reviews.yes_case: Film Room Sideline turns every practice call into game film. The spine of the product is one horizontal timeline strip that holds the whole call: persona and rep turns as coloured blocks, a playhead that follows audio time, and tagged moments (discovery, objection, pricing, close, filler, rapport) pinned to timestamps. The same strip runs through all three phases. On the live call, tags appear as they happen beside a 320px sideline HUD with six rubric meters that tween line by line, a checkpoint checklist, and one amber whisper at a time (20-second minimum gap) that the persona never hears. The debrief is timeline-first: grade ring and one-sentence verdict on top, a full-width film strip with green, amber and rose tags, and a moment inspector that opens the quote, timestamp and coach note. Every score links to a moment, and Replay this moment starts a retake with the same persona. Progress has four stat tiles with 30-day sparklines, a per-criterion trend chart, a Recurring misses list (for example, pricing transparency missed in 4 of 6 calls) and a filterable film table. The manager view adds a heatmap, an assign panel, pinned supervisor notes and consent labels. The library is a calm neutral catalogue: three-column cards with objection chips, difficulty dots, a detail sheet, a fork action, and built-in versus community badges. The five-step wizard extracts facts for review, validates each draft with one zod schema, strips PII from pasted calls, and exports a PR-ready file. It beats today's app because practice, live assist and post-call review become one object a rep can scrub, not three disconnected screens. The OpenAI story is concrete: a model strip with cost per call, plus Codex CLI reviewing persona-pack PRs in CI and drafting release notes, which are the exact qualifying uses in the Codex for Open Source program.
reviews.no_case: It keeps Sora and Inter and changes mostly surfaces, so on the library and progress screens a rep who knows today's app will see a recoloured version of it. The film metaphor (scrubbing waveforms, tag glyphs, a playhead) can feel like a video editor to a call-centre rep rather than a sales tool. The Tailwind 3 to 4 upgrade is scheduled for week one and touches every screen before anything visible ships. Text mode loses the audio strip's main value. The wizard fetches a URL only when the user asks, which is a weaker SSRF guard than a private-network block. The 150-persona pack is content work, and the D score depends on a latency harness that does not exist yet.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Console is a dark, command-first console built on shadcn/ui, cmdk and Radix, with Tailwind 3.4 kept so the change does not also carry a Tailwind migration. A 56px icon rail (Home, Library, Practice, Progress, Team) expands on hover and there are no header bars; each page has one title line. A centred Cmd-K bar holds every action: start a scenario, search personas, open the wizard, or copy a ready-made Codex prompt, with mono kbd chips on each row. The landing hero reads 'Practice the call. Get coached while you talk. Score every line.' beside a floating Cmd-K bar typed 'price objection, solar' with three results under it. The library shows counts (412 personas, 118 scenarios), a chip row for role, industry, difficulty meter and objection, Core and Community tabs, and a three-column grid of cards with monogram, two-line brief, difficulty meter, Run and a 5-second opening-line Preview. The AI wizard is a four-step sheet ('2 of 4') where AI-drafted fields carry a model-colour left border and a 'why' link to the source sentence, ending in a 60-second test call and Save or Export as PR. Pre-call is a 40-second readable brief with three objections and counters, a six-step talk track, a mic meter and quiet/normal/heavy intensity. The live call has three zones and no header: a flowing transcript with no bubbles, where whisper cues sit beside the exact caller line that triggered them; a 320px coach rail with a Next move line, a cue lane, an objection chip ('handled 1 of 3'), talk-track ticks and seven rubric bars marked est.; and a dock with push-to-talk and a coral End and grade. The debrief is two-pane, with evidence chips that jump and replay audio, and Drill your weakest is a single bar. Every AI output carries a provenance chip with model ID and cost, and Settings shows per-session spend. It beats today's app because the chat-app-with-a-drawer becomes a console and the coaching is finally visible on screen. The API contract is typed and the library schema is validated, so it is buildable by contributors.
reviews.no_case: Command-first is a developer-tool idea (Raycast, Arc) that may read wrong to a rep on a live call, whose main job is speaking, not typing commands. The dark-first brand switch is the kind of change an owner may reject, and the author's own D self-score of 5.6 is conditional on a coach event contract and latency that are not built. Keyboard-first design also makes the mobile and screen-reader paths thinner, which the proposal admits and then defers. The OpenAI showcase is weaker than it reads until the Realtime provider lands, and Codex appears only as copy-paste prompts and an AGENTS.md, with no CI or maintainer automation. The 400-persona target is a content job the design does not budget.

reviews.yes_case: Orb-First Coach Console is a conversation-first, voice-mode minimal product. The call screen is a dark stage with an audio-reactive orb (a shader driven by real input level) and a state label (Listening, Speaking, Your turn), the last four transcript turns below it, and a 360px light coach rail on the right. The rail holds three modules: a live rubric of five criteria with covered, partial or missed chips marked as live estimate; coach cue cards with the transcript quote and Accept or Dismiss; and a talk-track stepper. The persona voice never coaches. Coaching runs as a separate model call after each rep turn and returns typed cues within about two seconds, with a stated fallback to end-of-turn cues if latency fails. Coach intensity (Quiet, Cues, Full) controls volume, and Quiet still scores. The library has a 240px facet rail with counts, one semantic search box ('skeptical solar homeowner with an HOA'), portrait tiles, a pinned Create with AI card, filters that persist in the URL, and a persona detail drawer. Personas are Markdown files with front matter, so a contributor adds one by pull request without touching code. The wizard is two-pane and conversation-first: source chips, one clarifying question at a time, a live draft card with a rubric weight checksum to 100, a 60-second test call, and Save or Export as PR. The debrief is a grade hero with a per-turn timeline and criterion accordions that carry rewrite suggestions. Models appear as a status chip with cost in mono, and 'Built on OpenAI' is plain text with no logo, which handles trademark risk. The contribution path is the most concrete of the set: a Contribute page with draft-with-Codex links, persona lint in CI, and an AGENTS.md. It beats today's app because the call screen looks like a voice AI product and the coaching sits where the rep is looking.
reviews.no_case: A glowing voice orb on a dark stage is now the default look of every voice-AI vendor, and this proposal's lens is explicitly the ChatGPT Realtime aesthetic, so it reads as a borrowed look rather than a design of its own. A dark stage on the call and light everywhere else risks feeling like two products. The conversation-first wizard is slower than a structured form for a rep who already knows the persona they want. The 150-persona launch is ambitious, and the author's own plan ships about 40, which weakens the library claim. Semantic search adds an embedding dependency nobody has costed. The coaching latency target depends on a second model call per turn, and the risks section concedes that cues may arrive only at end of turn.

reviews.yes_case: Roster Arena is a hero-select front door for sales training. The persona library is a roster of 3:4 character cards with a stylised portrait, four stat bars (Brain for skepticism, Clock for time pressure, MessageSquare for talkativeness, ShieldAlert for objection load) drawn as 10-segment pips, a difficulty row from 1 to 5, and a voice preview button. A new-persona tile sits first in the grid. Clicking a card opens a 480px drawer with the brief, opening line, objections with triggers, rubric weights and a Practice button. The stat names are the rubric criteria, and the stats map to persona prompt parameters, so the game chrome is a readable vocabulary rather than decoration. Practice opens a pre-flight briefing with the buyer card, objection chips, talk track, a Voice or Text toggle and a Coach selector (Full, Quiet, Off). The live call is a three-column arena: waveform and timer on the left, a transcript with green and amber markers in the centre, and a coach rail on the right with five live rubric meters that flip to hit with a signal pulse, one whisper card at a time cited to its transcript line, and a next-best question. Certification mode hides the coach but records identical scores. The debrief is a match result with a score ring, five criterion stat lines with quotes, and three one-click drills. Progress adds unlock rules tied to real criteria (for example, 70 or higher on the skeptical CFO twice unlocks Hard), which gives a reason to return. The manager view has a team roster, a criteria heatmap, needs-attention cards, consent banners and an assignment queue. It beats today's dropdown and blurry orb because it makes difficulty, coaching and progress legible in one vocabulary, and it has the most memorable identity in the set. It also gives the F2 buyer a credible enterprise pitch with SCORM/LTI, SSO and certification mode.
reviews.no_case: Game framing reads as a toy to call-centre and enterprise buyers, and those are the paying market the F2 score assumes; the proposal flags this risk itself. Stylised illustrated busts need an asset pipeline and a budget nobody has priced, and they raise likeness questions. The migration is the largest in the set: Tailwind 4 and a Base UI shadcn move both land in phase 1 across every screen. The claim that Base UI became the shadcn default in July 2026 comes from a third-party write-up and is unconfirmed. Unlock rules and hero-select mechanics add gamification the brief did not ask for. The OpenAI showcase is conditional, with 'Built with Codex' shown only once Codex runs PR review, which it does not yet.

reviews.yes_case: Expressive Coaching Studio is a Material 3 Expressive system on MUI v7, where each persona's temperament (friendly, skeptical, hostile) generates a tonal palette from a seed using Google's Material Color Utilities. On the call screen the tint eases over about 600 ms as the persona's mood shifts, and a shader orb driven by agent audio sits in the centre. The desktop shell is an M3 navigation rail (Practice, Library, Progress, Team) with an avatar menu for settings and model configuration. The library is a responsive grid of temperament-tinted cards with objection chips, a playlist rail (for example, 'Solar door-knock, week 1'), URL-shareable filters, and an extended FAB that starts the wizard. The live call has a left column with interest and trust meters, a centre transcript with coach markers, and a right coach column where the newest cue springs in, with an objection alert, a next-best question, a talk-track stepper and seven provisional rubric meters badged until final grading. Coach level (Off, Subtle, Whisper) is set per session. If the coach fails, the call continues with a visible 'coaching paused' status, and a deterministic keyword checker keeps talk-track progress. The debrief is summary-first, with a live-versus-final sparkline that shows how provisional scores moved. The wizard turns any mix of job description, URL, CRM notes, ICP or pasted call into a persona, scenario, talk track and rubric, each traced to a source line, then saves locally or opens a GitHub PR with the YAML pack. The OpenAI model strip sits in the header with per-session cost, and a seeded demo team with a recorded sample call lets reviewers see coaching and scoring without keys. It beats today's app because it adds a manager surface and a debrief timeline, shows coaching during the call, and uses a design language maintainers already know from MUI.
reviews.no_case: M3 on MUI looks like a Material admin template. Most of the expressive layer (springs, morphing shapes, wavy score rings) is custom work the proposal admits is unverified, so the distinctive look can slide into noise. It is one of the most expensive rewrites in the set: XL effort, dropping Tailwind and lucide, and screen-by-screen parity across five phases. Temperament tints on the call screen spend design attention on mood colour that does not help a rep coach, and colour-coding personas by temperament invites stereotyping. The Codex PR-review workflow is planned, not shipped, so the OpenAI fund story is the weakest of the five. MUI X Data Grid, Recharts and three.js together add bundle weight that is only planned to be lazy-loaded.

reviews.yes_case: Geist Signal Console rebuilds the whole app as a calm monochrome console: Geist Sans and Geist Mono at 400/500/600, 1px hairline borders instead of soft shadows, black primary buttons, and a left shadcn Sidebar that collapses to an icon rail with a Cmd-K palette. Teal appears only when the AI coach has something to say. A 1px signal ring pulses only while a cue is live, so the rep's attention goes exactly where the coach has advice. The live call is three resizable panes: a call pane with a mono timer, mic meter, Mute, hold-to-talk and End and grade; a transcript with mono timestamps and inline markers such as 'Objection: price' or 'Discovery covered'; and a coach rail with a Next move card, a 'Why? line 6' evidence link, Accept or Dismiss, and live rubric meters that tick with a mono delta after each rep turn. The library is a faceted catalog covering the brief's exact filters (role, industry, difficulty, objection type), with about 200 persona-and-scenario pairs in 20 industry packs, and each persona opens in a Sheet with sliders, objections, rubric weights and Fork or View file on GitHub. The AI wizard streams a 'What I found' list with quote chips and include checkboxes before it drafts a single field, then runs a dry run and saves or exports a PR, and its zod schema doubles as the OpenAI Structured Outputs schema so wizard output is validated before the rep sees it. It beats today's app because the current app is a template with a three-item dropdown and a chat-style call, while this makes every surface a working tool. Every AI output carries a provenance chip with model and latency, the dashboard shows cost per session, and model roles are named in the product, which is exactly the legibility a Codex open source reviewer wants. The contributor path is obvious (a persona is a JSON file, the wizard writes the PR, and CONTRIBUTING gets a Built with Codex credit), and it ships in phases behind routes so the live demo keeps working.
reviews.no_case: It reads as a Vercel dashboard with a teal dot. The proposal itself warns that monochrome feels cold and invites a clone, and the teal signal is the only thing that makes it feel ours, so on the unique-design bar it is the least memorable of the three advancing options. A dev-tool console is an odd fit for a sales rep practising a phone call, and some reps will feel they are in an IDE rather than a coaching room. Its coaching depends on a 2 second p50 cue budget that roughly doubles per-turn API cost, with only a per-session cap as the answer. The 200 reviewed personas are a human-content bottleneck the proposal names but does not solve. The Geist licence is still unverified by the proposal's own account, and keeping Tailwind 3 in phase 1 leaves a second styling migration ahead.

reviews.yes_case: Strain and Form Console turns practice into a readiness story instead of a score list. Every call gets a Strain value from 0 to 21, computed from turns, objections faced and persona difficulty. Form, shown as fitness minus fatigue on a 7-day against 42-day ring, tells the rep whether they are sharp enough for a hard persona. Each persona card and the pre-call briefing carry a Strain forecast ('14 of 21, Hard'), the rep's Form for that persona, and the personal record to beat, so the load is known before dialing. The look is light by default, with a dark night canvas for the live call: 16px radius cards with 1px hairlines and no shadow at rest, 10px round-capped rings, and gold reserved for one pulse on a new personal record. The live call has a whisper cue rail that shows one typed cue at a time (Ask, Objection, Pace, Step, Close), a next-best-question chip, a six-step talk track, and rubric rings drawn dashed while provisional. An elevation timeline of the live score shows exactly where a call dipped, with coach markers. The persona wizard redacts phone numbers, emails and names before any model call, streams a live persona card, runs a 30-second test call and exports a PR-ready file. It beats today's app because the current app has no in-call feedback and four stat tiles, while this gives reps and managers a shared vocabulary for readiness. Model use is legible through an Under the hood panel on every debrief showing model, prompt version, tokens and cost, which fits the OpenAI fund's transparency story. Private PRs by default and an OpenAI Realtime voice option behind the same VoiceProvider as ElevenLabs show care for both the rep and OpenAI's voice products.
reviews.no_case: The fitness vocabulary (Strain, Form, PRs) risks reading as gamified to enterprise buyers, the same objection that weakens the Duolingo-style option, and the Strain number is a load model whose formula is only sketched. Form needs a fatigue model that the proposal never defines, so the number can look precise without being evidence-backed, which cuts against the product's own evidence-first grading. The Whoop and Strava patterns were not fetched, so the design rests on general knowledge, as the proposal admits. The cue target is 2.5 seconds p95, yet the proposal's own self-score drops to 4 if cues routinely arrive after 4 seconds, so the coaching baseline is conditional. Seeding 240 personas across 15 job families before launch is a large content commitment, and the proposal's own floor of fewer than 100 shipping personas drops the score to 4.

reviews.yes_case: Spatial Glass Call Window is the most visually arresting option in the set. It uses a canvas-ink dark stage with slow mesh light blobs, and the live call is a floating 960px window with a 28px radius and a persona orb at its centre that breathes at idle and displaces with mic or persona audio. Left and right ornaments hold the talk-track rail, where the current stop glows, and the coach HUD, with rubric meters that stay dotted until settled, a next-best-question card and an amber objection chip. The orb's rim turns amber when an objection lands and teal when the rep hits a rubric line, and tapping a quote chip in the debrief scrubs the replay to that exact second. The persona runs on OpenAI gpt-realtime, with ElevenLabs behind a flag, and the coach is a separate channel, so the persona never hears coaching and the realism claim can be tested. The library is about 300 JSON persona packs with facets for job, industry, seniority, difficulty, objection, channel and language, each validated in CI. The wizard fetches URLs and attaches a citation to every field, and reps accept or edit each one. It beats today's app because it says 'cutting-edge AI voice coaching' the moment the page opens, while the light paper-glass debrief and dashboard keep reading and printing practical. The fallbacks for reduced transparency and contrast show accessibility was considered, and the OpenAI Realtime centre of gravity is the strongest voice showcase for the fund.
reviews.no_case: Glass over transcripts is a readability problem: a 40px backdrop blur at 180 percent saturation on text-heavy panes hurts contrast and reading speed on long calls, and the 80 percent fill is a patch rather than a design. The coach timing contradicts itself: the coach reads a rolling window every 5 to 8 seconds, but the target is a cue within 2.5 seconds of the rep finishing a sentence, which a polling cadence cannot hit. The GPU cost of a blurred glass stack plus a transmission-material orb is high on the older laptops and phones many reps use, and the proposal's own fallback is a flat 2D gradient. The gpt-realtime voice path is a new adapter build, and the self-scored coaching D of 5.4 says the live channel is conditional. Roughly 300 packs at launch is aggressive for a content library that still needs human review, and the visionOS look is a trend that will date faster than the plainer options.

reviews.yes_case: Night Desk Cockpit is a dark, keyboard-first trading-desk layout built for power users and managers. It has a 56px icon rail that expands on hover, a Ctrl+K palette across personas, scenarios and past calls, and shortcuts (J/K, Enter, M, C, E, ?) that make a live call fast to run and to score. The live call has three resizable panes: a call clock and talk-track stages that tick live, a speaker-lane transcript with a cue dock holding up to two amber cues with Apply and Dismiss, and a right rubric tape with five criteria bars that move every turn and evidence pins that jump to transcript lines. The debrief has a call timeline with rubric total as a line and cue and objection markers that jump the transcript, plus a cue adoption log showing whether each cue was given, used or ignored and what score change followed, which is a genuinely useful test of whether coaching helps. The team view pins the top five and bottom five reps above the roster, with a coaching queue, a suggested drill per rep and saved Rep and Manager layouts. The persona library has 150 personas across 20 jobs with objection-tagged cards, and the wizard runs five steps one question at a time with Auto-answer, streams a live persona card, and exports a pack. It beats today's app by adding the in-call coaching, live scoring and manager surface the brief names, in a serious, dense layout that reads as professional tooling. The models-in-use footer names each OpenAI model with live latency, an honest showcase for the fund.
reviews.no_case: Bloomberg density is the wrong default for a rep practising a phone call. A first-time trainee faces three panes, five meters and a keyboard map before the first line, and the proposal admits density can overwhelm them. Dark and dense reads as a trading terminal, which is not the modern, cutting-edge look the brief asks for, and it is the least distinctive of the cockpit-style options. The coaching baseline is self-scored at 6.5 only if cues land under 1.5 seconds, a tighter budget than most of the field can promise. At 150 personas it is tied for the smallest library in the set, so the library reads as less large than the brief asks. The keyboard-first logic is strongest on desktop, and a rep on a phone gets a cut-down version of the cockpit.

reviews.yes_case: Game Tape Skill Path turns the whole app into a season. The Path home screen shows a skill tree of six branches (Opening, Discovery, Objections, Pricing, Closing, Booking) with five-level nodes that are grey when locked, green when mastered and carry a plus mark when open for contribution. A day streak with a seven-day dot strip, XP chips, and a streak flame that lights after three rubric hits in a row give reps a reason to come back tomorrow. The live call sits on a dark game-tape stage with a sports-broadcast feel rather than a cartoon mascot: a reactive orb, transcript criterion chips on credited turns, a violet now-cue card, a six-step talk-track path with checkmarks, and five live rubric meters with +delta flashes. Debriefs animate a grade ring, XP and a skill node moving from level 2 to 3, and a moment timeline jumps to each score's transcript line. Leagues are opt-in and team-scoped, and XP is withheld when a keyword heuristic grades the call, which fixes a real trust problem in today's debrief. The library is built as a curriculum, with at least 10 personas per job across 15 jobs, each carrying objection tags, difficulty and a talk track, and a Build with AI tile first in the grid. It beats today's app because progress gets a visible path that four stat tiles cannot give, and it is the only option in the set that explains why a rep should return tomorrow. For the fund, each OpenAI model has a named job in a Model lab panel with latency and token cost per call.
reviews.no_case: The gamification layer is the main risk. Streaks, XP and leagues read as a consumer language app to enterprise buyers, call-centre managers and grant reviewers, and the proposal's own mitigations only partly fix that. Reward mechanics can reward volume over quality, and leagues create comparison anxiety even when opt-in. Coaching is the weakest of the five against the brief's baseline: self-scored 5.2, meeting the bar only if cue latency stays under 2 seconds and throttling ships. Ten personas per job across 15 jobs is thin for a large, browsable library, and at 150 it is tied for the smallest in the set. A Duolingo-style skill tree is already a common pattern, so the distinctiveness is less of an edge than it looks. The skill tree, streaks, leagues and XP settlement add a whole product layer to build and test before the coaching rail, which is the part that carries the grant demo, and that is the wrong order for a fund application.

reviews.yes_case: Live Ledger makes the whole app one document-and-cockpit system. Library pages are Notion-style sections (Cold calls, Renewals and so on, each with a View all count). Every persona opens as a document with a properties header (persona, goal, difficulty, industry) and editable blocks for objections, rubric rows and scripted replies, edited with a slash menu. Library and debrief sit on a warm paper canvas (#F7F6F2) with white cards, indigo primary, Geist for interface text and Newsreader serif for evidence quotes, so it reads like an editorial workspace rather than a default Tailwind page. The live call is always dark: a 240px talk-track checklist with done, active and next states and a talk-ratio meter; the transcript as speaker turn rows with timecodes; a small orb that only shows listening or speaking; and a 320px rail with one whisper cue at a time (with a Why link to the rubric line it serves), a rose objection banner, and five rubric meters labelled live estimate that flash a teal delta chip when evidence lands. A separate coach model (gpt-4.1-mini, structured outputs) reads each finished turn, so the persona never coaches, and cues are rate-limited to one per 20 seconds. The debrief leads with a 0-100 score ring, a source badge ('Graded by gpt-4.1-mini', or an amber 'Estimate only, grader unavailable' when the fallback runs), a radar with the previous attempt overlaid, and expandable criteria whose quotes have a Replay moment that scrolls the transcript to the turn and shows the cue that should have fired. Against today's app it adds the live coaching and scoring that do not exist, a library where every persona is a reviewable file in the repo (and in Postgres when accounts are on), and a five-input wizard that streams a schema-validated draft with PII redaction on by default. For the OpenAI fund the contributor loop is concrete: a Good first persona board, bylines on persona docs, an Open PR button on each persona, Codex-assisted PR review of persona files and release checklists, and a model passport in Settings with cost per call. Mobile uses bottom tabs, a sticky composer and a bottom sheet for talk track and live rubric, with no horizontal scroll.
reviews.no_case: Scope is the main trap. A TipTap block editor with eight custom block types, slash menus, document properties and block-by-block streaming of generated content is weeks of work before a rep can run a call, and the proposal's own 'several months for one developer' is optimistic for the editor, wizard and cockpit together. The document metaphor is also a poor fit for a rep who only wants to practise: the editing surface serves managers and contributors, while the rep-facing screens carry more structure than they need. The split theme (warm light library and debrief, always-dark cockpit) doubles contrast and QA work, and the proposal itself lists the cockpit's WCAG and small-type pass as an open risk. Persona-as-document makes files harder to keep schema-valid for CI than plain YAML or Markdown, and the rich-text round trip to zod is not described. The 2-second cue target is unproven, and a six-step checklist, rubric meters, radar and replay together crowd a 390px screen. Self-rated F1 6 and F2 6 leave no clear licensing wedge; the proposal does not say why a call centre would buy this over an existing vendor.

reviews.yes_case: Call Canvas is the most distinctive of the five. Personas, talk-track steps and rubrics live as nodes on a 24px dot-grid infinite canvas (React Flow, lazy-loaded), on a dark #0B0D10 base with surface steps, hairline borders, Geist and Geist Mono, and a full light mode. The AI wizard is a wired graph: five source cards (job description, product URL, CRM note, pasted transcript, ICP form) connect with wires that draw in as each source attaches to a Persona Synth node, which emits Persona, Scenario and Rubric output cards. The inspector gives each field an Auto-generate or Edit manually toggle and a provenance list naming the sentence that produced it; output is schema-validated JSON, and manual edits survive regenerate. Browsing uses a 240px facet rail (role, industry, difficulty pips, objection type, mode) over a three-column card grid, with a board toggle where picked personas become nodes sequenced from warm-up to hard close. The live call is deliberately fixed, not canvas: a three-column cockpit with six talk-track step nodes (the current one pulses), a transcript with timecodes, and a right rail with a violet whisper card (cue colour kept off signal green so advice never reads as status), an amber objection alert with an acknowledge-then-anchor line, and six live rubric bars with delta chips and evidence pins, plus a pace gauge and coach-level toggle. The debrief has a score dial with a percentile against the last five calls, a replay timeline with cue markers showing whether the rep followed each cue, and evidence cards whose quotes scrub the replay. Mobile collapses to a violet cue pill, a rubric chip strip and a 56px hold-to-talk mic. Against today's app it adds the library, a creation path, live coaching and a reviewable replay where none exist. For the OpenAI fund it names Realtime for voice, gpt-4.1-mini for cues and grading and structured-output synthesis for the wizard, with cost chips on each AI surface; contributors get an Add a persona pack path, a CONTRIBUTING guide, AGENTS.md, and Codex-assisted PR review of pack files. It also says plainly that the $25K credit figure was not verified.
reviews.no_case: A canvas is a risky centre for a sales-rep product. The proposal itself concedes it can read as a diagram tool, and most reps who want to rehearse a call will not want to wire nodes before they start. A node-graph wizard is harder to build and test than a stepper and needs keyboard wiring, screen-reader labels and a touch fallback to meet the same accessibility bar as the rest of the app. React Flow, motion, Recharts and vaul add weight, and the bundle cost is a to-do in the risk list rather than a measured result. The dark cockpit and light library are effectively two visual systems, which the coherent-in-both-modes claim does not fully answer. Scores D 6.5 and E 6.5 depend on a latency target nobody has measured and on 40 reviewed packs that must ship before the 140 claim, so the content bill is large and the proposal admits it. A JSON pack format plus a node-graph builder raises the contributor barrier compared with one file per persona, which cuts against the open-source pitch. Self-rated F1 6 says the market is crowded, and the answer offered is open source rather than a clear feature gap.

reviews.yes_case: Shelf and Coach Studio is the library-first answer. The top bar holds Library, Practice, Progress, Team, a Contribute link and a search field with a Cmd-K hint. The library is a page of horizontal scroll-snap shelves of 1:1 cover cards at 192px, opening with Daily Mix: your weakest criterion and then Home services, Insurance, Mortgage, Solar, Auto, Medical devices, B2B procurement and Collections. Each card shows name, role, difficulty dots and objection tags; tapping opens a side sheet with the opening line and a Start button, and a queued bar holds the chosen scenario. Facets (role, industry, difficulty, objection, length) and a grid or list toggle handle dense filtering. Daily Mix makes the library adaptive, blending personas that target the user's weakest rubric line, which ties the catalogue to coaching in a way the other four do not. The palette is tokenised on :root (canvas #0B0E13, surface #141A22, signal green, cue amber, alert coral, persona violet) with a full light mode, 14px cards, 1px lines instead of shadows, and Geist Mono for scores and timers. The live call uses a Voicenotes-style coach rail rather than a music-player layout: a canvas waveform driven by real audio levels in place of the blurry orb, a transcript where the current line is highlighted, amber whisper cards that slide up over 200ms and fade after 12 seconds, coral objection alerts with an optional strong-reply line that stays locked until debrief, and top-strip rubric meters with live deltas. The debrief uses evidence cards with a replay-at-timestamp button. Mobile is a 390px stack with a swipe-up coach sheet, a centred 56px mic and a mini-player that persists across routes. For the OpenAI fund it shows 'Voice: OpenAI Realtime' in the footer, a model inspector with tokens and cost per call, cover art made with an OpenAI image model at build time, a /contribute good-first-persona board, a published YAML schema, and CI that validates persona files and rubric weights.
reviews.no_case: Spotify is the wrong mental model for a serious sales tool. Shelves and cover art make each persona look like a playlist item, which invites casual browsing rather than deliberate choice, and borrowing music-player patterns (queued bar, mini-player, lyrics-style transcript) risks reading as a music app. Producing 120 distinct cover images is a real cost and licensing question, and the fallback of deterministic gradients would make most covers look alike. The Tailwind 3 to 4 migration touches every screen and the custom classes in globals.css, and the proposal's own phase 1 requires screenshot regression tests before merge, a large cost before any new feature ships. The HeroUI licence is unresolved (MIT in the docs, Apache-2.0 in another index), and a component layer is more lock-in for contributors than the copy-in model that open-source contributors often prefer. The coaching score is self-rated 6, and its 1.5-second latency target is explicitly 'to be measured, not promised'. The Spotify Mobbin screen was not found, so the references lean on SoundCloud and Meetup, which is thinner evidence. F1 6 and F2 6 suggest nothing commercial beyond the open core.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Console is a command-first console: the Cmd-K bar drives every action, a 56px icon rail replaces header bars, and each page has one title line. The dark default uses surface steps and hairlines with Inter for UI and JetBrains Mono for timers, scores and model IDs, and light values are defined on the same tokens. The live call reads as one conversation: caller lines in ink, rep lines in signal teal, no chat bubbles, and each cue marked at the line that caused it. A 320px coach rail carries a Next move line, a cue lane of the last two whispers, an objection chip (handled 1 of 3), six talk-track ticks and seven rubric bars labelled est. Space talks, Cmd-period hides the rail, and Cmd-Shift-E ends. Its event contract is the strongest engineering of the five: the coach streams typed events (cue, next_question, objection, step_progress, criterion_estimate) that carry transcript line ids, and the debrief reuses the same ids, so a live cue and the final verdict point to the same quote. A visible latency gauge, a throttle and an off switch address whisper fatigue. Provenance chips show model ID and cost on every AI output. It keeps Tailwind 3.4 and shadcn, so contributors meet no Tailwind migration in the same change. The result looks like a developer tool, which suits the open-source audience. For the fund it makes the OpenAI Realtime provider first-class, adds a Contribute a persona command that runs the wizard and writes a validated file, ships AGENTS.md so Codex CLI can add personas, and lets the Cmd-K bar copy ready-made Codex prompts. The wizard redacts PII before model calls and blocks fetches to private-network URLs, a real safety point for a public tool.
reviews.no_case: A keyboard-first launcher is a poor centre for a rep who must be coached mid-call. Every action living in Cmd-K means hidden features for many users, and the proposal concedes that mobile and screen-reader users need visible buttons, so in practice it is two designs. Its self-rated coaching and library scores are the lowest here (D 5.6, E 5.3), and the proposal says the design alone does not clear baseline. The library depends on about 400 personas, a content problem with no path to that volume stated. The Raycast and Arc pattern is well worn, so the console could pass for any dev tool and distinctiveness is limited. Keeping Tailwind 3.4 means the new look rests on the old toolchain, and the migration is still owed later. The dark-first brand change is one the owner may reject, and the light fallback is defined but not designed. The default demo does not run on OpenAI end to end until the Realtime provider lands, which the proposal admits weakens the showcase claim.

reviews.yes_case: Orb-First Coach Console is calm and conversation-first. The top 40 percent of the live call is a dark voice stage (#0B0C0E) with an audio-reactive orb (canvas or shader driven by real mic and speaker levels) that replaces the blurry gradient, a state label (Listening, Speaking, Your turn), and the last four transcript turns with the newest emphasised. A 360px light coach rail holds a live rubric (covered, partial or missed chips labelled live estimate), cue cards with a transcript quote and Accept or Dismiss, and a talk-track stepper. On phones the stage, a row of five criterion dots, a cue card rising above the dock, and a press-and-hold End keep the call first, with no horizontal scroll. The library has a 240px facet rail with counts, one semantic search box (for example skeptical solar homeowner with an HOA), a card grid with portrait tiles, difficulty meter, objection chips and the user's best score, a pinned Create with AI card, and filters that persist in the URL. Each persona is one Markdown file with front matter, so a contributor adds one by pull request and the library renders it with no code change. The wizard is chat-first: one clarifying question at a time, a streaming draft card, a 60-second test call and a PR-ready export. Model chips appear on voice, coach, grader and wizard surfaces with per-call cost in mono, and Built on OpenAI is plain text with no logo, a careful trademark choice. For the fund it puts OpenAI Realtime voice at the centre of the screen, the clearest showcase of the five, and runs Codex persona lint and rubric-weight checks in CI alongside AGENTS.md.
reviews.no_case: The look is ChatGPT's voice mode with the logo removed, and the proposal's own references (ElevenLabs, Grok, Hume) are single-pane chat. Users and jurors are likely to see a clone rather than a distinct product, and an OpenAI-native look invites direct comparison with the vendor's own UI, a weak position for a community project. Orb plus chat is the default AI-voice template the brief criticises; swapping the blurry orb for a driven one keeps the same metaphor. Portrait tiles for 150 personas carry the same generation cost and licensing questions as cover art, and generated portraits of invented people look like real people. The chat-first wizard asks one question at a time, which is slower than a visible form or graph for a rep who already has a job description, and a streamed chat draft is harder to inspect than a structured form. The coach is still a separate call with a 2-second target, and the proposal's own fallback to end-of-turn cues concedes that latency may fail. Its self-rated A 8, B 8 and C 8 are the most generous of the five, and C 8 is not supported for a voice-chat look. Light is the default for the library and dark for calls, so the library's dark mode is not really designed.

reviews.yes_case: Night Desk Cockpit turns the working app into a dark, keyboard-first trading-desk workspace. Every screen after the landing page runs on one token set with Geist for text and Geist Mono with tabular numerals for scores, timers and timestamps, so the product reads like an instrument panel rather than a generic SaaS template. The landing page and README hero stay light and readable, with a product frame, a persona preview row, a models strip, a 'Powered by OpenAI models' line and a good-first-issue board fed by GitHub labels. The live call is the core. The left pane holds the call clock, talk-track stages that tick as the call moves, and a persona state meter (patience 0-10) driven by the grader. The centre is a speaker-lane transcript with timestamps. Above the composer sits a cue dock that holds at most two amber cues, such as 'Ask about timing before pricing' or an objection alert, each with Apply and Dismiss. The right pane is a rubric tape: five criteria bars that move every turn with plus and minus deltas, and evidence pins that jump to the exact transcript line that moved them. Cues never enter the persona's session, so the realism survives. Every cue is logged with whether the rep used it and what the score did next, which feeds the debrief. An Unassisted mode switch hides cues but keeps scoring, which gives managers a clean certification run. Today's app is a chat window that says nothing until the call ends. This version coaches while the rep is still talking, and it also has a real manager surface: a team roster with the top five and bottom five reps pinned, a coaching queue with one-click assign, and supervisor notes. The persona library is a 240px filter rail with counts for job, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel and source (Built-in, Mine, Community), saved presets, and a virtualized card grid. Opening a persona shows a 380px inspector with brief, talk track, rubric weights and a Practice button. Personas are JSON or YAML files validated by zod in CI, so a contributor can open a pull request for one persona and see it appear in the library. The wizard asks one question at a time and accepts a job description, product URL, CRM notes, an ICP or a pasted call. It streams a schema-valid persona into a live card, runs a 60-second dry-run call before save, and exports the file for a pull request. The footer on each call names each OpenAI model in use with its live latency, and AGENTS.md plus a one-click Codex prompt for adding a persona make the maintainer workflow visible for the Codex fund review.
reviews.no_case: Bloomberg density is a real risk. A first-time rep faces rails, a rubric tape, a persona meter, a cue dock and tabular numbers before they have said a word, and the Simple view and first-run tour are promised as mitigations without being designed. The stack adds shadcn, react-resizable-panels, cmdk, TanStack Table and Virtual, Recharts, Motion and zod all at once, and Tailwind 3 support for the component layer is unverified. The library score is only 5.5 and falls to 3.5 at today's three personas, so the claim depends on 150 seeded personas that do not exist yet. The coaching score is conditional on cues landing under about 1.5 seconds, which the author admits may not happen. The landing page is light while the product is dark, so the first impression and the product look like two different designs.

reviews.yes_case: Live Ledger treats each persona, scenario, talk track and rubric as an editable document, then wraps those documents in a dark live cockpit that coaches while the rep speaks. Most screens sit on warm paper (#F7F6F2) with white cards and thin hairlines. Geist handles interface text, Geist Mono handles timers and scores, and Newsreader serif sets doc titles and quoted evidence, so a debrief reads like a case file rather than a dashboard. The live call is the one exception: an always-dark, three-column cockpit. The left rail is a talk-track checklist with done, active and next states, plus a talk-ratio meter. The centre is turn-based transcript rows rather than chat bubbles, with a small orb showing whether the persona is listening or speaking, and grey coach notes on rep turns such as 'asked 2 of 4 diagnostic questions'. The right rail shows one whisper cue at a time, a rose objection banner when a trigger fires, and five rubric meters labelled 'live estimate' that flash a teal delta when evidence lands. Each cue names the rubric line it serves and has a Why link. Fallback scores are labelled as amber estimates, which fixes today's problem of a keyword fallback displaying as a red F. The debrief opens with a score ring, a goal-status chip and a source badge reading 'Graded by gpt-4.1-mini', plus a radar that overlays the previous attempt. Each criterion expands to evidence quotes with a Replay moment button that scrubs the transcript. The library is a set of sections such as 'Cold calls 24' with View all, a filter rail for job family, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode, and cards with initials discs (never stock faces), difficulty dots, objection chips and a use count. Opening a persona shows a document with a properties header and editable blocks, and a slash menu inserts an objection, a rubric row or a scripted reply. The wizard has a left stepper and five input tiles for job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP and pasted call. A live document fills block by block as the model streams, rubric weights must total 100 before save, PII redaction is on by default for pasted transcripts, and a two-minute test call follows. Each persona is a reviewable file in the repo, so a contributor opens a pull request on a persona doc. A Model passport in Settings lists which OpenAI model runs voice, coach, grader and wizard, with cost per call. That shows OpenAI where it does real work without a logo that implies endorsement.
reviews.no_case: The block editor is an open scope sink. TipTap with slash menus, properties headers and per-block editing can absorb weeks, and the proposal itself says it has to be capped at eight block types. Casual reps may find a persona library that behaves like a document system heavier than a picker, since opening a persona to reach Use in call is one step more than a card click. The visual identity is split between warm paper for most screens and a dark cockpit for calls, and light paper is less cutting edge than a dark-first look. Newsreader adds a third typeface beside Geist and Geist Mono. The proposal gives no self-scores for A through E, only F1, F2 and F3, so the design-category numbers here are the juror's own. Realtime voice cost falls on each user's own key, which the proposal flags but does not resolve.

reviews.yes_case: Shelf and Coach Studio makes the persona library feel like a place to browse, not a dropdown to pick from. It is dark by default on a near-black canvas with tonal surfaces, 14px cards, 1px hairlines and 12px cover-art tiles, all set in Geist with Geist Mono for numerals. The library opens with a Daily Mix shelf built from the rep's weakest rubric criterion, then horizontal scroll-snap shelves for Home services, Insurance, Mortgage, Solar, Auto, Medical devices, B2B procurement and Collections. Each cover card shows name, role, difficulty dots and objection tags, and tapping one opens a side sheet with the opening line and a Start button. Facet chips above the shelves (role, industry, difficulty, objection, length) filter them live, and a grid or list toggle serves dense filtering. A queued bar holds the chosen scenario. For reps, that discovery matters: a shelf can reveal a job they have never practised, and Daily Mix points them at the criterion they keep missing. The pre-call page has a large persona cover, a numbered talk-track checklist with a progress bar, five rubric weight bars labelled 'What you are scored on', and a Quiet, Balanced or Intense coach setting. The live call swaps the blurry orb for a waveform driven by real audio levels, shows a lyrics-style transcript where the current line is highlighted, and runs a coach rail. Amber whisper cards offer the next best question or talk-track step. Coral objection alerts can carry an optional strong-reply line, but that line stays locked until the debrief so practice still builds the skill. A top strip shows talk-track progress (step 3 of 6) and five live rubric meters with delta arrows. The debrief uses a grade ring, a goal chip, a one-sentence why-this-score, and criterion rows that expand to evidence quote cards with 'replay at 0:42' buttons beside a sticky transcript. The wizard has four steps with a counter, a streaming draft card whose fields cite the input line they came from, a rubric with five weighted rows that must sum to 100, a 60-second test call, and Save or Export YAML. The manager view turns a persona set into a team playlist with due dates. OpenAI is visible on the call footer (Voice: OpenAI Realtime), in a model inspector with tokens and cost per call, and in cover art generated at build time. CI validates persona files and rubric weights, and a good-first-persona board invites contributors.
reviews.no_case: The Spotify metaphor may make a serious sales-coaching product feel like entertainment, and the Mobbin research had no Spotify screen, so SoundCloud and Meetup stand in for the lens. Shelves are slower than a dense filter table for a power user comparing dozens of personas. Per-persona cover art from an image model adds build cost and licensing questions, and the proposal does not say what the art depicts, which invites stereotyped imagery of people by industry. The HeroUI license is reported as MIT in official docs and Apache-2.0 in another index, and it is unresolved. The Tailwind 3 to 4 migration touches every screen and the custom classes in globals.css. The coaching score rises above baseline only after cue latency is measured, and the lyrics transcript may distract during a live call.

reviews.yes_case: Call Canvas makes personas, scenarios and rubrics nodes on an infinite dot-grid canvas, and makes the AI wizard a wired graph. Source nodes (job description, product URL, CRM note, pasted transcript, ICP form) connect into a Persona Synth node that emits three output cards: Persona, Scenario and Rubric. Wires draw in as each source connects. Each generated field shows the source sentence it came from, can be auto-generated or edited by hand, and keeps manual edits through regenerate, so a reviewer can trace every line back to the input. The default library view is a three-column grid of cards with monograms, role, industry, objection chips and minutes, and a board toggle lets a rep wire picked personas into a sequence from warm-up to hard close. The live call is a dark cockpit. Six talk-track step nodes sit at the left, and the current step pulses and shows the next question. The centre has a persona header with a voice orb, a timecoded transcript and a hold-to-talk composer. The right rail has six live rubric bars with delta chips and evidence pins, violet whisper cues that hold the next question, and amber objection alerts with an acknowledge-then-anchor line. Each cue has Why and helpful or not buttons that feed prompt tuning. The debrief has a 0-100 dial with a percentile against the last five calls and a replay timeline that marks where cues fired and whether the rep followed them, which directly answers whether live coaching worked. Light and dark are both full modes. The OpenAI engine appears as a plain text chip (Realtime, gpt-4.1-mini), never a logo, which avoids any endorsement claim. It is the most distinctive proposal in this set and a clear break from the template look.
reviews.no_case: The canvas is the wrong default for most reps and many managers. The proposal admits it can read as a diagram tool, and the grid is the default library view, so the headline metaphor is secondary in practice. React Flow adds bundle weight and a graph model that contributors must learn just to add a persona pack. The wizard is a node graph, not the guided, one-question-at-a-time flow the brief describes, which makes first-time persona creation harder. Mobile is covered, but a wired canvas does not work sensibly on a phone. Only 40 of about 140 packs are reviewed, so the 140 claim is not yet earned. The phase estimates are optimistic for an XL build, the cue latency target is unproven, and the coaching score (6.5) falls back to post-call coaching if latency fails.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Console is a disciplined, keyboard-first shell. A 56px icon rail replaces header bars, each page has one title line, and a centred Cmd-K bar holds every action: start a scenario, search personas, build or contribute a persona, or copy a Codex prompt. Chords (G then L, G then P) move between sections. The palette is calm and dark-first, with teal signal, amber cues and coral risk, Inter for UI and JetBrains Mono for timers, scores and model IDs. The landing page leads with a floating command bar typed 'price objection, solar', which shows the product's core idea within seconds. The live call is a three-zone console. The transcript reads as one flowing conversation, with caller lines in ink and rep lines in teal, and each cue is marked at the line that caused it. A coach rail on the right has a 'Next move' line, the last two amber whispers, an objection chip ('handled 1 of 3'), six talk-track ticks and seven live rubric bars labelled 'est.'. Space talks, Cmd-. hides the rail, and Cmd-Shift-E ends. The debrief is a two-pane review with evidence chips that jump the transcript and replay audio, plus a 'Drill your weakest' bar. Phase 0 keeps Tailwind 3.4 and maps the existing .card and .btn-primary classes onto new tokens, so the team can ship in increments without a stack migration. It is the cheapest and lowest-risk path for an owner who wants a clear improvement without a full brand overhaul.
reviews.no_case: It is a command palette wrapped around a mostly conventional interface, and the brief asks for a total UI change, not a shell change. Inter, rounded cards and the same token shapes map onto the existing classes in Phase 0, so much of the app looks the same until late phases. Keyboard-first hides features from mobile and screen-reader users, which the proposal admits and leaves open. These are the weakest self-scores in the set: D 5.6 and E 5.3 sit barely above baseline, and the author concedes that without the event contract the console is a prettier chat. The persona library is a card grid with Run and Preview buttons, not a multi-facet browse, and the wizard is a form with a chat toggle. Dark-first is a brand change the owner may reject, and the OpenAI showcase is weaker until the Realtime provider ships.

reviews.yes_case: Spatial Glass Call Window is a whole-app redesign on a visionOS-style glass system. The live stage is dark (#070B14) with a frosted call window floating on it, a glass persona orb at its center, and a coach HUD held in space around the orb. Navigation becomes a floating glass dock that collapses to one red End control during a call. Inside the call, the talk-track rail sits on the left, the transcript runs as glass bubbles below the orb, and the coach HUD on the right shows rubric meters that stay dotted until they cite a transcript turn. Cues slide in from the window edge, fade after eight seconds, and are budgeted to one per 20 seconds. The orb's rim flashes amber on an objection and teal on a rubric hit. The debrief switches to a light paper-glass theme with a replay ribbon: tap a quote and the transcript scrubs to that second, and a drift readout shows how provisional live scores settled into the final grade. The library is a three-column facet catalogue with a Cmd+K palette, a virtualized grid of about 300 persona packs, and a glass preview sheet. The wizard turns one paste into a streaming draft where each field carries a citation chip that highlights its source sentence in a split view, with Accept and Edit per field. Against today's app (a three-item select, a chat-bubble call with no coaching, a long debrief scroll and four stat tiles), this is a practice product a rep can see and use: it coaches while the call happens, scores with evidence, and builds personas from real source material. For the Codex fund it puts OpenAI on screen: a models ribbon with latency, tokens and cost per call, and an Open prompts drawer that links to the real prompt, rubric JSON and schema in the repo. That is the cost transparency a credit reviewer looks for.
reviews.no_case: The headline feature is still a promise. Live coaching is self-scored 5.4 and conditional on a coach channel that does not exist yet, and cue latency is unmeasured. The glass system also carries real costs: backdrop blur plus a transmission-material orb is heavy on older laptops and phones, and translucent panels over live transcripts hurt contrast and reading speed unless the 80 percent fills hold. Glass is the trend most likely to date fast, and the dark-first stage may read as a gimmick to buyers who print debriefs. The library commits to about 300 reviewed packs at launch, a content effort the proposal admits Codex PR review does not cover. At XL effort with four migration phases and a Radix plus glass token rewrite that touches every screen, it is among the costliest options here.

reviews.yes_case: Strain and Form Console turns the whole product into a performance readout for the rep. Call Strain (0 to 21) rates how hard a call was from turns, objections and persona difficulty. Form (fitness minus fatigue) shows whether the rep is sharp for a hard persona, and personal records mark bests per persona. Visually it uses Geist and Geist Mono with 10px rings and 16px cards on a light canvas for practice, library, debrief, progress and team, and a night canvas for the live call, briefing and landing hero. Practice is a Today page: your Form ring, one recommended persona with its target strain, and your latest PR. Library cards show expected strain before a rep starts, with a Form ring for their recent score, across a 240-persona catalogue in 15 job families with facets for role, industry, strain, objection, channel and voice or text. The live call has a strain ring, a talk-ratio bar with a shaded target band, an elevation timeline of the live score with coach markers, and a right rail with one whisper cue at a time (Ask, Objection, Pace, Step, Close) plus rubric rings drawn dashed while provisional. The wizard has four entry points, redacts phone numbers, emails and names before any model call, streams a schema-valid persona, runs a 30-second test call, and exports a PR-ready file. The debrief links every quote to its transcript line and has an Under the hood panel with model, prompt version, tokens and cost. Against today's app (four flat stat tiles, a three-item dropdown and no coach), it gives reps a reason to come back and a clear readiness signal, and it puts the OpenAI models on every surface. The metaphor is specific and memorable, not a template look.
reviews.no_case: The fitness metaphor is a liability. Strain and Form can read as performance surveillance to call-center reps, and the manager view that flags overloaded reps by load is the feature a labor-side buyer will object to first. The coach must answer within 2.5 seconds at p95, and the self-rated coaching score drops to 4 if cues routinely arrive after four seconds, so the core need rests on an unmeasured number. The look is clean but close to the default dashboard template the brief calls generic: rings, cards and stat tiles on a light canvas. The 240-persona promise is a large content lift, and E is rated 6.5 only if all 240 ship. The stack claims are unverified in this run (shadcn on Base UI as the default since July 2026, and bundle sizes from a single blog), and the Whoop and Strava research was not fetched, so the analogy is unsourced.

reviews.yes_case: Shelf and Coach Studio reframes the product as a studio of persona shelves, the way a music app reframes a catalogue. The library opens as stacked horizontal carousels: a Daily Mix built from the rep's weakest rubric criterion, then shelves for home services, insurance, mortgage, solar, auto, medical devices, B2B procurement and collections. Each shelf is a row of 192px square cover cards with difficulty dots and objection tags. Tapping a cover opens a side sheet with the opening line and a Start button, and a bottom queued bar holds the chosen scenario. Facet chips for role, industry, difficulty, objection and length filter the shelves live, with a grid or list toggle for dense work. The live call is a dark three-column view: the persona cover with a canvas waveform driven by real audio levels, a lyrics-style transcript where the current line glows, and a Coach rail with amber whisper cards (next-best question, talk-track step) and coral objection alerts with an optional strong-reply line. The top strip shows talk-track progress and five rubric meters with delta arrows. A minimized call becomes a mini-player with timer and coach pill on every route. The debrief is a two-column review with quote chips that jump the replay to the exact second. Against today's three-item dropdown and chat-bubble call, a rep can find a price objection in a given industry in two taps, and the product feels like a modern consumer app. The wizard drafts a persona with source-cited fields and exports YAML for a pull request. OpenAI shows in a Voice: OpenAI Realtime footer badge and a model inspector drawer with tokens and cost per call.
reviews.no_case: The metaphor fights the job. Shelves are a browsing metaphor, and a rep who wants a pricing objection in insurance with a hard persona is running a multi-facet search that carousels handle poorly; the grid is a toggle, not the main path. The lyrics transcript and music-app chrome signal consumer entertainment, the wrong register for enterprise training buyers and for a grant reviewer. The live coach is self-scored 6.0 and reaches baseline only with sub-1.5 second cues that are not measured yet. The library's 12 industries omit real estate, a sales job the brief names, and its self-scored E of 8 looks high for 120 personas. The HeroUI license is unresolved (one index says Apache-2.0), and generated OpenAI cover art adds per-persona cost and rights questions.

reviews.yes_case: Night Desk Cockpit is a dark, keyboard-first workspace for reps and managers, built as dense multi-pane panels. It uses tabular Geist Mono numerals, 6px radii, 1px hairlines and stepped surface tones instead of shadows, with a 56px icon rail that expands on hover. Ctrl+K jumps to any persona, scenario or past call, and keys J/K, Enter, M, C, E and ? keep a rep in flow. The live call is three panes: a left rail with the clock, talk-track stages that tick live and a patience meter from the grader; a centre speaker-lane transcript with a cue dock holding up to two amber cues with Apply and Dismiss; and a right rubric tape with five criteria bars that move each turn and evidence pins that jump into the transcript. Cues stay out of the persona's session so the character cannot hear the coaching, and a logged cue-adoption record shows whether a rep used each cue and what score change followed, a real evaluation loop. The debrief adds a replay timeline with cue and objection markers, a sticky index, and Print or Export Markdown. The library is a filter rail with job, industry, difficulty, objection, channel and source facets (built-in, mine, community) over a virtualized grid, and the wizard asks one question at a time with Auto-answer. Managers get a pinned top-five and bottom-five roster and a coaching queue. Against today's app it trades a generic page for a workspace that looks like a serious instrument. The contributor story is strong: AGENTS.md, a one-click Ask Codex to add a persona prompt, and a good-first-issue board fed by GitHub labels.
reviews.no_case: Density is the strongest cut reason. The proposal names the risk that first-time reps will be overwhelmed by a three-pane terminal with rubric tape, a cue dock and a patience meter, then offers a Simple view as a promise rather than a designed flow. The look sits closer to a trading terminal than to a modern sales product, which scores low on the brief's user-friendly and modern criteria. The live coach pipeline is handed to separate backend work, and the self-scored coaching depends on sub-1.5 second cues that are unproven. It keeps Next.js 15 and Tailwind 3 and defers the upgrade, so the cutting-edge claim rests on a stack the proposal itself leaves unverified. Its library target of 150-plus personas is rated 5.5 by its own author, and the competitor and OpenAI program claims rest on vendor blogs and search snippets, since Firecrawl was rate-limited.

reviews.yes_case: Game Tape Skill Path wraps every rep in a skill tree and a streak system. The app canvas is light, and a dark game-tape stage holds the live call, the debrief header and the landing hero. Navigation is a 72px icon rail on desktop and bottom tabs on mobile, with a streak flame chip and an XP ring always visible in the top bar. The Progress home is a hand-built SVG skill tree of six branches (Opening, Discovery, Objections, Pricing, Closing, Booking) with five-level nodes: mastered nodes glow green with a gold ring, and open contribution nodes carry a plus mark. The pre-call briefing shows where this call sits in the tree, the XP at stake (Earn 40 XP if goal met), and a checklist of three wins tied to rubric criteria, each with the rep's last score. The live call has a violet now-cue card (one whisper at a time), a Coach rail with a six-step talk-track path and five rubric meters with +delta flashes, criterion chips on credited transcript turns, and an Off, Subtle or Active coaching toggle. The debrief pays out a +48 XP chip and moves a skill node from level 2 to 3, with a moment timeline and timestamped evidence quotes. Its honesty is a strength: heuristic scores show an Estimate badge and withhold XP, so reps are not rewarded for noise. The library ships at least ten personas per sales job, with a Build with AI tile first, a detail sheet and best-score rings. Against today's four stat tiles and flat list, it gives a visible path and a reason to return tomorrow, which matters for real practice habits. A Model lab shows which OpenAI model ran each step, with latency and token cost.
reviews.no_case: Gamification is the wrong register for the audience the brief names. XP, leagues, streak flames and a skill tree read as an edtech app for learners, and enterprise training buyers and call-center managers (the F2 customers) will see a toy, a risk the proposal itself flags. Among these five it is the least modern and the least distinctive: streaks and XP are a mature pattern, and the sports-broadcast palette is the only fresh element. Live coaching is self-scored 5.2 and reaches baseline only if cues land within two seconds with throttling in place, and ten personas per job is a thinner catalogue than the 120 to 300 the other proposals commit to. Its best ideas, such as honest grading that withholds XP on heuristic scores and the dry-run gate before save, can be lifted into a stronger design, so cutting it loses little.

reviews.yes_case: Film Room Sideline turns every practice call into game film. The call is a scrubbable timeline strip: persona and rep turns as coloured blocks, moment tags (discovery, objection, pricing, close, filler, rapport) pinned as they happen, and coach or manager notes on the same timestamps. One spine serves practice, live assist and post-call review, which is the gap the market currently splits on. Visually it is calm: a light canvas (#F6F7F9) for landing, library, progress and team, and a film-dark stage (#0B0F14) for the live call and debrief, with teal primary, a mint signal for the live playhead and good scores, and amber for whisper cues. The live HUD has six tweening rubric meters marked est., a talk-track checklist, and one amber cue at a time with a 20-second minimum gap. The persona never hears the cue. The debrief is a film room: a grade ring, a full-width tagged strip, a moment inspector showing the quote and coach note, and Replay this moment, which starts a retake from that timestamp with the same persona. Versus today, the chat screen with no feedback gains live coaching and live scoring, the long scroll becomes a scannable review, and the progress page names recurring misses (for example, pricing transparency missed in 4 of 6 calls) instead of four static numbers. The library is one versioned JSON pack of 150+ persona-scenario pairs, each with a rubric and two scripted replies for offline tests, validated by one zod schema shared with the wizard and CI. For the OpenAI fund it has the most concrete Codex story in the set: Codex CLI runs in the repo's CI to review persona-pack PRs for schema, bias and rubric weights, maintainer automation drafts release notes, and a model strip names Realtime, coach and grader with cost per call. Its first milestone is a measured harness over recorded calls, which is the right order for a coaching product.
reviews.no_case: The density the proposal itself warns about is real. A timeline strip, tag pills, six meters, a checklist and a cue card in one rail can overwhelm a rep mid-call, and the Hudl lens may read as sports-coded to insurance and mortgage reps, which the proposal says must be tested before the palette locks. It is the least sleek of the top three: Sora and Inter are kept so the change stays recognisable, which undercuts the brief's call for a new look. The film metaphor thins out in the library and wizard, which are mostly filtered card grids. The Tailwind 4 upgrade touches every screen, and a 150-persona target against about 40 hand-checked launch personas makes the library fit a content promise rather than a delivered one. Its own D and E self-scores of 6 concede the baseline is met only if the harness proves the cues.

reviews.yes_case: Live Ledger is the most coherent visual system in the set. A warm paper canvas (#F7F6F2) and white doc pages carry the library, wizard, debrief and progress. A near-black cockpit (#0B0D12) takes over only for the live call, with one soft teal glow on the active cue. Typography does real work: Geist for interface, Geist Mono for timers and weights, and Newsreader serif for doc titles and transcript evidence quotes, so the evidence reads like evidence. Personas, scenarios and rubrics are block documents edited with a slash menu, and the library is the same data the coach and grader read, so nothing in it is decorative. The live call is a three-column cockpit: a talk-track rail, transcript turns, and a right rail with one whisper cue at a time, an objection banner and five live rubric meters. Cues are rate-limited to one per 20 seconds, objections jump the queue, and each cue names the rubric line it serves. Live scores are labelled estimates that the final re-run over the full transcript replaces. The debrief has a 0-100 ring with a source badge that turns amber on fallback, a radar with the previous attempt overlaid, and a Replay moment action that scrubs to the turn. The library covers 120+ personas across 12 job families with filters for job, industry, difficulty, objection and mode, and the wizard validates rubric weights to 100 and redacts PII by default. For the fund, a Model passport in Settings lists which OpenAI model does voice, coach, grader and wizard with cost per call, and Codex runs PR review on persona files and a release checklist. Versus today it replaces the blurry orb and the fake debrief bars with the real product.
reviews.no_case: The cost is the problem. shadcn, a Tailwind v4 migration, TipTap, cmdk, Motion, Recharts, vaul, sonner and three font families, rated XL and several months for one experienced developer, with a block editor the proposal itself says can absorb weeks. The proposal does not say what format the repo files use. If personas are TipTap JSON, a pull request diff is unreadable, which undercuts the reviewable-file promise central to the open-source pitch. The warm paper plus near-black cockpit is a two-theme system that must pass WCAG AA on every text pair, and the Notion lens risks reading as a productivity tool rather than a sales-call product. The two-second cue target is asserted, not measured, and the proposal commits to no measurement harness before building the UI.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Console makes ⌘K the spine of the product. One centred command bar starts any scenario, searches the library, builds or contributes a persona and copies a Codex prompt, with a 56px icon rail, no header bars, Enter to start a drill, and chords such as G then L and G then P. The look is dark-first, with depth made from surface steps and hairlines instead of shadows: canvas #0B0D12, surface #141821, raised #1C2230, teal signal #2DD4BF for rep speech and the active coach, amber for whisper cues, coral for objection alerts and End and grade, and a blue-violet #8FA8FF reserved for AI provenance chips. The live call is one flowing conversation with cue markers placed at the caller line that triggered each cue, plus a 320px coach rail with a Next move line, a cue lane, an objection chip (handled 1 of 3), six-step talk-track progress and seven live rubric bars marked est. The coaching contract is the most rigorous on evidence in the set: typed events (cue, next_question, objection, step_progress, criterion_estimate) carry transcript line ids, the debrief reuses those ids so a cue and the final verdict point at the same quote, a latency gauge is visible, and there is an off switch. The wizard uses one structured-output schema, strips PII before any model call and blocks private-network URL fetches. It keeps Tailwind 3.4, so the redesign avoids a second migration in the same change. For the fund, provenance chips show model ID and call cost on every AI surface, Settings lists the model roles with spend, and an AGENTS.md lets Codex CLI add personas and tests. Versus today it turns a dropdown and a chat app into a coached console.
reviews.no_case: Command-first is a power-user pattern, and the proposal concedes coaching cannot hide behind ⌘K, so the identity is partly a label on a conventional rail-and-grid app. Keyboard-first design can hide features from phone users and from reps who never learn the chords, and the proposal admits every ⌘K action needs a visible button. Dark-first is a brand change the owner may reject, and the light set is only a fallback. The v1 target of 400 personas and 120 scenarios is a content job the proposal calls the real risk, and its own self-score puts the library at 5.3, so the design clears baseline only if content and the wizard both ship. The Codex story is thinner than Film Room or Live Ledger: AGENTS.md and a copyable prompt are real, but nothing shows Codex doing CI or maintainer work. The look is a competent dark console with teal and amber accents, close to a familiar Raycast-style template, so it will not stand out in a crowded market.

reviews.yes_case: Orb-First Coach Console is a voice-first call stage. The top of the live call is a dark stage with an audio-reactive orb whose state reads Listening, Speaking or Your turn, with the current line as a caption and the last four transcript turns below. A light 360px coach rail holds a five-criteria live rubric with covered, partial or missed chips marked live estimate, cue cards that show the transcript quote that triggered them with Accept or Dismiss, and a talk-track stepper. A bottom dock holds mute, timer, model chip and End and grade. Light is the default for library, wizard, debrief and progress, and all screens share one token set. Geist 600 for display and Geist Mono for timers and model IDs, a 16px card radius, one soft shadow reserved for floating cues, and the orb as the only glow, so the product looks quiet and expensive. The coach runs as a separate call after each rep turn with the rubric and last six turns, returns cues with transcript references within about two seconds, and Quiet mode still scores, so certification and open-source users can run the same rubric silently. The persona library is the most contributor-friendly format in the set: each persona is one Markdown file with front matter, so a pull request adds a persona with no code change. The wizard asks one question at a time, streams a draft card, runs a 60-second test call and exports a PR-ready file. The fund angle shows on the screens reviewers touch: model chips on voice, coach, grader and wizard with per-call cost in mono, a Built on OpenAI line, and Codex-run persona lint and rubric-weight checks in CI. Versus today it replaces a blurred gradient orb and a chat screen with a call-first layout.
reviews.no_case: It is the most derivative of the five. The lens is ChatGPT and OpenAI-native, and the inspirations are ElevenLabs, Grok and Hume voice screens, so the orb-plus-transcript stage will look like the voice demo every AI vendor shows, and the cutting-edge claim rests on a pattern rather than an idea. Self-scoring C at 8 is generous for a design whose own description is minimal and conversation-first. The wizard is chat-first with one question at a time, which is slower than a five-input source picker for a rep who wants a usable persona in about a minute. Copying another company's product aesthetic also invites brand-confusion questions for an open-source project, even though the proposal says no logo and no OpenAI colours. Tailwind stays on v3 until phase 4, which pushes the styling migration to the end, and the launch is about 40 personas with 150 on the roadmap, so the library promise is mostly deferred.

reviews.yes_case: Roster Arena turns the persona library into a character-select screen. Each buyer is a 3:4 portrait card with four stat bars (skepticism, time pressure, talkativeness, objection load) drawn as ten-segment pips, a difficulty tier, a voice preview button, and a New persona tile first in the grid that opens the wizard. Portraits are stylized illustrated busts with a difficulty-tinted rim, so no real faces ship. The stat names are the rubric criteria, and the stats map to real persona prompt parameters in the JSON, so the buyer you pick and the score you get share one vocabulary. The live call has a portrait and waveform rail on the left, a transcript with green hit markers and amber coach flags in the centre, and a 360px coach rail on the right with five rubric meters, one citation-backed whisper at a time, and a next-best question. Certification mode hides the coach but records identical scores, which suits training firms and call centres.
