The debrief reads like a match result: a score ring with a tweening number, a scrubbable timeline, five stat-line criterion cards whose quotes jump the timeline, and three one-click drills. The fund angle is a Models in this call strip naming each OpenAI model's role and cost, OpenAI Realtime as a first-class voice provider beside ElevenLabs, and an Export as PR action for persona JSON. It is the most distinctive proposal here, and its F2 story (SCORM and LTI, SSO and SCIM for training firms, BPOs and call centres) is the most explicit of the five. Versus today, the three-item select and the blurred orb become a roster a rep can read at a glance.
reviews.no_case: The game frame is the main risk, and the proposal knows it. A hero-select roster with stat pips reads as a toy to the call-centre and enterprise buyers its F2 story depends on, and the proposal keeps the stat-and-pip chrome while dropping only rarity borders and fantasy art. Its own needs-fit self-scores (D 5.3, E 5.2) sit barely above baseline, and the coach and library both depend on a latency benchmark and a human review pass that are not built yet. The portrait system means about 150 illustrated busts, an art budget the proposal does not cost. The Codex story is the weakest in the set: Built with Codex appears only once Codex runs PR review, which is a promise rather than a plan. The stat-to-prompt mapping is asserted, and the proposal admits reviewers will check the JSON. It is the most distinctive design here, but distinctiveness is not what the council's basic-needs and fund criteria reward first.

reviews.yes_case: Call Canvas makes the whole product one dark, spatial studio. A 64px icon rail sits beside an infinite dot-grid canvas where personas, talk-track steps and rubric criteria are nodes you wire together, so a sequence from warm-up to hard close reads at a glance and the library can be browsed as a board. The AI persona wizard is the clearest version of the wizard idea in this set: a job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP and a pasted call feed a Persona Synth node, which emits Persona, Scenario and Rubric nodes, and each generated field cites the sentence it came from. Manual edits survive regeneration. Live calls do not use the canvas. They use a fixed, glanceable three-column cockpit: a talk-track rail, a transcript with a voice orb, and a right rail with a violet whisper card for the next question, an amber objection alert with an acknowledge-then-anchor line, and six live rubric bars with evidence pins. The debrief settles the live numbers into a 900ms score-dial sweep and shows whether the rep followed each cue. It beats today's app on every axis the brief names: the live call is a chat app now, the library is a three-item dropdown, and no wizard exists. On the OpenAI fund question, this is the strongest of the set on visible model use. A model rail names Realtime for voice and gpt-4.1-mini for cues and grading, each call shows its cost, Settings lists each model, and an AGENTS.md lets Codex CLI draft packs and review PRs.
reviews.no_case: Strongest reason to cut: a canvas is a diagram tool, and the proposal admits the risk. Most reps will never want to wire nodes, and a 140-persona library shown as a React Flow board is slower to scan than a grid. The most distinctive idea does not touch the live call, which falls back to fixed panels, so the baseline requirement the brief cares about most is served by ordinary layout. React Flow and the wizard graph add real bundle weight and build cost for an XL effort, and its own self-scores (D 6.5, E 6.5) say the baseline is met only if latency and the content both ship. The two-week phase estimates are optimistic. The OpenAI fund claims rest on Codex program terms the proposal did not fully read, so the fund angle is unverified.

reviews.yes_case: Live Ledger treats everything a rep touches as one kind of document. Each persona, scenario, talk track and rubric is a block page with a properties header and a slash menu (checklist, rubric row, objection, scripted reply, cue, callout), and the coach and grader read the same structure. That gives the open-source core its strongest contributor story: each persona is a reviewable file in the repo, and each persona doc has an Open PR button. The library uses Klaviyo-style sections (Cold calls 24, View all) with cards showing an initials disc, role, difficulty dot, objection chips and a use count, and filters for job family, industry, difficulty, objection and mode. The launch target is 120+ personas across twelve job families, at least eight each. The wizard takes five input types, streams a live document block by block (persona, objections, talk track, rubric rows whose weights must total 100 before save), redacts PII by default in pasted transcripts, and ends in a two-minute test call. The live cockpit is always dark: a talk-track checklist on the left, turn-based transcript rows with a small persona orb in the centre, and on the right one whisper cue at a time, a rose objection banner, and five rubric meters labelled live estimate that flash a teal delta when evidence lands. The coach is a separate gpt-4.1-mini structured-output call, limited to one cue per 20 seconds, and the persona never coaches. The final grade re-runs the same rubric over the full transcript with quotes, so live and debrief scores agree. When the grader falls back, the debrief says so in amber rather than showing a red F. A Model passport in Settings shows which OpenAI model did each job and what it cost. The migration keeps the current API routes and grading contract. Against today's app, it reworks every screen the brief names and adds the missing manager view.
reviews.no_case: Strongest reason to cut: the block editor is the largest scope risk in the set. TipTap, slash menus and persona-as-document editing can absorb months before the live cockpit ships, and the cap of eight block types is a hope, not a decision. The visual language is familiar: a warm cream canvas, hairlines and Notion-style card rows. Nothing about it says cutting-edge tech the way a canvas or a film timeline does, and a serif for evidence quotes beside a sans UI can read as editorial rather than sleek. The proposal estimates several months for one experienced developer, and the two-second coach latency target is unproven.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Console is the most keyboard-literate design in the set. A 56px icon rail with no header bars, and one centred command bar that holds every action (start a scenario, search personas, build or contribute a persona, copy a Codex prompt), with chords such as G then L for library and G then P for progress. The live console has three zones and no header: a flowing transcript where caller lines are ink and rep lines are signal teal, cue markers placed at the exact line that triggered them, and a 320px coach rail with a Next move line, a whisper lane, an objection chip (handled 1 of 3), talk-track ticks and seven live rubric bars marked est. Its coaching contract is the most rigorous in the set: the coach streams typed events (cue, next_question, objection, step_progress, criterion_estimate), each carrying the ids of the transcript lines it refers to, and the debrief reuses those ids, so a live cue and the final verdict point at the same quote. Whispers are throttled to one per 20 seconds, with quiet, normal and heavy intensity. Security is handled properly: URL fetches are allowlisted against private networks, and transcripts are PII-redacted before any model call. The library is data, not code: validated YAML or JSON personas and about 120 scenarios, which makes contribution easy. It beats today's app because a command-first shell and a coached console replace a dropdown and a chat app. Its self-scoring is also the most candid: D 5.6 and E 5.3, with the stated condition that the event contract and the content ship.
reviews.no_case: Strongest reason to cut: it is the least visually distinct proposal, and the brief asks for a cutting-edge look. The Raycast and Arc lens reads as a developer tool. A call-centre rep under a headset is not a power user, and the proposal itself concedes that keyboard-first can hide features from mobile and screen-reader users. It keeps Tailwind 3.4 and Inter for all UI, which leans on the system the brief calls generic. Under the command bar the screens are cards and chips, so the new look is mostly chrome. Its own E of 5.3 says the design alone does not clear the baseline, and the 400-persona target is a content job nobody has priced. The OpenAI showcase also waits on a Realtime provider that is not built yet.

reviews.yes_case: Orb-First is calm, conversation-first and OpenAI-native. The library, wizard, debrief, progress and team sit on a warm light canvas with white surfaces, and the live call and landing hero use a dark voice stage, both on one token set. On the call, an audio-driven orb sits in the top third of the dark stage and labels its state Listening, Speaking or Your turn, with the last four transcript turns beneath it. A 360px light coach rail holds a live rubric with covered, partial or missed chips marked live estimate, cue cards that carry a transcript quote with Accept or Dismiss, and a talk-track stepper. The coach is a separate model call after each rep turn that returns structured cue and criterion data with transcript references, aiming for about two seconds. Quiet, Cues and Full set the volume, and Quiet still scores. The debrief grader chip reads Graded by GPT, or Heuristic fallback with a Re-grade button, which replaces the current warning banner. The wizard is conversation-first: source chips, one question at a time, a draft card that streams in, a 60-second test call and an Export as PR action. The library is about 150 personas in 15 job families, each one Markdown file with front matter, so a contributor adds one by PR with no code change. Filters persist in the URL. Model chips sit on every surface with per-call cost in mono, and Built on OpenAI appears as plain text with no logo, which keeps trademark use clean. Against today's app, it replaces the chat-only call, the three-item dropdown and the blurred gradient orb.
reviews.no_case: Strongest reason to cut: the look is the voice-AI template. An orb centred, a transcript beside it and a light rail mirror the ElevenLabs, Grok and Hume screens the proposal cites, so its distinctiveness is low. The brief criticised the blurry orb, and this keeps the orb as the only glow in the product, now audio-driven rather than decorative. Self-scoring C at 8 is generous for a layout most voice products already ship. The migration keeps Tailwind 3 until phase 4 and only then evaluates v4, so the system stays one generation behind. A chat-led wizard asks one question at a time, which is slower than a structured five-source intake for a rep who already has a job description and a CRM note. The 150-persona target is content work that the proposal itself says to cut to about 40 at launch.

reviews.yes_case: Film Room turns every practice call into game film, and the unifying idea is a timeline spine. A scrubbable waveform strip runs across the top of the live call, the debrief and the library, with persona and rep turns as coloured blocks, a playhead at now, and tagged moments (discovery, objection, pricing, close, filler, rapport) that appear as the call happens. Every rubric score, coach note and cue is pinned to a timestamp on that same strip, so practice, live assist and post-call review share one view instead of three products. The live call is a film-dark three-column stage: the timeline across the top; the transcript with inline tag pills in the centre; and a 320px sideline HUD with six rubric meters that tween, a talk-track checklist, one amber whisper cue at a time with a 20-second minimum gap and Esc to dismiss, two suggested replies drawn from the cue, and an objection alert chip. The debrief is timeline-first: a grade ring and verdict, a full-width film strip with green, amber and rose tags, and a click on any tag opens the matching transcript line, quote and coach note. Replay this moment starts a retake from that timestamp with the same persona. Progress ranks recurring misses by frequency (for example, Pricing transparency missed in 4 of 6 calls) and links each to its moments. The manager view carries consent and visibility labels on rep data, which a sales org needs. The library is one versioned JSON pack with 150+ target entries, each with a rubric and two scripted replies, validated by one zod schema shared by the wizard, the importer and CI. Codex CLI in CI reviews persona-pack PRs for schema, bias and rubric weights, which is a concrete Codex for Open Source use. Against today's app, it replaces a chat with no feedback and a dropdown with a coached review cockpit.
reviews.no_case: Strongest reason to cut: it borrows its metaphor from sports analytics, and the proposal itself flags that the density may read as sports-coded, or as a video editor, to insurance and mortgage reps. The timeline is strong on desktop but shrinks to a 48px scrubber on a 390px phone, which is where most reps will take a call. The library is the least designed part: a conventional filter rail and card grid, not film-like. The Tailwind 4 upgrade touches every screen and needs frozen visual baselines first, a real cost before any UI ships. Its self-scored D 6 and E 6 mean the baseline is met only with a measured latency harness that does not exist yet. The Codex review badges on merged personas depend on CI that is not yet built.

reviews.yes_case: Orb-First Coach Console rebuilds the whole app on shadcn/ui (owned copy-in components), Geist and Geist Mono, Motion and a Realtime-style voice stage, with one token set for a dark call screen and light library, debrief and team views. The live call has a dark stage with an audio-reactive orb in the top third that visibly listens and speaks, the last few transcript turns beneath it, and a 360px light coach rail on the right. The rail holds a live rubric (labelled as a live estimate), one cue card at a time with its transcript quote and Accept or Dismiss, and a talk-track stepper. Coaching is a separate model call, so the persona never coaches. Cues aim for about two seconds after the rep finishes a turn, and when latency runs long the UI falls back to end-of-turn cues and says so. The library is a 15-job catalogue with facets for role, industry, difficulty, objection and mode, filters that persist in the URL, and a pinned Create with AI card. The wizard is a two-pane chat with source chips that asks one question at a time, streams a draft card with a rubric checksum at 100, runs a 60-second test call and saves or exports a PR-ready file. OpenAI appears in the chrome as model chips for voice, coach and grader with per-call cost, and Codex runs persona lint and rubric checks in CI. It beats today's app because a chat-bubble call with no feedback becomes a cockpit that coaches and scores as you talk, and three scenario choices become a browsable catalogue.
reviews.no_case: The voice-stage look sits very close to current ChatGPT and Realtime demos, so judges may read it as derivative rather than distinctive, and leaning on that pattern invites a brand-adjacency question. The per-turn coach call is unproven on latency, and the Quiet-still-scores rule has no benchmark behind it. The wizard has no PII step for pasted real calls, which is a compliance gap. Roughly 150 personas is a large writing job with 40 at launch. The Codex CI checks are described, not built, so the fund claim depends on work not yet done.

reviews.yes_case: Film Room Sideline turns every practice call into game film. A scrubbable timeline strip (wavesurfer.js with coloured regions for tagged moments such as discovery, objection, pricing, close, filler and rapport) runs across the live call, the debrief and the library, so practice, live assist and post-call review share one spine. The live call is a film-dark, three-column surface: a turn timeline with a playhead, a transcript with inline tag pills, and a 320px sideline HUD with six rubric meters that tween as each turn lands, a talk-track checklist, and at most one amber whisper cue (20-second minimum gap, Esc to dismiss) shown to the rep only. The debrief is timeline-first: a grade ring, a film strip with green, amber and rose tags, a moment inspector that jumps to the quote and coach note, and a Replay this moment button that starts a retake from that timestamp. Progress lists recurring misses, such as pricing transparency missed in 4 of 6 calls, and the manager view pairs a rep-by-criterion heatmap with consent labels. The wizard runs five steps, strips PII from pasted calls before any model call, shows what it extracted for editing, and keeps sources in the browser unless a key is set. The OpenAI story is concrete: a model strip with cost per call, and CI that runs Codex CLI to review persona-pack PRs for schema, bias and rubric weights and drafts release notes. It beats today's app because a chat-like scroll with no coaching becomes a film room where every score points to the exact moment that caused it.
reviews.no_case: Hudl-style density can read as sports-coded to insurance and mortgage reps, and the film metaphor is untested with buyers. The 20-second minimum gap between cues can hold back the objection alert at the moment it matters most, which is the core coaching promise. The claim that live and final scores cannot disagree is an overstatement, since a rolling live estimate and a final grade are different computations. The library facets name six job families and eight industries, short of the fifteen the brief asks for, and real estate is missing from the industry facet. The Tailwind 4 move touches every screen, and voice cues risk bleeding into the mic without headphones.

reviews.yes_case: Expressive Coaching Studio is a Material 3 Expressive redesign on MUI. Tonal palettes come from seed colours through Google's Material Color Utilities, with 28px corners, pill buttons, springy motion and Roboto Flex. Each persona's temperament (friendly, skeptical, hostile) is a seed, so the call screen eases to a new tint as the persona's mood shifts, and the tint never touches body text. The live call is three columns: a shader orb with interest and trust meters, a transcript with speaker-tinted bubbles and inline coach markers, and a coach column with a stack of at most three cues, an objection alert, a next-best question, a talk-track stepper with the current step pulsing, and seven live rubric meters labelled provisional. The coach is a separate model channel the persona never sees. If it fails, a keyword checker keeps the talk track moving and a status line says coaching is paused, so the failure is never silent. The debrief shows a sparkline of provisional live scores against final scores, with markers where cues fired, so reps can judge how trustworthy the live estimates were. The library holds 120+ YAML persona packs across fifteen job families, with playlists, tinted cards and URL-shareable filters. The wizard traces each generated field to its source line, runs a 60-second test drive and saves or opens a GitHub PR. OpenAI models are named in the header with each job and its cost, and a seeded demo team with a recorded call lets reviewers see coaching and scoring without keys. It beats today's blue-on-slate template and chat screen with a console that looks designed and shows its own scoring.
reviews.no_case: MUI does not ship Material 3 Expressive shapes or spring motion, so the signature look is custom theme work that could drift into noise, and porting every screen off Tailwind is a large rewrite of a working app. MUI's default look is itself recognisable as a template, which is the diagnosis the brief rejects. Tinted persona backgrounds must hold WCAG AA in every temperament, and the proposal does not address PII in pasted real calls. The Codex PR-review workflow is only planned, so the fund claim leans on the model strip more than on working CI.

reviews.yes_case: Roster Arena is a dark, roster-first training arena where every buyer is a character. The front door is a grid of tall cards with illustrated portraits, four stat bars named after the rubric criteria (skepticism, time pressure, talkativeness, objection load), difficulty pips and a five-second voice preview, with a New persona tile that opens the wizard first. Practice opens a pre-flight briefing with objection triggers, a talk-track checklist, weighted scoring rows and a coach setting (Full, Quiet, Off), where Off is certification mode and still records scores. The live call has three zones: persona and waveform on the left, a transcript with green and amber markers in the centre, and a coach rail on the right with five live rubric meters, one whisper card at a time, a coral objection chip with a suggested reply, a next-best question and a talk-track stepper. The coach runs out of band and emits typed events (whisper, objection, next question, criterion hit), each citing a transcript line, capped at one whisper per 20 seconds, with a latency benchmark in the repo. The debrief is a match-result layout with a score ring, a scrubbable timeline and quotes that jump the timeline. Progress uses unlock rules tied to real criteria, which gives reps a reason to return. The wizard drafts a persona in five steps with a source citation on every trait, redacts PII before a pasted call reaches a model, lints the draft, and saves or exports as a PR. It beats today's app because a three-item dropdown becomes a roster people want to work through, and the call gets a coach and a scorecard.
reviews.no_case: Game chrome reads as a toy to some enterprise and call-centre buyers, which is the risk the proposal itself lists, and a reviewer scoring sleekness may mark the glow-and-pip HUD down. The fund angle is thin: Codex appears only as a CONTRIBUTING page and a footer badge that waits for CI use, so the story rests on Realtime and model cost. The 150 illustrated portraits with rim tints are an art pipeline the proposal never costs. Gamified unlock tiers can feel like grind inside a workplace tool.

reviews.yes_case: Mantine Coaching Console applies one Mantine v8 kit across all nine screens: an AppShell with a collapsible navbar, Spotlight on Ctrl or Cmd+K across personas, scenarios, debriefs and actions, Stepper and Drawer flows, Tabs, RingProgress and Mantine charts, all driven by one token set. The live call is a fixed dark console: a 280px persona panel with a dual-channel waveform (rep in indigo, persona in teal), a transcript with objection alerts pinned to the top, and a 320px right rail with an amber whisper strip above the composer, a six-step talk-track Stepper, and provisional rubric bars with delta arrows and evidence chips that jump to the transcript line that moved them. Scores stay dimmed until two consecutive turns agree, a sensible stability rule, and a keyword heuristic takes over with a visible notice if the model fails. The library is grouped by sales job with facets for role, industry, difficulty, objection and channel, and preview and practice actions on each card. The debrief leads with a Coach's one fix card and a Re-run weakest criterion action, and the team view adds an Approve for live calls switch. The model stack, per-session tokens and cost sit in Settings and the README. It beats today's app with a coaching rail, a talk-track tracker and search-first navigation built on one well-documented kit that contributors can learn quickly.
reviews.no_case: Mantine's defaults are the generic template look the brief rejects, and the proposal's own fix, a custom token set and dark console, is a promise rather than a designed system. The coaching architecture is thin: there is no separate coach channel, no latency target, and audio whisper has no headphone or bleed guard. A whisper strip visible for about four seconds is too brief to read mid-call. The launch library is 50-plus personas, short of the large catalogue the brief asks for, the wizard is four steps with no PII handling, and the OpenAI fund story is mostly a Settings panel plus a can-draft-and-review promise.

reviews.yes_case: Game Tape Skill Path turns the whole app into a season of practice. The light app (white cards on a pale canvas, a 72px icon rail for Path, Library, Live, Debriefs, Progress and Team, and a top bar with a streak flame chip, an XP chip with a level ring and the avatar) sits around a dark game-tape stage that is reserved for the live call, the debrief header and the landing hero. The progress story is a skill tree of six branches (Opening, Discovery, Objections, Pricing, Closing, Booking), each with five-level nodes: grey when locked, green with a gold ring when mastered, and marked with a plus where contributions are open. On the live call a 320px coach rail shows one violet now-cue line, a six-step talk-track path with checkmarks, five rubric meters that flash deltas, and objection alerts that name the criterion they threaten. The debrief states which grader ran. A keyword-heuristic score gets an Estimate badge and no XP, which fixes a real flaw in today's app. The library has five facets (role, industry, difficulty pips, objection type, Done by me) over a three-column card grid with best-score rings and a right sheet with rubric weights, replacing the three-item dropdown. The AI wizard is a four-step stepper with source tiles and a streaming persona card, and nothing saves until a two-minute dry run passes. The stack is well known and buildable (shadcn on Radix, Tailwind v4 tokens, Motion, Recharts, Lucide, next/font). For the Codex fund, a Model lab panel lists each model's latency and token cost per call, and contributor XP on profiles plus persona badges give open-source contributors something to work toward.
reviews.no_case: Gamification is the bet, and it is the most familiar bet of the five. Streaks, XP, leagues and bite-size levels are a Duolingo pattern that call-center buyers may read as childish, and the sports-broadcast styling is mostly a skin over the same mechanics, so this is the least distinctive design in the advancing set. The proposal does not show how XP avoids rewarding volume over quality beyond withholding it on heuristic grades, so reps can farm streaks with low-value reps. The hand-built SVG skill tree of about 30 nodes plus a Path home screen is a second product to build before the coaching core, which the proposal itself calls the grant demo. Its own self-score for live coaching is 5.2, and it only clears baseline if cue latency stays under two seconds and throttling ships.

reviews.yes_case: Strain and Form Console is the most coherent new identity in the set. Every rep gets a Form ring (fitness minus fatigue, so the rep sees whether they are sharp for a hard persona), every call gets a Strain score from 0 to 21 that forecasts load before dialing, and personal records mark bests per persona. The look is a clean instrument panel: 16px cards with hairline borders and no shadow at rest, round-cap rings that fill over 900ms, a night canvas for the live call, briefing and landing hero, and a light canvas for practice, library, debrief and team. It beats today's app by replacing four stat tiles and a blurry orb with readable trends, and by replacing the chat app with a live coach: one whisper cue at a time (Ask, Objection, Pace, Step, Close), a next-best-question chip, dashed provisional rubric rings that settle into the graded score, and an elevation timeline with coach markers showing where the call dipped. The coach runs as its own server-side channel, so the persona never hears advice. The library is 240-plus persona JSON files checked by one zod schema, faceted by job family, industry, strain, objection, channel and voice or text. The wizard has four entry points, including a pasted call transcript that is redacted for phone numbers, emails and names before any model call. It streams a persona card, runs a 30-second test call and exports a schema-valid file for a pull request. For the Codex fund it is the strongest OpenAI showcase here: the grader, coach and wizard use OpenAI structured outputs, OpenAI Realtime is a switchable voice engine next to ElevenLabs, and an Under the hood panel shows model, prompt version, tokens and cost on every debrief.
reviews.no_case: The metaphor carries the main risk. Strain and Form borrow the vocabulary of a consumer biometrics wearable, and a call-center manager may hear a health-tracking app instead of a sales coach, so the concept needs careful onboarding to land. Scope is heavy: the six-step migration is XL, touches every screen, and removes the three.js orb. The 240-persona launch is far beyond what a volunteer project can review for stereotyping and objection quality in one cycle, and the proposal's own risk list concedes that personas need a review rubric and a verified badge. The Base UI-as-shadcn-default claim and the bundle-size figures rest on a single blog post that was not checked here, so the stack credibility is only as good as that one source.

reviews.yes_case: Night Desk Cockpit is the most rigorous live-coaching design in the set. It is a dark three-pane cockpit. On the left: a call clock, talk-track stages that tick during the call, and a persona patience meter (0 to 10) that the grader updates. In the centre: a speaker-lane transcript with timestamps and a cue dock holding up to two amber cues with Apply and Dismiss, kept out of the persona's session so the character never hears coaching. On the right: a rubric tape with five criteria bars that move every turn and evidence pins that jump to the transcript line. Unassisted mode hides cues for certification runs and still scores. Every cue is logged with whether the rep used it and the score change that followed, and the debrief shows that adoption log beside a replayable timeline with cue and objection markers. The library is a filter rail (job, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel, source: built-in, mine, community) over a virtualized card grid, with an inspector, saved presets and a New persona split button. The wizard asks one question at a time with an Auto-answer option, streams a persona card and runs a 60-second dry run before save. Keyboard shortcuts (J/K, Enter, M, C, E) make it fast for power users and managers. Against today's chat app and dropdown, it gives reps and managers the data they act on. For the fund, a footer names the model for each job with live latency, and a per-call cost chip shows real token spend.
reviews.no_case: It looks like a trading terminal, and reps are not traders. Bloomberg density is the wrong default for a first-time rep, and the proposal concedes it needs a Simple view and a first-run tour; if those slip, the first impression is a wall of panels. Modern is weak: dark terminal chrome, dense 13 to 14px type and monospace numerals read as a developer tool rather than a sleek, cutting-edge product. The stack also stays on Tailwind 3 and Next 15 with the upgrade deferred, so the redesign sits on the older system, and shadcn Tailwind 3 compatibility is unverified in its own text. The best coaching engine in the set is wrapped in the least approachable skin, and the brief judges look and user experience as much as coaching.

reviews.yes_case: Shelf and Coach Studio makes the persona library feel like a catalogue worth browsing. The library is stacked shelves: a Daily Mix built from the rep's weakest rubric criterion, then rows for Home services, Insurance, Mortgage, Solar, Auto, Medical devices, B2B procurement and Collections. Each row is a horizontal scroll-snap strip of 192px cover cards with name, role, difficulty dots and objection tags. Facet chips for role, industry, difficulty, objection and length filter the shelves live, a grid and list toggle serves dense filtering, and a side sheet opens each persona with its opening line and a Start button. The live call is a lyrics-style transcript where the current line glows as the rep speaks. The coach rail on the right carries amber whisper cards (next question, talk-track step), coral objection alerts with an optional strong-reply line, and a Quiet, Balanced or Intense setting, while five rubric meters with delta arrows run along the top. Strong-reply lines stay locked until the debrief, so practice still builds the skill. The debrief is a two-column review with a grade ring, criterion bars, evidence quotes with replay buttons and a sticky transcript. On mobile a bottom tab bar and a mini-player keep the timer and coach pill visible on every route. It beats today's three-item dropdown and bare list by making the library personal and browsable. For the fund, GPT drafts personas in the wizard, OpenAI image generation makes cover art at build time, the call footer names Realtime, and a contributor page with an Open PR button brings persona authors in.
reviews.no_case: The Spotify metaphor is the most consumer-facing in the set, and a sales manager may read a music app with cover art and playlists as entertainment rather than a training tool. The lyrics-style transcript and Daily Mix are charming but add little coaching value. Coaching is the weakest-supported non-negotiable: latency is 'to be measured, not promised', the proposal's own coaching self-score is 6, and the cap of one whisper per 20 seconds limits coaching in fast objection exchanges. Cover art for about 120 personas adds generation cost and a licensing question for every persona. The HeroUI licence is uncertain, as the proposal admits (MIT in official docs, Apache-2.0 in another index), which matters for an open-source project that asks to be trusted. The launch list covers 12 industries but leaves out real estate, which the brief names explicitly.

reviews.yes_case: Call Canvas makes the whole product a spatial studio. Personas, talk tracks and rubrics are nodes on a dot-grid canvas. The library is a faceted card grid by default, with a board mode that wires picked personas into a sequence from warm-up to hard close. The AI wizard is a visible graph: source nodes (job description, product URL, CRM note, pasted call, ICP form) feed a Persona Synth node that emits Persona, Scenario and Rubric nodes, and each generated field cites the sentence it came from. The canvas is for building and browsing only; the live call and debrief keep fixed, glanceable layouts. On the live call a six-step talk-track rail pulses the current step, a speaker-labelled transcript with timecodes sits in the centre above a voice orb or hold-to-talk composer, and the right rail holds five rubric bars that move each turn with delta chips and evidence pins that jump to the transcript line. A violet whisper card carries one next question and an amber objection card carries the strong reply. Each cue has Why and helpful buttons that feed prompt tuning. The debrief is a replayable timeline with markers for cues and objections. It beats today's app because the chat layout gives no feedback until the grade, and the dropdown becomes a browsable, faceted library. The stack is real and sensible (shadcn on Radix with Tailwind 4, React Flow lazy-loaded, cmdk, vaul, Motion, Geist). The light landing page with a text-mode demo gives Codex reviewers something to try in one click. The footer names each OpenAI model with its live latency, and AGENTS.md plus a contributor board give maintainers a Codex-ready workflow.
reviews.no_case: The canvas is a risky bet for reps and for accessibility. Node graphs are hard to operate with a keyboard or a screen reader, and a three-output Persona Synth graph asks a sales manager to think like a pipeline builder when the brief asks for a wizard that turns a job description or pasted call into a persona. The proposal itself says the canvas can read as a diagram tool. The build cost is high: React Flow wiring, animated connections, per-field provenance, regenerate-per-field and a synth progress state are a large new surface, while the coaching pipeline is still backend work and the 2-second latency target is marked unproven. The launch library is thin by the proposal's own account (ship 40 reviewed packs before claiming 140), and the coach has no unassisted or certification mode.

reviews.yes_case: Roster Arena makes the whole app a dark, roster-first training arena. The old three-item scenario dropdown becomes a grid of named buyer cards, each with four stat bars that map to real persona parameters (skepticism, time pressure, talkativeness, objection load), 10-segment difficulty pips, and a five-second voice preview before you commit. Every screen (landing, roster, pre-call briefing, live call, debrief, progress, manager, mobile) uses one token set built on shadcn/ui over Base UI, Tailwind v4 and Motion, with signal teal for the rep, coach amber for cues, green for criterion hit and coral for misses. The live call has three columns: persona and waveform on the left, a transcript with green criterion-hit markers in the middle, and a coach rail on the right with five rubric meters that move every turn, plus at most one amber whisper every 20 seconds, each citing the transcript line it refers to. The coach runs out-of-band on OpenAI Realtime or a text model, so the persona never hears coaching, and the debrief is built from the same event log so live and final scores agree. The plan says coaching only counts if a latency and restraint benchmark ships in the repo, which is the right gate. Against today's chat-style call with no feedback, a rep watches the rubric move while talking and can scrub the debrief to the exact quote that cost points. For the Codex fund it makes OpenAI visible on screen: a Models strip with per-call cost, Realtime as a first-class voice next to ElevenLabs, and an AI persona wizard that drafts from a job description, product URL, CRM notes or pasted call, cites a source line for every trait, redacts PII before any model call, and exports a persona as a PR. Contributors get reviewable JSON persona files, good-first-persona issues and a CONTRIBUTING page for Codex-assisted PRs. The library covers roles, industries, difficulty, objection type and mode with 150+ personas as the target.
reviews.no_case: The game hero-select chrome (stat bars, pips, portrait cards, a voice-preview button on every card) is the most likely of the five to read as a toy to call-center buyers and enterprise procurement, and the stats only earn their keep if reviewers confirm they map to real prompt parameters. The plan also claims 20 sales jobs while naming 15, and it depends on a shadcn/Base UI move plus a Tailwind v4 rewrite of every screen that the proposal itself rates XL effort with a budget risk.

reviews.yes_case: Expressive Coaching Studio is a Material 3 Expressive redesign on MUI where the persona's temperament is the organizing idea. Each persona is a seed color (friendly teal, skeptical amber, hostile red) that generates a full tonal scheme with Google's Material Color Utilities, so the live call screen re-tints as the buyer's mood shifts, library cards carry the tint, and the morphing Start button and wavy progress indicators give a bolder, more tactile feel than today's blue-on-slate template. Navigation is an M3 rail on desktop and a bottom bar on mobile, and Library merges today's scenario editor into one browsable place with editing in a drawer. The live call is three columns: a shader orb driven by agent audio, a transcript with coach markers, and a coach column where cues spring in (at most three, pinned until read, each highlighting the transcript line it refers to) above seven live rubric meters labelled provisional. Coaching runs on a separate model channel the persona never sees, with Off, Subtle and Whisper levels per session, a 2-second target, and a keyword fallback that keeps the call going with a visible 'coaching paused' status instead of failing silently. The debrief shows live scores against final scores as a sparkline, a live-versus-final story today's app cannot tell. The library is 120+ YAML persona packs grouped by the sales jobs in the brief, filterable by role, industry, difficulty, objection and temperament, with filters shareable in the URL. The wizard traces each trait to its source line and can open a GitHub PR with the YAML pack. For the Codex fund it is the most reviewer-friendly: the header and landing page name each OpenAI model with its job and per-session cost, and a seeded demo team plus a recorded sample call let reviewers see coaching and scoring without setting up keys.
reviews.no_case: The Material 3 Expressive layer is unverified in MUI, and the proposal admits the shapes, springs and per-persona tints are custom work that can drift into visual noise or the generic Google Material look. It also drops Tailwind and lucide for a whole new icon and type system, and it carries a heavy bundle (three.js plus MUI X) on phones. The 120-persona library is content work the proposal itself says may have to launch smaller.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Desk is a dark-first, editorial redesign built on Ark UI behavior, Panda CSS semantic tokens and Park UI-style copy-in components, so every component lives in the repo as source that contributors can read and PR. The look is a quiet dark live console (near-black canvas, teal signal, amber cues, coral alerts) with Geist and Geist Mono for numerals and model IDs, and an Instrument Serif verdict line on the debrief that sets it apart from the usual SaaS cards. The live call is three columns: a persona transcript in the middle, and on the right a coach rail with one amber whisper card at a time (visible about 8 seconds, with a Why link that expands the rubric line), a talk-track stepper, and five rubric meters that show tracking ranges rather than grades, labelled as live estimates. A cue should land within about 2 seconds of the turn ending, with a fallback to after-turn cues, and the final grade reruns the full evidence-backed grader so the debrief never contradicts the live view. The library has about 150 reviewed personas across roles, industries, three difficulty tiers and five objection types, and the wizard drafts persona, scenario and rubric from a job description, product URL, CRM note, ICP or pasted call, with a provenance chip on every field and nothing saved until the rep approves. For the Codex fund it is the most explicit about OpenAI: model chips on every stage show model ID, latency and cost per call, OpenAI Realtime is a voice option beside ElevenLabs, a human-labelled grader eval and Trust panel live in the repo, and AGENTS.md plus a Codex-run PR review workflow give reviewers a concrete Codex-for-Open-Source story.
reviews.no_case: The stack is the least familiar to contributors. Panda CSS, Ark UI and Park UI have much smaller ecosystems than Tailwind or shadcn, so the project would be adopting a styling engine and component source it must maintain itself, and the migration rewrites every Tailwind component, which the proposal names as its biggest risk. Its D and E scores are conditional on the coach channel and the reviewed library both shipping, and the look leans on one serif and a canvas ring after the proposal itself admits a dark SaaS skin can read generic.

reviews.yes_case: Friendly Coach Studio is a warm, rounded redesign on HeroUI v3 with a warm paper canvas (#F6F4F0), a violet coach accent, Bricolage Grotesque display type and soft 20px cards, with dark mode in v1. It is the friendliest of the five: a Practice home screen, a persona library with a left filter rail (sales job, industry, difficulty slider, objection, source) and a 3-up grid of glyph-tile cards that open a drawer preview, and a four-step wizard with a live preview pane and a 'Generated with GPT' badge. The live call has three visible lanes: the persona lane (voice or text, never sees coaching), a coach lane that emits at most one whisper every 20 seconds, each 12 words or fewer with a why link to the transcript line, and a grader lane that streams rubric deltas in under about 1.5 seconds, labelled as live estimates. Spring-animated whisper cards and a shared-element morph from library card into persona header give motion a purpose. The library target is about 150 personas across 16+ sales jobs with two or three scenarios each (340 scenarios), the most scenario coverage stated by any proposal here. For the fund, a per-session cost meter, a 'Build a pack with Codex' button that opens a pre-filled Codex task, and a Codex review checklist on pack PRs give a concrete open-source story.
reviews.no_case: It is the least cutting-edge look. The proposal's own risk is that soft HeroUI defaults read as every AI SaaS, and a friendly consumer tone may read as less serious to call-center and enterprise buyers. It rests on HeroUI v3, a new library that dropped its motion layer, and it is marked L effort even though it touches every screen, so the schedule is likely understated.

reviews.yes_case: Mantine Coaching Console rebuilds all nine screens on one mature kit (AppShell, Stepper, Tabs, Drawer, RingProgress, Spotlight, Mantine charts), with a fixed dark live console and a light library, debrief and dashboard. The live call has three layers: an amber whisper strip above the composer, a six-step talk-track stepper ticked by the model, and a live rubric with provisional bars, delta arrows and evidence chips that jump to the transcript line that moved each score. Scores stay dimmed until two consecutive turns agree, a good restraint rule, and the debrief reuses the same rows so live and final numbers match. The library is grouped by sales job with a facet rail and counts. The four-step wizard (Source, Persona, Scenario, Dry run) streams drafts tagged with their source sentence, enforces rubric weights that total 100, and saves a persona file that can go into a PR. Spotlight gives Ctrl+K search across personas, debriefs and actions such as 'Build persona from this JD'. For the fund there is a Model stack panel, per-session token and cost chips, and an AGENTS.md explaining how Codex CLI can draft and review persona PRs. Mantine is the lowest-risk kit to ship, and it removes Tailwind and globals.css in one stroke.
reviews.no_case: The proposal says its own Mantine defaults look like a generic template, so the look depends on a custom token set and a dark console that are not designed yet. The persona library is seeded at 50+ personas, well short of the roughly 150 scale the other proposals target for every sales job, so the library criterion meets the standard only narrowly.

reviews.yes_case: Expressive Coaching Studio is a whole-app Material 3 system built on MUI. Desktop gets a navigation rail (Practice, Library, Progress, Team), mobile gets a bottom bar, and the avatar menu holds model and voice settings. The call screen re-tints to each persona's temperament through Material Color Utilities, so the caller's mood shows up as colour across the whole screen, and a shader orb reacts to agent audio. In the live call a coach column springs cues into place: one objection alert, a next-best question, talk-track steps and one-line whispers. Seven rubric meters run live with a provisional badge, and each cue links to the transcript line that triggered it. The debrief is summary-first, with a live-versus-final sparkline and every debrief kept in history. The library folds today's scenario editor into 120+ YAML persona packs grouped by sales job, filtered by role, industry, difficulty, objection type and temperament, with filter state shared in the URL. The AI wizard takes a job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP or a pasted call and drafts a persona, scenario, talk track and rubric, each traced to its source line, then runs a 60-second test drive before saving locally or opening a GitHub PR. OpenAI is a visible product feature: Realtime as a voice option, chat models writing coach cues, grading and persona drafts, and per-session cost shown in the UI. Against today's app, a chat window with no feedback, a three-item dropdown and four flat numbers become a coached, scored, browsable cockpit with a distinctive visual identity.
reviews.no_case: MUI v7 does not ship Material 3 Expressive shapes or spring motion, which the proposal admits, so the expressive layer is custom work that can drift into noise. A tinted call screen, springing cues, morphing buttons and a shader orb all moving at once is a lot for a rep who is trying to listen to a caller. The Material look is familiar, and familiar Google styling is not automatically cutting edge. The rewrite is XL, touches every screen, drops Tailwind and lucide, and is a large phased lift for a small open-source maintainer. The 120-persona library is content work the proposal itself says is larger than the UI work. Per-turn coaching and seven live meters add model cost and latency on every turn, and the 2-second cue target is aspirational on a voice call.

reviews.yes_case: Mantine Coaching Console is a dark, fixed live console set against light working screens, all on one complete kit: Mantine v8 AppShell, Stepper, Spotlight, charts, Dropzone, notifications and forms. The whole app reads as one serious tool. Ctrl or Cmd+K opens Spotlight across personas, past debriefs and actions, including 'Build persona from this JD'. The live call shows a dual-channel waveform (rep and persona in separate colours), a talk-track Stepper that ticks as steps are detected, an amber whisper strip that fades in above the composer without blocking typing, and live rubric rows with provisional bars, delta arrows and evidence chips that jump to the transcript line that moved them. Scores stay dimmed until two consecutive turns agree, so the rep is not chased by noise. The debrief reuses the same rows, so live and final numbers match. The library groups personas by sales job with a facet rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection, channel, length) and counts, and the wizard tags each drafted field with the source sentence it came from. The proposal also gives a model stack panel naming the model for each job, with token and cost chips per session. Against today's app, a chat window that gives no feedback and a three-item dropdown become a coaching rail, a live rubric and a faceted library.
reviews.no_case: Mantine's defaults look generic, and the proposal admits that only a custom token set and a fixed dark console keep it from repeating the template problem. That rescue depends on design discipline the repo may not sustain. The persona library is seeded at 50+ personas in Phase 3, well short of the 120 to 150 that the brief's 'large, browsable' library implies, and the proposal's own E self-score of 5.2 barely clears baseline. Rewriting nine screens behind flags, with Tailwind dropped last, is a long fork risk. Per-turn grading with gpt-4.1-mini adds cost and latency to a call that is supposed to feel live, and the two-consecutive-turns rule means scores can lag what the rep just did. A fixed dark console next to light working screens means two visual systems must both pass contrast and reduced-motion checks.

reviews.yes_case: Friendly Coach Studio is a warm, rounded, motion-led training studio. A violet whisper card springs in from a coach rail on the live call, and one tap uses its line. A library card morphs into the persona header through a shared-element transition, and rubric rings tick mint only when the rep earns evidence, so progress can be felt during the call. The debrief has a replay scrubber where each scored moment lights up in the transcript, plus 'Drill this moment', which replays the turn that cost points. The library covers about 150 personas across 16+ sales jobs, with a filter rail, illustrated tiles, and a preview drawer showing transcript and rubric. The wizard drafts from five source types, streams fields into editable cards with per-field regenerate, runs a 60-second dry run, and then saves or exports a PR-ready pack. OpenAI is named on the landing page and in each session footer, with a token and cost meter. Against today's app, a cool blue-on-slate template with a blurry orb and a dropdown becomes a warm, guided practice space with coaching you can act on.
reviews.no_case: Warm paper, rounded shapes and a soft consumer look read as 'every AI SaaS', which the proposal admits, and that is the opposite of the serious, cutting-edge feel the brief asks for. HeroUI v3 is new, its API may churn, and the Tailwind v4 migration in Phase 0 could stall before any user-facing value ships. The wizard does not show source provenance for drafted fields, so the 'where did this come from' trust gap stays open. The one-whisper-per-20-seconds ceiling can hold back an objection alert the rep needs right now. Only about 60 personas are reviewed at launch, and the rest are labelled community drafts, so the library's quality varies.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Desk is a dark-first cockpit that reads as a serious AI product rather than a template. The debrief opens with one Instrument Serif verdict line over a score ring, a goal chip, and a Replay weakest moment button. Each rubric row expands into evidence quotes that jump to transcript timestamps, and a radar compares this attempt with the last one. The live call has a persona audio-level ring, a speaker-labelled transcript and a coach rail with one amber whisper at a time, each showing its evidence quote and a Why? link into the rubric line. The rubric meter fills as the rep speaks, and every tick links to the quote behind it. Live numbers are labelled as tracking ranges, not grades, and the final grade reruns the full evidence-backed grader, so the debrief never contradicts the live view. Model chips on each stage (caller, coach, grader, wizard) show model ID, latency and cost per call, which makes OpenAI usage visible and auditable, exactly what a fund reviewer checks. The library is a faceted catalogue of 150+ reviewed persona files, and the wizard drafts persona, scenario and rubric with provenance chips such as 'from product page, para 2'. Nothing saves until the rep approves. Against today's app, a chat with no feedback becomes a coaching cockpit, and a three-item select becomes a browsable, forkable library.
reviews.no_case: This has the heaviest migration in the set: Tailwind, the globals.css component classes and every component move to Panda recipes and Ark behaviour, and the copy-in Park model makes the repo own a large body of UI source. The proposal itself says the two styling systems must not coexist for long. Panda CSS and Ark have smaller contributor ecosystems than Tailwind or MUI. Coaching falls back to after-turn cues whenever the 2-second target is missed, so the live promise is conditional. The proposal's own council scores put D at 5.3 and E at 5.4, and only if the coach channel and 150 reviewed personas actually ship. The 'look collapse' risk is real: a dark SaaS skin with cards and chips can still read as generic, and only three real reps testing it would prove otherwise.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is the most accessible and internationalised of the five. It is a calm, keyboard-first cockpit built on React Aria Components, with a 64px top bar, a bottom tab bar on phones, a dark call mode, and a Cmd or Ctrl+K command bar. Every score reads as a word, a meter and a quote rather than colour alone. Coaching cues go to a polite live region and never steal focus, with Full, Captions and Off modes. The live call uses a three-column layout with a tabbed coach panel (Cues, Talk track, Live score) and a Jump to latest control. The debrief starts with a text summary and a grader chip ('Graded by gpt-4.1-mini' or a heuristic fallback notice), and it is collapsible by criterion with quotes that link to the transcript line. Persona language is separate from UI language, so one pack serves an English-speaking rep practising against a Spanish-speaking buyer. The library has a RAC tree, TagGroup filters, shareable URLs, and a wizard that tags AI-drafted fields and requires human confirmation of each one. It beats today's app on what training buyers and public-sector or BPO customers audit: skip link, forced-colors support, 14px minimum text, CI axe gates and seven launch locales, while keeping Tailwind 3 and the Prisma data model, so migration risk is low.
reviews.no_case: The look is calm and enterprise-neutral by its own description, which is the opposite of the cutting-edge AI feel the brief asks for, and the dark call mode is the only visual edge. It keeps Inter, Sora and Tailwind 3, so the redesign is a well-run reskin on a familiar base rather than a new system. Seven locales with Arabic and Hebrew RTL is a large scope for an open-source project, and LLM-drafted non-English personas need native-speaker review per locale. Coaching is quieter by design, with one-glance cues rather than whispered prompts, so it may under-deliver on the live coaching the brief asks for. The OpenAI showcase is less visible in the product than in P14 or P17, and the proposal's own D and E self-scores of 5.3 and 5.2 barely clear baseline.

reviews.yes_case: Mantine Coaching Console rebuilds all nine screens on one kit, Mantine v8: AppShell for navigation, Stepper for the wizard and talk track, Tabs and Accordion for the debrief, RingProgress for the grade, Drawer for previews, Dropzone and Notifications for uploads and toasts, and @mantine/charts for the radar and trends. Spotlight is the Ctrl+K bar across personas, scenarios, past debriefs and actions such as 'Build persona from this JD', replacing today's three-item dropdown. The live call is a fixed dark three-zone console: a left panel with a dual-channel waveform (rep in indigo, persona in teal) and a Geist Mono timer; a centre transcript with turn numbers and objection alerts pinned on top; and a right rail with one amber whisper cue, a talk-track stepper that ticks as steps are detected, and live rubric rows with provisional bars, delta arrows and evidence chips that jump to the transcript line that moved them. The debrief leads with a large grade ring, a goal chip and one 'coach's one fix' sentence, then a criteria radar, then quote-linked accordions with 'Re-run weakest criterion' as the main action. The progress dashboard and a team view use the same kit, so the manager surface the data model already supports finally appears. The wizard has four steps (Source, Persona, Scenario, Dry run), takes a job description, product URL, CRM notes, an ICP or a pasted call, keeps the zod contracts the repo already uses, and exports a persona file for a pull request. A Model stack panel names the OpenAI model behind each feature and shows cost per session. The main advantage is delivery: one documented kit with native components for nearly every screen, and a phased migration that removes Tailwind last.
reviews.no_case: Mantine defaults are a recognisable component look, and the proposal concedes they read as a generic template. The look only holds if the custom token set and dark console are finished, which is the part a volunteer team is most likely to cut short. The persona library is the thinnest content commitment in the set: phase three seeds 50-plus personas, which falls short of the large, browsable library the brief asks for, and the proposal's own needs-fit scores (D 5.6, E 5.2) sit at or barely above baseline. Live grading is a per-turn model call under a token budget with a keyword-heuristic fallback, so the live rubric can be weaker than the debrief on a bad night, and the design only shows a notice when that happens. The OpenAI and Codex story is present but generic (a models panel and cost chips), and the contributor path leans on a wizard export rather than on a concrete Codex workflow such as PR review or release automation. A reviewer looking for a striking, cutting-edge first impression will see a competent dashboard kit, not a new look.

reviews.yes_case: Friendly Coach Studio is a full re-skin and re-structure of the trainer into a warm, rounded, motion-led studio on HeroUI v3 and Tailwind v4, with Motion for choreography and Bricolage Grotesque, Inter and Geist Mono for type. All nine screens share one token set on a warm paper canvas, with a violet 'Coach Violet' accent reserved for AI-sourced elements, so it stops looking like a default blue SaaS template. On the live call the rep sees three separate lanes: the persona (voice or text) who never sees coaching, a coach rail of violet whisper cards capped at one every 20 seconds and 12 words each, and a rubric column of five criteria shown as mint, amber or coral rings that tick as evidence lands. Each whisper has a one-tap 'Use this line' and a 'why' link to the transcript turn, and live estimates reconcile with the debrief because both use one rubric. The debrief adds a replay scrubber with a marker per scoring event and a 'Drill this moment' loop that replays the 60 seconds that cost points. The library is the biggest content commitment of the five: about 150 personas across 16-plus sales jobs, each a plain JSON or YAML file with two or three scenarios, filterable by job, industry, difficulty, objection and source (built-in, community, yours). A library card morphs into the persona header of the live call through a shared-element transition. The four-step AI wizard takes five source types, streams a draft into editable fields, proposes a weighted rubric that must total 100, runs a 60-second dry run, and exports a PR-ready pack. Against today's app, which has a three-item dropdown and a chat screen with no feedback, this is a whole product: a coaching cockpit, a browsable catalogue, a creation path and a manager surface. The OpenAI story is visible: gpt-realtime as a voice option, gpt-4.1-mini for coaching and grading, a cost meter on each session, a 'Generated with GPT' badge on drafts, a 'Build a pack with Codex' button, and a Codex review checklist on pack pull requests. That is a credible route to a Codex open source fund application.
reviews.no_case: Soft, rounded, friendly polish is the look of a lot of AI SaaS, so the cutting-edge claim rests on motion and copy more than on a distinctive system. The stack is the riskiest in the set. HeroUI v3 is new, has dropped its framer-motion layer, and needs a Tailwind v4 migration first, and a one-week Phase 0 for that is optimistic. Adding HeroUI, Motion, cmdk, Recharts, react-three-fiber and a Tailwind v4 move at once puts many moving parts into a volunteer-maintained repo. The 150-persona target is a content project of its own; the plan ships about 60 reviewed and labels the rest community draft, so most of the library will be drafts on day one. The sub-1.5-second grader and coach latency target is tight for a per-turn model call, and the whisper rhythm depends on hitting it. The warm, friendly tone may read as too light for enterprise sales managers who want a serious scoring tool, and the 'friendly' brand is the first thing a skeptical reviewer will call generic.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Desk has the most editorial and most distinctive look of the five. It is dark-first: a near-black canvas with surface steps, a teal signal colour for live state and primary actions, amber for cues, and one red End and grade button. It uses Geist for UI and Geist Mono for timers, scores and model IDs, and sets only the debrief verdict line in Instrument Serif. It drops the blurry orb for a 2D canvas audio-level ring that shows real mic and caller levels, and takes three.js out of the app shell. The system is Ark UI for accessible behaviour, Panda CSS for typed semantic tokens with a dark condition, and Park UI-style copy-in components in src/components/ui, so contributors read and PR the source rather than patch a package. On the live call, a coach model runs after each finished turn and returns at most one cue every 20 seconds, an objection tag, talk-track progress and rubric deltas, each tied to a verbatim quote, with the cue visible within about 2 seconds and a fallback to after-turn cues if slower. The meter shows tracking ranges rather than grades, and the final grade reruns the full evidence grader, so the debrief never contradicts the live view. The debrief is a scannable scorecard: each criterion expands to evidence quotes that jump to the transcript timestamp, with a radar against the previous attempt, and a 'Heuristic estimate' trust badge replaces the old fallback warning. The library covers 150-plus personas on a clear taxonomy of role, industry, difficulty and objection type, each a versioned, reviewed file. The wizard turns a URL or description into persona, scenario and rubric drafts with provenance chips such as 'from product page, para 2' before a dry run, and nothing saves until the rep approves. For OpenAI, model chips sit on every stage (Caller, Coach, Grader, Wizard) with model ID, latency and cost per call, Realtime is a first-class voice option, and a human-labelled grader eval lives in a Trust panel. That is a strong fit for the fund's visibility criterion.
reviews.no_case: This is the heaviest migration on the list. Panda CSS, Ark UI and copy-in Park components mean rewriting every Tailwind component and the globals.css classes, and the proposal says the two styling systems should not coexist for long, which is hard to hold while a shim covers untouched routes. Contributor friendliness suffers: Panda recipes and Ark's headless patterns are less familiar than shadcn or Mantine, and copy-in source only helps once a contributor learns the token system. The live coach is an every-turn model call that the proposal's own risk list says multiplies cost, and cues slower than about 2 seconds 'feel wrong', so the feel depends on a latency the design cannot guarantee. Its needs-fit scores are conditional (D 5.3 and E 5.4) on the coach channel and a reviewed library shipping, so at the spec as written both sit at baseline, not above it. The commercial case is the weakest on the SaaS side (F1 5.5 by its own count). A dark-first look with serif verdicts also risks reading as a design showcase rather than a tool a rep opens twenty times a week.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is a calm, keyboard-first call cockpit built on React Aria Components, Adobe's accessibility and internationalisation layer, styled with Tailwind 3 through data-attribute states and a single focus-ring rule. Its defining strength is that it is the most accessible and most localisable product in the set: seven UI locales through next-intl with ICU catalogues, RTL support, and locale-aware dates, timers and rubric weights through @internationalized. Arabic, Hebrew and CJK fonts load only for the locales that need them. Persona language is kept separate from UI locale, so an English-speaking rep can practise against a Spanish-speaking homeowner, with persona packs launching in en-US and es-US. The live call is three columns: a transcript on the left, a 380px coach panel with Cues, Talk track and Live score tabs on the right, and a bottom dock with text input, mute and End and grade behind a Ctrl or Cmd+Enter confirm. Cues are one-glance lines of 12 words or fewer in a polite live region that never moves focus, with Full, Captions and Off modes and per-criterion mute. Only compliance warnings use role=alert. Live meters update at turn boundaries with text values and trend arrows, and reuse the debrief rubric so the two score views compare directly. The debrief is a scannable summary with collapsible criteria, evidence that links to the exact transcript line, and the old yellow fallback banner becomes a labelled chip. Every chart has a table alternative, and CI gates on axe, forced-colors and reduced-motion projects. The five-step wizard requires a human to confirm each AI-drafted field, marked with a source chip and an AI draft badge, and exports a pack that opens a prefilled PR. It keeps Tailwind 3, the Prisma model and the API routes, which makes it the lowest-risk migration in the set.
reviews.no_case: Cadence is the most conservative look of the five, and the proposal says so: it chose not to adopt Spectrum's style system and added a dark call mode because pure calm reads as enterprise-generic. What results is a clean, accessible enterprise app that could be any B2B tool, which falls short of the brief's 'modern, sleek, cutting edge' and 'unique' criteria. Keeping Tailwind 3 and hand-built styling means the new system is mostly a behaviour layer and token set, not a visual step change. Its own council self-scores put UX and uniqueness at 7, and its needs-fit scores (D 5.3, E 5.2) sit at baseline. The 120-persona launch target is ambitious for a 12-job, 12-industry launch, and each non-English locale needs native-speaker review that the plan leaves to later. The Codex fund angle is the thinnest: Codex appears as 'planned Codex-assisted PR review' and CONTRIBUTING notes, with no concrete action of the kind the program funds. Accessibility is a real strength, but neither the brief's OpenAI-usage criterion nor the fund rewards it directly.

reviews.yes_case: Live Coach Studio turns the trainer into a call cockpit on one shadcn/ui system: Radix primitives copied into the repo, Tremor-style KPI, BarList and Tracker blocks restyled on the same tokens, Recharts for trends, and motion for the cue entrance. At desktop width the live call has three lanes. The transcript on the left puts a criterion dot on each rep line once evidence is found. The centre coach rail shows one amber cue at a time: the next best question, an objection alert with its trigger quote, and a six-segment talk-track progress bar. The right rubric column shows five criteria with hatched provisional fills that turn solid only when a transcript quote confirms them. The rule that makes it trustworthy is that live scores use the same grader prompt as the debrief, so the two differ only in whether a quote is confirmed, and the coach never touches the persona's channel. The debrief adds a call timeline strip with one tick per turn coloured by criterion, clickable to replay that moment, and every number sits one click from its transcript line. Managers get a calibration chart that sets the AI score against the manager score for each call, plus flags and a coaching queue, which the app does not show today. The persona library is YAML under /personas, validated by the same zod schema the wizard uses, so a contributor's file and an AI draft have an identical shape. It launches with 120 personas across 15 sales jobs, 40 reviewed and the rest marked Draft, with facets for job, industry, difficulty, call type and objection. The four-step wizard (Source, Draft, Shape, Dry run) traces each drafted field to the sentence it came from, and a violet provenance chip shows model, latency and token count. For the Codex fund it has the most concrete contributor path in the set: AGENTS.md, a 'Contribute a persona' button that opens a prefilled YAML PR, a Codex-powered PR review action that checks persona files against the schema, and Codex-drafted release notes. Those map directly onto the program's PR-review and release-workflow criteria, and the proposal correctly says to confirm the terms before applying.
reviews.no_case: The look is the weak point. shadcn/ui is the most common component kit in new React apps, and the proposal admits that without a distinct chart and cue language the app reads as another default template. The palette is a blue primary on a near-neutral canvas, close to today's blue-on-slate look with a new coat, so many users will feel this as cleanup rather than a new product. The proposal calls shadcn the system of record but leans on Tremor patterns, so two chart idioms have to be kept consistent. Tailwind 3.4 stays for phase one, so the styling engine is not modernised. The library is thin at launch: 40 of 120 personas are reviewed, so most of the catalogue ships as drafts, and the wizard's review checklist is not resourced. Live scoring has not been checked against human raters, the proposal says so, and the cue target of under 2 seconds after the rep stops speaking adds a per-turn GPT call to every session. On look it is the least adventurous of the leading three (its own self-score is 7.5), so a reviewer who wants a cutting-edge first impression will not get one from this design.

reviews.yes_case: Live Coach Studio is a whole-app system on one shadcn/ui base: a collapsible sidebar with Cmd+K, one token set, and Geist with tabular Geist Mono so timers and scores do not jitter. The practice call is a cockpit. The persona speaks, a single amber cue rail offers the next question or an objection alert with its trigger quote printed beneath, a six-segment talk-track bar advances, and the rubric fills in as provisional until a transcript quote confirms each criterion. Every debrief score links to the exact transcript line, and the footer names the grading model, turn count and latency. The persona library is a faceted rail covering all 15 sales jobs, with difficulty, call type and objection filters and a live result count. The AI wizard runs Source, Draft, Shape and Dry run, and each drafted field is traced to its source sentence. Analytics sit where a manager needs them: Tremor-style KPI, BarList and Tracker blocks on Progress and Team, plus a calibration chart of AI score against manager score. It beats today's app because the live call stops being a chat window and the debrief stops being one long scroll. It is also the most buildable plan of the five. It defers the Tailwind 4 move, keeps every existing route, and reuses the zod schema the repo already has for persona files and AI output. The fund story is concrete: a Codex-powered PR review action, release notes drafted with Codex, AGENTS.md, and visible GPT-4.1-mini attribution on every debrief.
reviews.no_case: shadcn is now the most common default in React, and the proposal admits the look may drift into another template. Stacking Tremor-style analytics on top adds a lot of dashboard surface to a training product, which can make it feel like a BI tool rather than a practice room. The cutting-edge signal is modest: beyond the amber rail there is no distinctive motion or cue language. Cue latency and cue quality are unproven, and a 120-persona library with only 40 reviewed is a heavy content lift.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Call Studio is the most visibly cutting-edge option. The landing page sits on a full-bleed dark Aurora background with an Animated Beam diagram that draws voice, live coach and rubric as one moving path, so the product explains its mechanism on the first screen. The live call is a three-zone cockpit: a rubric ring that tweens as criteria land, a Tracing Beam talk-track rail that lights steps as they are covered, a persona orb that reacts to speech, and a transcript that highlights the words counting toward each criterion. The coach rail holds dismissible cue cards labelled Next question, Objection, Pricing, Talk track or Pace, and the persona never hears the coach. The debrief is a navigable replay timeline with markers for coach cues, objections and score jumps, where a click plays that moment back. The library is a Bento Grid of persona cards with a facet rail and cmd-K search, and the wizard uses an Animated Beam to carry source snippets into the draft. Mono chips show the model, latency and grading model on each cue. It beats today's app on first impression and on showing the coaching working. The author also keeps dense rubric tables free of glow and gives motion reduced-motion and low-power fallbacks, which is what keeps it workable.
reviews.no_case: Glow, beams and Aurora backgrounds on dark are now the default look of AI landing pages, so it runs straight into the template problem the author flags. It depends on copy-in Magic UI and Aceternity pieces whose licences are still unverified for an MIT repo. The coach channel that makes the live-call story real does not exist yet, and the author self-scores live coaching at 5.4, the lowest of the five. The 1.5-second cue target is untested, and the Codex PR-review path is deferred to a later CONTRIBUTING note, so the fund story is thinner than the visuals suggest.

reviews.yes_case: Loud Dial Neo-Brutal is the most distinctive proposal here. Every control and card has a 3px ink border and a hard 4px offset shadow, the fills are flat and loud (yellow, pink, mint, blue, orange), and headlines are Archivo uppercase at 88px. It looks nothing like the blue-and-white enterprise look that every competitor in AI roleplay uses. The live call is a stamped scorecard: a yellow whisper cue card tilts and peels off when marked Used, a six-step talk-track rail ticks off, and five criterion bars stamp when evidence lands and stay hatched until a transcript quote confirms them. A talk-ratio meter and a coach latency chip sit beside them. The persona library reads like a deck of trading cards, with an industry colour block, difficulty stamps (Easy, Hard, Brutal), objection badges and grouped sections with counts. The six-step wizard is a split pane where the persona card fills field by field with a yellow flash. The debrief opens with a grade tile and a rotated score stamp, and each 'Replay this line' chip jumps to and flashes the matching transcript line. A paper reading mode keeps long transcripts legible. It beats today's app by making practice feel like a game with stakes. The model chips on each cue and score, the Built with Codex footer and the Reviewed with Codex badge make the OpenAI and Codex story visible without a footnote.
reviews.no_case: Neo-brutalism is loud and chunky, not sleek. An enterprise buyer may read it as playful or consumer-grade, and a sales manager may find it toy-like. Hard shadows and ink borders on every element add visual noise, which the proposal itself admits hurts long debriefs. It scores weakest of the five on modern and cutting edge, because the look signals playfulness rather than AI sophistication. The loud fills with ink text still need the contrast audit the author has not yet run.

reviews.yes_case: Editorial Ledger is a whole-app system built on one idea: paper, ink, hairline rules, a single signal red, a serif display voice (Newsreader) over Inter and JetBrains Mono for data. Cards and shadows go, so the app reads like a well-set magazine or a ledger. Each screen has a clear job. The landing page pairs a headline with a real annotated transcript excerpt and a numbered feature ledger. The library has a 240px facet rail, removable filter chips and a result count. The pre-call briefing reads like a document, with a numbered talk-track checklist and a sticky start sheet. The live call is a night-theme room: a talk-track ledger, the transcript as one column of turns, and coach notes pinned in the margin to the exact line that caused them. The debrief is a two-level report with a large serif score, goal status as one plain sentence, strengths and gaps linked to transcript lines, and a criteria ledger whose verbatim quotes sit one tap down. The wizard shows a source snippet for every generated field, requires rubric weights to total 100, runs a dry run, and ends in Save or Export as PR. The colophon names the OpenAI models on each screen, and the plan includes AGENTS.md and Codex review of persona PRs. It beats today's blue-on-white SaaS default by being calmer, more legible and more distinct. It is also the most incremental migration of the five, so it can ship screen by screen behind flags.
reviews.no_case: Restraint can read as austere. A serif-led, Swiss look may feel like a publishing tool rather than an AI product, and it has little motion to signal live intelligence, which weakens the cutting-edge brief.
