The author's own self-score for the persona library (5.5) is the lowest of the five, and the 200-persona target is still a real content lift. Base UI's maturity for complex comboboxes and multi-select is unproven, and the proposal itself names a React Aria fallback as a possible cost.

reviews.yes_case: Switchboard Console is a complete and distinct redesign. The live stage is a dark phosphor console and the debrief, library and dashboard are a light paper mode, with IBM Plex Mono for timers, scores and labels. Nothing else in AI roleplay looks like it. An oscilloscope replaces the blurry orb, the transcript is a teleprinter with CALLER and YOU tags, and a six-jack talk-track patch panel lights each step as it is hit. The amber whisper ticker types each cue (OBJECTION, ASK, NEXT STEP, TIME), allows one cue per 20 seconds, and stays silent when confidence is low, so the rep is not flooded. The five rubric LEDs are labelled 'live estimate, unverified' and show their evidence on hover, and the debrief reuses the same evidence objects, so the cue, the live LED and the final quote share one trail. The library is a faceted, cmdk-searchable board of 300 seeded persona JSON files across more than 30 jobs, with difficulty LEDs and Built-in, Community and Mine badges. The wizard is conversational, with numbered question cards answered by keys 1 to 4, a streaming build log, a live persona card, a rubric that must total 100 percent, a two-minute test call and Export as PR. It beats today's app on personality and on clarity about what the model is doing. The model switchboard tray names the OpenAI model behind voice, coaching, grading and the wizard, with cost per call, which is the most direct way to show a Codex fund reviewer what the project uses.
reviews.no_case: The retro terminal look is a niche bet. Scanlines and glow on the live stage can hurt legibility and can read as cosplay to a sales manager buying a training tool. The switchboard vocabulary (jacks, patch, board) asks users to learn metaphors before they can use the app. Phase 1 packs a Tailwind 3 to 4 migration, a shadcn Base UI move, new fonts and a shell rebuild into one or two weeks, which is optimistic, and it leans on a third-party claim about Base UI being the shadcn default. The 300-persona target is the largest content promise of the five and would look padded if the entries are thin.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: Film Room Sideline treats every practice, live and debrief call as game film on one scrubbable timeline. Look: a calm light canvas (#F6F7F9) for home, library, progress and team, and a film-dark stage (#0B0F14 family) for the live call and debrief. Teal (#5EEAD4) marks the playhead and good scores, amber marks whisper cues. Sora, Inter and JetBrains Mono type, 14px cards, hairlines instead of soft shadows, Lucide icons plus six custom moment-tag glyphs. How it works: a top bar with Practice, Library, Calls, Progress and Team (Team only when an org exists), a Cmd-K palette and one New call button. Library is a filterable catalogue (Job, Industry, Difficulty, Objection type, each with counts) of 150+ forkable personas. Each card shows objection chips, difficulty dots and the user's best score, and a sheet shows the opening line, behaviour, rubric preview and a Practice button. The live call puts a timeline strip across the top with persona and rep turns as coloured blocks and tags appearing as moments happen, a transcript with inline tag pills, and a 320px sideline HUD with six tweening rubric meters, a talk-track checklist, one amber whisper card at a time (20-second minimum gap, Esc to dismiss, never sent to the persona), an objection alert chip and two suggested replies. The debrief is the same film strip with green, amber and rose tags. Each tag opens the transcript line, quote and coach note, so every score points to a timestamp. Why it beats today: the chat screen with no feedback, the three-item dropdown and the long vertical debrief are replaced by one spine. OpenAI Fund fit (the strongest in this set): a model strip names the Realtime voice model, the coach model and the grader model, with a per-call token and dollar cost. The repo's CI runs Codex CLI to review persona-pack PRs for schema, bias and rubric weights, maintainer automation drafts release notes, and a Contribute page shows those checks as badges on merged personas. That maps directly onto the Codex for Open Source uses of PR review, maintainer automation and release workflows, and the wizard's Export as PR file gives contributors a concrete path in. The calm neutral palette deliberately avoids a sports-app look that insurance and mortgage reps would reject, and PII is stripped from pasted calls before any model call, which a serious open-source product needs.
reviews.no_case: The timeline-as-spine concept borrows Hudl's sports metaphor, which the author admits can read as sports-coded to the reps who buy this, and the calm palette is an unverified mitigation. The live HUD's six-meter scoring and whisper cadence are unproven until a recorded-call harness exists (self-scored D 6). The 150-persona launch is a content job that ships about 40 first, the industry facet omits real estate, which the brief names, and the L-effort Tailwind 4 migration touches every screen.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: Roster Arena makes the persona library the front door, styled as a dark roster-select screen where every buyer is a character card. Look: a dark canvas (#0A0E14) with #121923 surfaces, teal signal (#2DD4BF) for the rep's turn and primary actions, amber coach cues, green hit and rose miss states, Sora headings, Inter body, Geist Mono for stats, timers and model costs, 14px card radius, 1px hairlines, and stylized illustrated busts with a difficulty-tinted rim instead of photos. Light mode uses the same tokens. How it works: Roster is the first nav item. The library shows 3:4 cards, four across at desktop, each with a bust, role line, industry chip, four stat bars drawn as 10-segment pips (skepticism, time pressure, talkativeness, objection load), difficulty pips and a voice preview. Filters cover role, industry, difficulty, objection type, mode and voice accent. A click opens a 480px drawer with the brief, opening line, objections, rubric weights and Practice. Pre-call is a two-column briefing that states what gets scored and what the buyer will push on. The live call is three columns: a portrait with a live waveform and timer on the left, a transcript with green and amber criterion markers in the centre, and a coach rail on the right with five live rubric meters and one whisper card at a time that cites its transcript line and fades after 8 seconds. The persona never voices coaching, and Certification mode hides the coach while recording identical scores. The debrief is a match-result layout with a 900ms score ring, five criterion stat lines and quotes that scrub the timeline. Progress has explicit unlock rules tied to real criteria, such as 70 or more on the skeptical CFO twice to unlock Hard. Why it beats today: the three-item dropdown and blurry orb become a catalogue of 150 personas across 20 sales jobs, and live coaching appears where there is none. The coaching spec is the most rigorous in the set: at most one whisper per 20 seconds, never mid-sentence, every whisper cited, a 2-second latency target and a restraint benchmark shipped in the repo. The wizard has five steps with a source citation on every trait, PII redaction before a pasted call reaches a model, and Export as PR writes persona JSON. Folder-per-job JSON means contributors edit data, not code. For OpenAI Fund purposes it shows a Models in this call strip with each model's role and cost, makes OpenAI Realtime a first-class voice provider, and reserves a Built with Codex footer for when Codex really runs PR review. It is the most distinctive proposal here and the one most likely to stand out in a crowded field.
reviews.no_case: Game hero-select framing is the biggest threat to the brief's serious, modern bar. Stat bars, pips and portrait busts read as a toy to call-centre, insurance and enterprise buyers, which hurts the F2 licensing story and the Codex reviewer's first impression. The author's own self-scores are barely above baseline (D 5.3, E 5.2), the 150-persona library is XL content work, and the Codex PR-review story depends on Codex actually running in the repo.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: Expressive Coaching Studio is a Material 3 Expressive redesign on MUI v7 in which each persona's temperament seeds the colour of the whole call screen. Look: M3 tonal palettes generated from seed colours with Google's Material Color Utilities (friendly teal, skeptical amber, hostile red), a light default with a dark mode (#0D1424 surface, #B3C5FF primary), 28px corners on hero and persona cards, full-pill buttons and chips, tonal surface steps instead of drop shadows, Roboto Flex with the width axis for expressive headlines, and Material Symbols Rounded with fill on active states. Motion springs handle taps, cue entrance and chip reflow, and the Start button morphs from pill to a rounded square on press. How it works: a desktop M3 navigation rail with Practice, Library, Progress and Team, an avatar menu for settings, voice and model configuration, and a mobile bottom bar. Practice is three steps (Briefing, Live call, Debrief) and every debrief stays in history. The live call has three columns: a shader orb driven by agent audio with interest and trust meters, a transcript with speaker-tinted bubbles and inline coach markers, and a coach column where at most three cues stack and fade, with an objection alert chip, a next-best question, a talk-track stepper whose current step pulses, and seven rubric meters labelled provisional. The debrief is the standout: a wavy score ring that morphs from provisional to final, and a sparkline of live scores against final scores with markers where coach cues fired, so the rep can see how the call moved and whether coaching helped. Coaching runs on its own channel the persona never sees, with coach levels Off, Subtle and Whisper, a 2-second cue target, a keyword fallback and a visible coaching-paused line instead of silent failure. Why it beats today: the blue-on-slate hero and generic feature cards become a tonal hero with a visible OpenAI model strip, and the chat app becomes a coached call. OpenAI: the Realtime voice option, coach model, grader and wizard are each named in the header with per-session cost, and the wizard traces each generated element to its source line. MUI is the component base most open-source contributors already know, and persona packs are YAML grouped by sales job with URL-shareable filters, which suits a 120-persona library. It is the most visually novel option here and the only one that makes the persona's emotional state a visible design token.
reviews.no_case: The expressive layer is custom work on top of MUI that the author admits is unverified, so springs and shape morphs can drift into visual noise. Tinting a whole call screen by persona risks contrast failures and fatigue for reps on long calls. It is an XL rewrite that drops Tailwind for MUI, the proposal gives no self-scores, the wizard has no PII handling for pasted calls, and the Codex PR-review workflow is only planned.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: Friendly Coach Studio is a warm, rounded, motion-led redesign on HeroUI v3 with Tailwind v4 and a separate Motion package for choreography. Look: a warm paper canvas (#F6F4F0), white 20px cards, pill chips and toggles, a violet Coach accent (#5B4BFF) reserved for primary calls to action and AI-sourced elements, Bricolage Grotesque headings, Inter body text, Geist Mono for timers and scores, and a dark theme that ships in v1. Persona avatars are gradient industry glyph tiles, not photos. How it works: a slim left rail with Practice, Library, Progress, Team and Settings, a Cmd+K palette, a persistent Create persona button, and a mobile bottom tab bar that hides during calls. The landing page has a live animated call mock with a violet whisper and a rubric ring ticking from 58 to 64, a model strip naming gpt-realtime, gpt-4.1-mini and ElevenLabs, and three contributor cards (Add a persona, Build a pack with Codex, Self-host with Docker). The library has a filter rail for sales job, industry, difficulty, objection type and source (built-in, community, yours), a 3-up card grid, and tabs for Personas, Scenarios, Rubrics and Community. The pre-call brief is a readable card with three things the persona cares about, the goal as a success checklist and a six-stage talk track, plus a sticky start panel with Voice or Text, coach intensity (Quiet, Balanced, Chatty) and a large Start button. The live call has rubric rings for five criteria on the left, the persona and transcript in the centre, and a glass coach rail on the right where violet whisper cards of 12 words or fewer slide in with a one-tap Use this line and a why link to the transcript turn. Persona and coach lanes stay separate, and grader deltas arrive within about 1.5 seconds, labelled live estimate. The debrief has a replay scrubber and a Drill this moment action that replays the 60 seconds that cost points. Why it beats today: a dropdown becomes a 150-persona library across 16 sales jobs, and a chat screen becomes a coaching cockpit. OpenAI and Codex: each session footer shows models used with token and cost meters, Build a pack with Codex opens a pre-filled Codex task, pack PRs run a Codex review checklist, and a contributor wall shows merged-pack counts. The friendly tone suits sales reps, who are the actual end users. Its coaching limits (one whisper per 20 seconds, 12 words, 1.5-second grader) are measurable.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive of the serious options. Its own risk list concedes that soft HeroUI defaults look like every AI SaaS, and the coach rail and palette are its main differentiators. HeroUI v3 is new, with API churn risk and a motion layer the team must rebuild. The Codex PR-review story is described as a checklist rather than a specified CI job, pasted calls get no PII step, and the 150-persona launch is still a content job the author would cut to about 60 reviewed.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: Mantine Coaching Console is a Mantine v8 command console applied across all nine screens, with a fixed dark live console and light surfaces everywhere else. Look: Geist for UI and display with Geist Mono for timers and scores, a light canvas (#F6F7FB) for library, briefing, debrief, dashboard and team, and a fixed dark live console (#0B1020 canvas, #131A2E surfaces) with indigo rep actions, a teal persona channel, amber whisper cues and rose alerts. Radii are 10px on controls and 16px on cards, with pill chips, hairlines instead of shadows except on floating elements, and Tabler icons at 1.5 stroke. How it works: a collapsible AppShell navbar on desktop (Home, Practice, Library, Create persona, Progress, Team, Settings) and a bottom tab bar on mobile. Ctrl or Cmd+K opens Mantine Spotlight across personas, scenarios, debriefs and actions such as Build persona from this JD. The main path is Library card, Pre-call briefing, Live call, Debrief, then a targeted re-run of the weakest criterion. The library has a 260px facet rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel, length, each with counts), grouped sections by sales job with See all links, and a three-column card grid with initials avatars, temperament meters and objection tags. The live call has a dual-channel waveform (rep in indigo, persona in teal), a transcript with objection alerts pinned at the top, a whisper strip of about four seconds above the composer that never blocks typing, a six-step talk-track Stepper, and live rubric rows with provisional bars, delta arrows and evidence chips that jump to the transcript line. Scores stay dimmed until two consecutive turns agree, a sensible anti-jitter rule. The debrief shows a grade ring, a goal chip, a single Coach's one fix card and a radar, with accordions and quote chips. Progress has KPI sparklines, an area chart, a first-five versus last-five radar and readiness bars per sales job. The team view has a roster table, a heatmap and an Approve for live calls switch. Why it beats today: the three-item select becomes a grouped, filterable catalogue with Spotlight search, and the chat screen becomes a coached console. It is the most credible build in the set: one mature kit with forms, charts, notifications, dropzone and command search, zod schemas the repo already uses, and a phased migration with per-route screenshot diffs. A Model stack panel and per-session cost chips make OpenAI usage visible.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive and least ambitious of the five. The author concedes that Mantine defaults look generic, the persona catalogue is seeded only to 50-plus personas in Phase 3, well short of the large library the brief requires, and the Codex angle is only can draft and review with no concrete workflow, which is the weakest fit for the fund.

reviews.yes_case: Live Coach Studio keeps every existing route (/trainer, /trainer/scenarios, /trainer/debrief/[id], /dashboard) and the Prisma and API layer, then rebuilds the front end on one shadcn/ui system: Radix primitives copied into src/components/ui, Geist and Geist Mono type, a warm-neutral light canvas, and an ink-dark live call that defaults on. Tremor-style KPI, BarList and Tracker blocks sit on the same tokens, but only on analytics screens. A collapsible sidebar, a Cmd+K palette and a bottom bar on mobile replace the glass header, and focus mode strips the chrome during a call. The live call has three lanes. The persona orb and transcript sit on the left. The centre coach rail shows one amber cue at a time: a next best question, an objection alert with its trigger quote printed beneath, and a six-segment talk-track bar. The right rubric meter starts each criterion hatched as provisional and turns solid only when a transcript quote confirms it. Cues appear under two seconds after the rep stops speaking, in Silent, Light or Full modes, and the persona never hears the coach. The debrief uses the same grader prompt, so live and final numbers compare directly. Its timeline has one tick per turn, coloured by criterion, and every score is one click from its quote. The manager view adds a calibration chart of AI score against manager score for each call, the strongest trust feature in the set. Personas are YAML files checked by the same zod schema the wizard uses, and the wizard traces each field to its source sentence. The Codex case is the most concrete of the five: AGENTS.md, a Codex-powered PR review action that checks persona files, Codex-drafted release notes, and a Contribute button that opens a Codex CLI prompt. Those map directly to the fund's named PR review, maintainer automation and release workflows, and each debrief footer shows the model, token count and latency. Against today's chat app and blurry orb, it is a coaching cockpit with an audit trail.
reviews.no_case: Its modern and distinctiveness scores rest mostly on the live call, and it has the least motion identity of the top three. Shadcn plus Tremor on one token set is a very common admin-dashboard stack, and the proposal concedes the look could read as another default template. Only 40 of 120 personas are reviewed at launch, which is thin against the 150-plus open-source bar. The Codex fund terms, which the proposal itself says need confirming, are unverified.

reviews.yes_case: Friendly Coach Studio turns the trainer into a warm, rounded, motion-led practice studio built on HeroUI v3 primitives, Motion for choreography, and Tailwind v4 tokens on a warm paper canvas (#F6F4F0) with a violet Coach accent. A slim left rail (Practice, Library, Progress, Team, Settings) and a Cmd+K palette replace the sticky glass header. The live call is three columns. On the left, five rubric rings tint mint only when evidence lands, each showing a live estimate. The persona orb and transcript sit in the middle. A glass coach rail on the right stacks violet whisper cards that slide in on a spring: 12 words or fewer, at most one every 20 seconds, and typed as objection alert, next question, don't-say or talk-track step. Each card has a one-tap 'Use this line' and a 'why' link to the exact transcript turn. The grader target is under 1.5 seconds, with a fallback to turn-end scoring. The library is a 3-up grid of industry glyph tiles with a left filter rail for sales job, industry, difficulty slider, objection type and source (built-in, community, yours). It holds about 150 JSON or YAML personas across 16 jobs, and unreviewed ones carry a 'community draft' label. The AI wizard has four steps: one prompt with five source types (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP, pasted call), a streamed draft into editable field cards with per-field regenerate, weight sliders that must total 100, and a 60-second dry run. It ends in save locally or export a PR-ready pack, with a cost meter in the footer. For the Codex fund, OpenAI is visible throughout: gpt-realtime and gpt-4.1-mini are named on the landing page, each session footer shows models with tokens and cost, Settings allows a model swap, and a 'Build a pack with Codex' button opens a pre-filled task. Against today's three-item dropdown, blank form and blurry orb, it reads as a coaching product with a clear voice.
reviews.no_case: It bets the redesign on a young library. HeroUI v3 is new, has just dropped the motion layer that its signature moments depend on, and Phase 0 needs a Tailwind v4 migration plus a second animation package, so the schedule can slip before any screen ships. Soft rounded defaults are a very common look in AI SaaS, as the proposal itself flags, and friendly-consumer polish reads less serious than the sales-pro tone the owner wants. 150 personas is a large writing load, with only about 60 planned as reviewed at launch.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Desk is a dark-first, source-owned design system: Ark UI for behaviour, Panda CSS semantic tokens with a _dark condition, and Park UI-style copy-in components in src/components/ui that contributors read and PR directly. The canvas is near-black (#0B0E13), with a teal signal accent (#5EEAD4) for live state and primary CTAs, a cue amber (#F5B942) for whisper coaching, and coral for objection alerts. Every status pairs an icon and a word with its colour. Type is Geist for UI, Geist Mono for timers and model IDs, and Instrument Serif only for the single debrief verdict line, an editorial touch no other proposal in this set uses. The shell is a collapsible left rail (Practice, Library, Progress, Team), a Cmd+K combobox over personas, calls and settings, and a five-step wizard whose fields carry provenance chips such as 'from product page, para 2'. The live call has a centre transcript with an audio ring and speaker labels, a right coach rail with one amber cue at a time and a Why? expansion, a rubric meter that shows tracking ranges rather than grades, and an End and grade button behind a confirm dialog. Model chips on every stage show model ID, latency and cost, so OpenAI use is visible and auditable. The debrief is a scorecard: each criterion has a status, a weight and evidence quotes that jump to transcript timestamps, plus a visx radar against your last attempt. The old fallback warning becomes a Heuristic estimate badge. For the Codex fund, AGENTS.md and a Codex-run PR review workflow are part of the design, and a human-labelled gold-debrief eval lives in the repo with a Trust panel, the kind of reproducibility open-source reviewers look for. Against today's glass header, dropdown and blurry orb, it reads as a serious pro tool with a point of view.
reviews.no_case: It is the least familiar stack in the set: Ark UI, Panda CSS and copy-in Park UI. Panda's build-time codegen adds a step for every contributor. The plan removes Tailwind outright, which makes it an XL rewrite of every component, and the proposal concedes the two styling systems should not coexist for long. Its own self-scores put D at 5.3 and E at 5.4, both conditional on work not yet built, so it clears the basic-needs bar only if the coach channel and 150 reviewed personas both ship in full.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Call Studio is the most visibly AI-native design in the set: a dark-first Signal theme on near-black (#05070B), with cyan coach cues, violet persona voice and green model-trace chips, built on shadcn/ui with Magic UI and selective Aceternity pieces. The landing hero has an Aurora background and an Animated Beam drawing a live path from persona voice to live coach to rubric, a Text Generate headline, and a Moving Border 'Try a demo call' button. The library is a Bento Grid with Magic Card spotlight hover. Each card has an industry-tinted orb, objection chips, minutes to finish and your own last score ring. It targets 200-plus personas with difficulty and objection facets on every entry, and cmd-K search plus a 'Describe a buyer' field that opens the wizard. The wizard has five steps: an Animated Beam carries source snippets into the draft, a streamed preview fills in, weight sliders must total 100, a two-minute test call runs, and an Export as PR toggle finishes. The live call is a three-zone cockpit. A rubric ring and a Tracing Beam talk-track rail sit on the left. In the centre, the orb reacts to speech and the transcript highlights words that count toward a criterion. The coach rail on the right holds dismissible cue cards labelled Next question, Objection, Pricing, Talk track or Pace, arriving about 1.5 seconds after the rep's turn, and the persona never hears the coach. The debrief has a replay timeline with markers for cues, objections and score jumps, each playable. Mono chips read 'voice', 'coach gpt-4.1-mini' and 'grade gpt-4.1-mini' with latency. Settings exposes an OpenAI-compatible base URL and key, which is good bring-your-own-key open-source design. Against today's blurred orb and chat app, it is the proposal that most directly answers the 'nothing says cutting-edge AI voice coaching' diagnosis.
reviews.no_case: It is the most borrowed-looking design of the five. Magic UI and Aceternity supply the glow, beam and shimmer pieces seen across many AI landing pages, and the proposal itself warns that overuse makes the app read as a template again. Glow and WebGL cost battery and contrast on phones, several components need licence checks before vendoring, and Codex is only 'once wired' in the future, so the fund story is thin.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is a calm, keyboard-first, fully localized cockpit built on React Aria Components with Tailwind 3 CSS-variable tokens. It has a light default, a dark call mode for the live screen and a density switch. It keeps the current stack, Prisma model and API routes, so it is the lowest-risk rebuild in the set. The 64px top bar holds Practice, Library, Dashboard, Team and a Cmd+K command bar, plus a language selector that shows native names. Filter and sort state live in the URL, so a view can be shared. The practice flow is visibly three steps: Brief, Call, Debrief. The library has a RAC Tree of industry and sales job, TagGroup objection facets, Easy/Medium/Hard, and a persona-language select, over a GridList with arrow-key navigation. It targets 120 launch personas as YAML packs validated by zod. Persona language is separate from UI language, so an English-speaking rep can practise against a Spanish-speaking homeowner, a real multilingual wedge for call centres and BPOs. The live call has a 380px coach panel with Cue, Talk track and Live score tabs. Cues are one-glance, 12 words or fewer, and go to a polite live region so they never steal focus. Coach modes are Full, Captions and Off, with per-criterion mute. The debrief is text-first, with collapsible criteria whose quotes jump to the transcript line, and a grader chip that reads 'Graded by gpt-4.1-mini' or 'Heuristic fallback'. Its accessibility is the strongest in the set: axe checks in CI, forced-colors and reduced-motion projects, and contrast-tested tokens. Against today's dropdown and blurred orb, it is a cleaner, more usable product that an enterprise buyer would trust.
reviews.no_case: It is the least cutting-edge of the five: calm neutral surfaces on Tailwind 3, Inter-led type, and a stated worry that pure calm reads as enterprise-generic. It would score low on look and distinctiveness, and it does not answer the owner's 'nothing says cutting-edge AI' diagnosis. The Codex story is a planned Codex-assisted PR review, and the 120-persona and sub-1.5-second coach latency targets are both unproven.

reviews.yes_case: Strain & Form Console is a whole-app redesign built on one idea that repeats on every screen: a Whoop-style performance console. Each screen carries three numbers about the rep: Call Strain (0 to 21, how hard a call was, from turns, objections faced and persona difficulty), Form (fitness minus fatigue, so the rep can see whether they are sharp enough for a hard persona), and personal records per persona. Rings, trend charts and a PR wall replace today's four stat tiles and flat list. The live call has a coach rail beside the conversation: one typed cue at a time (Ask, Objection, Pace, Step, Close) that fades after six seconds, an elevation timeline of the live score with coach markers, and rubric rings drawn dashed while provisional until the final grader replaces them with quoted evidence. Today's call screen is a chat app with no feedback until the end, so this is the clearest answer to the coaching requirement. The library covers 240-plus personas across 15 job families, filterable by family, industry, strain tier, objection, channel and voice or text, and each card shows the rep's Form ring or a 'New' tag. The AI wizard offers four entry points in a 2x2 (job description, product URL, CRM or ICP notes, real call transcript), streams a persona card as the model writes, checks that rubric weights total 100, runs a 30-second test call and exports a file for a pull request. Visually it is coherent: Geist with tabular numerals for scores and timers, one token block per theme (light, dark and a night mode for the live call), custom ring and strain components, and hairline borders instead of shadows. For the OpenAI fund it names the model doing each job (grader, live coach, wizard, Realtime voice), and each debrief has an Under the hood tab with model, prompt version, tokens and cost, so a reviewer can audit how a score was produced.
reviews.no_case: The Whoop metaphor is borrowed from athletic training load, and it may not hold for sales managers. Strain and Form are invented scores with no validation, and the proposal's own self-scores show the basic needs depend on things not yet built: coaching is 6.5 only if cues arrive within about 2.5 seconds p95, and the library is 6.5 only if 240 personas ship, falling to 4 under 100. Rings on every screen, plus a rail, rings and a timeline during a live call, risks overloading a rep who is trying to hold a conversation. Gamification is acknowledged and PRs are private by default, but a manager can still use Strain as a performance number and a rep can read Form as a verdict. The Whoop and Strava patterns come from general knowledge and were not checked, and the claim that Base UI became the shadcn default in July 2026 is unverified. The 'Built with Codex' chip on the landing page is decoration unless there is real maintainer workflow behind it, and the proposal does not show one.

reviews.yes_case: Night Desk Cockpit is a dark, keyboard-first desk for power users and managers, modelled on a trading terminal: resizable multi-pane layouts with saved Rep and Manager arrangements, dense 36px tables, tabular Geist Mono numbers, a Ctrl+K palette and single-key shortcuts (J and K to move, Enter to start, M to mute, C to toggle coach, E to end, ? for help). The live call is the most structured of the five. A left rail shows the call clock, talk-track stages that tick during the call and a persona patience meter; the centre has a timestamped transcript and a cue dock holding up to two amber cues with Apply and Dismiss; the right rail is a rubric tape of five criteria bars that move each turn, with evidence pins back into the transcript. Coaching runs on a separate model path, so the persona never hears it, and each cue is logged for whether the rep used it and what the score did next. Unassisted mode hides the cues but keeps scoring, which makes certification runs fair. The debrief is a replay timeline with the rubric total as a line and cue and objection markers that jump the transcript, a real step beyond today's long scroll. Progress gives eight KPI tiles with 14-day sparklines, five criterion small multiples, a criteria-by-scenario heatmap and a sortable session table with saved views. The library has the most complete facet set in the group (job, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel and source: built-in, mine, community) with saved presets, beside a virtualized grid. The wizard asks one question at a time with an Auto-answer button and ends in a 60-second dry-run call before save or export. Every call footer names the models in use. Its self-scores are candid (E at 5.5, and it says three personas exist today against 150 needed), and its risks say where the density will bite.
reviews.no_case: It is the densest of the five, and the proposal admits Bloomberg density can overwhelm first-time reps. Its answer is a Simple view and a first-run tour, which means maintaining two interfaces. A trading-terminal look is an established dark-dashboard archetype, so it is less distinctive and less sleek than the canvas, editorial or shelf concepts, even though the brief asks for modern and user-friendly. It keeps Next.js 15 and Tailwind 3 and defers the Tailwind 4 move to a separate change, which makes it a less complete system refresh than the brief asks for, and its shadcn-on-Radix support on Tailwind 3 is unverified. Coaching is self-rated 6.5 only if cues land under about 1.5 seconds, a figure with no measurement behind it, and the library is 5.5 because it needs 150-plus personas. Keyboard shortcuts are excellent for power users and invisible to most reps. The landing page and library are light while the product is dark by default, so the first impression and the product a reviewer opens can feel like two different apps. Its competitor claims rest on vendor blog snippets because Firecrawl was rate-limited.

reviews.yes_case: Shelf & Coach Studio turns the persona library into a streaming-style set of shelves. The top shelf is Daily Mix, a made-for-you row that blends personas aimed at the rep's weakest rubric criterion, followed by rows for Home services, Insurance, Mortgage, Solar, Auto, Medical devices, B2B procurement and Collections. Each row is a horizontal scroll-snap strip of 1:1 cover cards showing name, role, difficulty dots and objection tags. Tapping a card opens a side sheet with the opening line and a Start button, and a queued bar holds the chosen scenario. A grid and list toggle with facet chips handles precise filtering. Cover art on every persona gives the library a visual identity none of the other proposals has, and the shelves make coverage of every sales job visible at a glance. On the live call, a lyrics-style transcript highlights the current line, and a coach rail on the right carries amber whisper cards for the next-best question and talk-track step, coral objection alerts with an optional strong-reply line, and live rubric meters with delta arrows. A coach setting (Quiet, Balanced, Intense) lets the rep choose how much help they get, and strong-reply lines stay locked until the debrief, so practice still builds skill. The wizard is four steps (source, draft persona with source-cited fields, rubric with weights that must total 100, then a 60-second test call) and ends in a YAML export for a pull request. The system is coherent: Geist, one token set for dark default and light, tonal surfaces with hairlines, a mini-player that keeps the coach visible on every route, and bottom tabs on mobile. For the fund, a model inspector lists the model behind the persona, the coach and the grader, with tokens and cost per call, and the call footer reads 'Voice: OpenAI Realtime'. It is the easiest of the five to browse and the most approachable for a rep who is not technical.
reviews.no_case: The Spotify framing is the most familiar of the five. Shelves and carousels are a well-worn pattern, and dressing a sales trainer as a music app may read as playful rather than serious to managers, buyers and Codex fund reviewers. Cover art for about 120 personas is a generation and licensing cost; the proposal covers it with a deterministic fallback and build-time pre-rendering, but that is still work. The live coach is the weakest part of the proposal: one whisper per 20 seconds is a hard cap that is loosest exactly when a rep needs help, and coaching is self-rated 6 with a 5.1 gate that depends on latency nobody has measured. Horizontal scroll rows are awkward with a mouse and for keyboard users, and facets are secondary to the shelves, so precise multi-facet search (role plus objection plus difficulty) is weaker than in the grid-first proposals. The HeroUI license is an unresolved question the proposal itself flags (MIT in official docs, Apache-2.0 in one index), a real adoption risk for an MIT open-source project. The wizard is a conventional stepper, fine but not distinctive, and the business case is middling (F1 and F2 at 6).

reviews.yes_case: Call Canvas makes the whole app a spatial studio. Personas, scenarios and rubrics are nodes on an infinite canvas, and a library board lets a manager or rep wire picked personas into a sequence from warm-up to hard close. The most distinctive part is the AI persona wizard built as a graph: source nodes (job description, product URL, CRM note, pasted call, ICP form) feed a Persona Synth node, which emits three outputs (Persona, Scenario, Rubric). Each generated field cites the source sentence it came from, and manual edits survive regeneration, so a black-box draft becomes a traceable build that a user can inspect and correct. The grid stays the default library view, with filters for role, industry, difficulty and objection type, and the canvas is opt-in. The live call is deliberately fixed rather than free-form: a rail of six talk-track step nodes with the current step pulsing and showing the next question, a transcript with timecodes, a voice orb, six live rubric bars with evidence pins, and a violet whisper card kept apart from the amber alert colour, so the rep can tell advice from status. Cues come from a separate evaluator, so the persona prompt never sees coaching. Each cue has Why and helpful or not buttons that feed prompt tuning, and the debrief has a replay timeline with cue markers that show whether the rep followed the advice. The look is dark-first with a dot grid, violet for coaching and teal for signal, with no logos or gradients, which reads as current AI tooling rather than a template. For the fund, a model rail names Realtime, gpt-4.1-mini and the synthesis step on screen, with a per-call cost chip from real token usage, and Codex is used for persona pack generation and PR review.
reviews.no_case: The canvas is the biggest risk for a sales-training app. The proposal itself warns it can read as a diagram tool, and most reps will not want to wire nodes to practise a cold call. A node graph is also not obviously a guided wizard: a first-time contributor or a sales manager may find it harder than a step flow, so the 'wizard' is really a graph editor with a provenance panel. React Flow adds weight, and every node is state to test. The launch library is 40 reviewed packs against a 140-pack target, so the library is thin at launch, and real estate, which the brief names, is not among the industries listed. Its basic-needs self-scores are D 6.5 and E 6.5, just above baseline, so it does not clearly beat the field there. The latency target (about 2 seconds in text, 3 in voice) is unproven, and the roughly two-week phase estimates look optimistic for a Tailwind 4 migration plus new primitives. It depends most on a new evaluator endpoint. The fund case is thin on proof: the model rail and cost chip are good, but the Codex role is described as a plan, not shipped work. The dark-first look with violet cues and a dot grid is distinctive but could feel cold and technical to the non-technical reps who are the main users.

reviews.yes_case: Live Ledger treats personas, scenarios, rubrics and talk tracks as editable documents. A persona is a block document (TipTap with a slash menu, capped at eight block types) with a properties header, so a contributor edits objections or talk-track steps in place and opens a pull request from the same screen. Personas are validated files in the repo, and one zod schema runs through the repo files, the wizard and the API, so what a user browses is what the coach and grader read. The library is organized as browsable sections ('Cold calls 24' with View all) with a filter rail for job family, industry, difficulty, objection type and voice or text mode, and each card shows initials, role, difficulty and objection tags. The AI wizard has four steps and five input tiles (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP text, pasted call), a live document that fills in block by block as the output streams, PII redaction on by default for pasted transcripts, and a two-minute test call before the persona is saved. The live call stays dark: a talk-track checklist with done, active and next states, transcript rows instead of chat bubbles, one whisper cue at a time (rate-limited to one per 20 seconds, with objections jumping the queue), a rose objection banner, and five rubric meters labelled 'live estimate' that flash a teal delta when evidence lands. The debrief is replayable: a score ring with a source badge that reads 'Graded by gpt-4.1-mini', or an amber 'Estimate only, grader unavailable' when the fallback runs, a radar with the previous attempt overlaid, and a Replay moment on each quote that scrolls the transcript. The proposal says today's keyword fallback shows as a red F with 'Needs practice', so labelling estimates honestly fixes a trust problem as well as adding features. The look (warm paper canvas, indigo primary, Newsreader serif for evidence quotes, Geist and Geist Mono for interface and numbers) reads as a modern, editorial AI product rather than default SaaS. For the fund, a Model passport in Settings shows which OpenAI model does each job and what each call costs.
reviews.no_case: Scope is the main risk. Personas as block documents, a four-step wizard, a dark cockpit, a debrief timeline, progress, team and a rep drawer add up to several overlapping systems, and the proposal itself says TipTap can absorb weeks, so 'several months for one experienced developer' is probably optimistic. Notion-style documents are an established pattern in AI products, so the distinctiveness depends on execution more than on the concept. The look runs two visual systems (light for most screens, always-dark cockpit) that must stay consistent. The coaching is conservative (one whisper at a time), and the two-second cue target depends on a coach pipeline the proposal says is scoped separately. The persona bar (120-plus across 12 families, at least eight per family) depends on contributor content, and the proposal does not say what ships if packs are thin. Real estate, which the brief names, is not in its job-family list. It gives no numeric self-scores for the basic-needs categories, so the coaching and library claims have to be judged from the text, and its business view is asserted rather than evidenced. The OpenAI credit case is argued rather than shown.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Desk is a total redesign on one token system: Ark UI for accessible behaviour, Panda CSS semantic tokens with a dark condition, and Park UI-style components copied into src/components/ui so contributors PR the source. It is dark-first (near-black canvas, teal live state, amber whisper cues) with Geist and Geist Mono for timers and scores, Instrument Serif for one verdict line, 1px hairlines, and status always shown as icon, word and colour. On a live call, persona and transcript sit in the centre and a 320px coach rail on the right shows one amber whisper card at a time (never more than one every 20 seconds) with its verbatim trigger quote, a talk-track stepper and a next-best question, while a five-criterion meter shows tracking ranges rather than grades. The debrief is a scannable scorecard where each criterion expands to quotes that jump to timestamps, with a radar against the last attempt. The library is a faceted rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection) with a count line and 150-plus reviewed persona files; the AI wizard is five Ark steps with provenance chips, rubric weights that must total 100, a 60-second dry run and no save until the rep approves. Against today's three-scenario dropdown and blurry orb, it reads as a different product. For the fund it is the most complete pitch: model chips on every stage, OpenAI Realtime as a first-class voice engine, a human-labelled gold-debrief eval in the repo behind a Trust panel, AGENTS.md, and a Codex-run PR review workflow.
reviews.no_case: It is the most expensive plan in the pool. The XL migration removes Tailwind and globals.css and rewrites every component on Panda and Ark while the two styling systems coexist, with shims on untouched routes. Panda recipes are an unfamiliar setup for the open-source contributors the brief wants to attract, which works against the contributor-friendly goal. Dark-first with teal and amber is also a fashionable AI-product palette, and the proposal itself flags the risk of a generic dark SaaS skin. D and E are self-scored 5.3 and 5.4 only if the coach channel and 150 reviewed personas ship, so the strong design depends on backend and content work that does not exist yet. The OpenAI Realtime voice engine and the gold-debrief eval are promised, not built.

reviews.yes_case: Live Coach Studio runs on one rule: a rubric bar starts hatched as provisional and turns solid only when a transcript quote confirms it, so the live meter and the final grade can be compared line by line. On a live call, the persona orb and transcript sit on the left, the centre rail shows one amber coaching cue at a time with its trigger quote and a six-segment talk-track bar, and the right side carries the live rubric meter. Charts stay off the call so it stays calm, and if the coach times out the lane says 'Coach paused' and the call goes on. The debrief opens with a Geist Mono score, a delta against attempt three and a call timeline with one tick per turn that replays that moment; a sticky scorecard links every number to its transcript line. The team view is the richest screen in the pool: a rep-by-criterion matrix, flag cards, and a calibration chart that sets AI score against manager score, which is what makes a manager trust the grader. The library covers all fifteen sales jobs in the brief with a Draft badge on unreviewed personas, so it is honest about depth, and the wizard traces each field to its source sentence. On the fund it is the most concrete: 'Graded by GPT-4.1-mini' footers with token count and latency, a Models page, AGENTS.md, a Codex-powered action that validates persona files against the zod schema, and Codex-drafted release notes, which map directly onto the program's named PR review, maintainer and release workflows.
reviews.no_case: shadcn/ui is the most common React kit, so the look can read as a default template, and the proposal admits the drift risk without offering a strong signature beyond the hatched rubric and the timeline. Analytics-first on the debrief, progress and team screens risks a practice tool turning into a BI dashboard, the opposite of the call-cockpit feeling the brief wants. The 'one system' claim is weaker than it sounds, because Tremor blocks are copied in and restyled on shadcn tokens, which gives contributors two sets of conventions to learn. Only 40 of the 120 launch personas are reviewed at v1, a thin library for a fund reviewer judging against open-source level. The calibration chart is only meaningful once a team has manager scores, which most open-source installs will not have.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Call Studio is the most visibly AI-native design in the pool. It runs on a dark stage with an Aurora hero, an Animated Beam that draws the live path from persona voice to live coach to rubric, and a headline that generates as you read. During the call the persona orb reacts to speech, the rubric ring tweens on each criterion hit, the matching word glows in the transcript, and cue cards slide into a rail with a traveling Border Beam pulse. The coach runs on its own text channel and never reaches the persona. The debrief is a replay timeline where coach cues, objections and score jumps are clickable markers that play that moment, a more direct answer to 'every score links to its moment' than a list. Mobile is rebuilt for thumbs: a rubric pill opens a sheet, cue cards swipe away, and End and grade sits in the thumb zone. The library is a Bento grid with Magic Card hover, faceted by role, industry, difficulty, objection and channel, with a 'Describe a buyer' field that starts the wizard. The dark Signal and light Paper themes share one token set, each targeting WCAG AA. Against today's chat app with a collapsed talk-track drawer, this is the clearest statement of cutting-edge AI voice coaching in the pool.
reviews.no_case: Glow, beams and aurora are now a common AI-startup template, so the look can date quickly; the proposal warns about overuse, and its own design leans on these effects heavily. Three component sources (shadcn, Magic UI and selected Aceternity pieces) mean a licence audit before anything is vendored into an MIT repo, and a larger surface for contributors to learn. Coaching is the least specified of the top three: the 1.5-second cue target is asserted, but no fallback, rate limit or cost cap is described, and the OpenAI Realtime voice path has to be built before the Realtime showcase is real. A WebGL orb, beams and glow cost battery on phones and need reduced-motion work the proposal has not yet proven. Its own D self-score of 5.4 is honest: the design is clearer than the engine behind it.

reviews.yes_case: Loud Dial is the one design a reviewer will remember. Every card, button and chip gets a 3px ink border and a hard 4px offset shadow on flat yellow, pink, mint and orange fills, with an 88px uppercase poster headline and a tilted live-call card in the hero. The persona library is a deck of collectible trading cards: an industry colour block, a flat avatar, difficulty stamps (Easy, Hard, Brutal) and objection badges, grouped in sections with counts. On a live call, the coach cue is a yellow sticky note that tilts and peels off with a Used tick, an orange stripe flags objections, and five criterion bars stamp when evidence lands and stay hatched until a quote confirms them. The debrief has a 120px grade tile and a 'Replay this line' chip that jumps to and flashes the matching transcript line. Progress adds a levels ladder (Explorer, Closer, Objection Hunter), which gives reps a reason to come back. It keeps Tailwind 3 and the existing routes, so the migration is the smallest in the pool. It stands apart from the blue-and-white look of Second Nature, Hyperbound, Yoodli and Mindtickle, which is a real brand asset for an open-source project.
reviews.no_case: Neo-brutalism is loud, chunky and playful. The brief asks for sleek, modern and cutting-edge, and enterprise buyers in call centres and training firms may read a poster-style skin as consumer or indie rather than serious AI infrastructure. Hard shadows and 3px borders on every element add noise to long debriefs and dense rubric tables, which the proposal concedes. The OpenAI tie-in is thin: a model router dropdown, a Realtime engine option beside ElevenLabs, a 'Built with Codex' footer and a 'Reviewed with Codex' badge with no described mechanism behind it. The fund's named workflows (PR review, maintainer automation, release) are not part of the design. And 200-plus seeded personas with objection sets is content work the design cannot shortcut, which the proposal's own risks admit.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is a calm, light-first cockpit: a warm neutral canvas, white cards, the current blue primary, Inter for UI and transcript, Sora for display headings, 1px hairlines, and a dark ink-navy call mode for the live screen. Practice is a visible three-step flow (Brief, Call, Debrief). The library is a left facet tree with a grid of persona cards, a live result count and shareable URLs, and persona language is its own facet, so an English-speaking rep can practise against a Spanish-speaking homeowner from the same pack. Underneath, React Aria Components supply focus, keyboard, screen-reader and RTL behaviour for every control, with seven launch locales through next-intl. The live call is designed not to steal attention: cues go to a polite live region and never move focus, coaching has Full, Captions and Off modes with per-criterion mute, and whispers go to the rep's headset only. The wizard is strong on provenance: each AI-drafted field carries a source chip and needs a human confirmation, and a contributor can export a pack and open a prefilled PR. CI runs axe, forced-colors and reduced-motion checks. It is the easiest of the five to ship (Tailwind 3, Prisma and the API routes stay) and the strongest on accessibility, which an enterprise buyer will test first.
reviews.no_case: It changes the look the least. The primary is still today's #1D4ED8, the canvas is close to today's #F8FAFC, and Inter and Sora stay, so the brief's requirement of a coherent new look is only partly met. Calm and accessible is also the enterprise-generic register the brief warns about, and the dark call mode is the only real visual move. The 12 launch sales jobs and industries leave out SaaS, real estate, retail and customer success, four areas the brief names, which weakens the 'every sales job' claim. The OpenAI showcase is light: visible OpenAI presence is attribution text ('Powered by', 'Graded by') and a Settings page, Codex review is only planned, and the Realtime adapter is new code that must pass the same tests as ElevenLabs. Styling by hand on top of React Aria data attributes also means real custom component work, which claws back some of the migration saving.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Call Studio is a dark-first, motion-led AI call studio on shadcn/ui with Magic UI and selected Aceternity pieces, set in Geist and Geist Mono with a violet and cyan palette. It reads as an AI product, not a SaaS template. The landing is a full-bleed aurora hero with one animated beam running from persona voice to live coach to rubric, so a visitor sees the mechanism before reading copy. In the live call, a central persona orb reacts to speech, a left rail shows an overall circular rubric ring and five criterion bars that tween when a criterion is hit, and a right coach rail holds dismissible whisper cards (Next question, Objection, Pricing, Talk track, Pace) that type on in a line. Every score change links to the exact transcript words, which is the evidence-first behaviour the brief asks for. The debrief is a replay timeline with markers for coach cues, objections and score jumps; clicking a marker plays that moment. The library is a Bento grid of persona cards with industry-tinted orbs, objection chips and the rep's last score ring, behind a facet rail for role, industry, difficulty, objection type and channel, with cmd-K search. The wizard labels every extracted field with its source chip, enforces rubric weights that total 100, runs a two-minute test call, then saves locally or exports a pull request. Against today's app it turns a three-item dropdown into a catalogue, a chat window into a cockpit and four numbers into a replay. For the fund, OpenAI models appear as mono chips on the orb, on each cue and on each criterion, with latency shown, and the 'Powered by OpenAI' text rule avoids the logo. A first-time visitor is most likely to think this is a serious AI product.
reviews.no_case: The aurora hero, Moving Border CTA and Text Generate effects are the same motifs as a generic AI landing template, and the proposal itself warns that effects can make the app read as a template again. The brief's own diagnosis was a default template. Glow and motion during a live call cost battery and legibility on phones, and the reduced-motion fallback is described, not built. Licensing is unverified: Magic UI and Aceternity are copy-in libraries with their own terms, and the proposal says to verify before vendoring without doing it. The Codex angle is thin: 'once Codex is wired into PR review' is a future promise, so this proposal does less for the fund's maintainer-automation criterion than rivals that already name a Codex workflow. D is self-scored 5.4, which the proposal admits only clears baseline once the coach channel and its 1.5-second latency are proven. The 200-persona launch target is a content promise the interface cannot deliver alone.

reviews.yes_case: Switchboard Console is the most distinctive of the five, and its metaphor runs through every screen. A voice call is a switchboard: talk-track steps are jacks on a patch panel that light as they are covered, persona selection draws a patch cord, and the console is dark phosphor on near-black with IBM Plex Mono and Sans. The live call is a three-zone cockpit: a 240px patch panel on the left, a centre with a canvas oscilloscope that runs on real audio level and a teleprinter transcript tagged CALLER and YOU, and a right Coach column with an amber whisper ticker above five rubric LEDs labelled 'live estimate, unverified'. Each LED shows its evidence on hover. The strongest architectural idea is the shared evidence trail: the live cue, the live LED and the final debrief quote are one object, so advice and grade cannot drift apart. The debrief is a paper-white receipt with an LED score ring, a radar of five criteria with the previous attempt dashed over it, and a waveform timeline with score markers that play the moment. The library is a faceted board of 300-plus seeded personas across 30-plus jobs, with source badges for Built-in, Community and Mine and a dense table view for managers. The wizard is conversational, with numbered question cards that take keys 1 to 4. For the fund, it shows the models best of the five: a Model switchboard tray names gpt-4.1-mini for coaching, grading and the wizard and shows cost per call in mono, and CI runs Codex review on persona-schema changes. It beats today's chat app by making the call itself the place where feedback arrives.
reviews.no_case: The retro-terminal look risks cosplay: phosphor glow, scanlines and switchboard vocabulary can read as a gimmick to enterprise sales managers and to the training-company buyers in F2, and the proposal's own risk list says the same. The navigation renames core areas to Board, Patch, Call, Ticket and Log, which is harder to learn than Library, Practice and Progress, and the routes make contributors guess what each page does. The 300-persona, 30-job launch is the largest content commitment of the five, with no curation plan beyond a rubric test. Moving to Tailwind 4 is a real migration cost for a repo that runs Tailwind 3 today. The Base UI-as-default claim comes from third-party write-ups the proposal says to verify, and the model name gpt-realtime-1.5 cannot be confirmed from the brief or the proposal's own sources; it must be checked against OpenAI's model list before it goes on a screen. Dark phosphor on paper is distinctive but less sleek than the brief asks for, and the paper mode doubles the QA work.

reviews.yes_case: Editorial Ledger is the most serious of the five, which matters for an open-source AI product that a fund reviewer has to trust on first look. It is a Swiss-grid, paper-and-ink system: a 12-column grid with a Newsreader display serif, Inter for UI, JetBrains Mono for every score and timestamp, hairline rules in place of cards and shadows, and one vermilion signal colour for coaching and objections. The landing replaces the blurry orb with a real annotated transcript excerpt that shows the product working. The live call is the most original coaching layout of the five: a night-theme room where coach notes sit in the margin, pinned to the transcript line that triggered them, so a rep can see why each cue appeared. A right rail of thin bars shows six criteria as provisional 'est.' numbers that become quoted evidence in the debrief. The debrief is a two-level report: a 120px serif score, a one-sentence goal status and numbered strengths and gaps, each linked to a transcript line, then a criteria ledger with weights and expandable verbatim quotes. The library is a facet rail for role, industry, difficulty, objection and source, with built-in personas forkable so contributors can start from a real example. The wizard shows the source snippet behind each generated field, weight sliders that must total 100, a 60-second dry run, then Save or Export as PR. For the fund, the colophon names the grader, voice model and rubric version on every debrief, and the proposal describes a concrete Codex path: AGENTS.md, plus Codex review on each persona pull request beside schema lint. The stack is nearly unchanged (Next.js 15, Tailwind 3, shadcn on Base UI), so contributors keep their current knowledge. Against today's app it turns four tiles and a dropdown into an evidence-first product.
reviews.no_case: The restraint can read as austerity: no cards, no shadows and one accent colour can look like a document or a blog, and the brief asks for modern, sleek and cutting-edge AI, which is closer to a premium editorial than to a voice product. Its only looping motion is a waveform strip, so the live call may feel like a text transcript with a margin, not a living AI voice conversation. Its signature idea, margin notes, is less visually striking than the orb, beams or LEDs of rivals, and it has the lowest distinctiveness of the three advancing proposals. The quiet serif landing and paper palette may not show a visitor the live voice product behind them. F1 is self-scored 4, and the proposal concedes that differentiation rests on self-hosting and bring-your-own keys rather than design. The Base UI default is a third-party claim left unverified. Its 200 personas across 20 jobs is still a large content lift.

reviews.yes_case: Loud Dial Neo-Brutal is the most memorable of the five and the one a demo audience is most likely to remember. It is a paper-and-ink system, Gumroad-style: 3px ink borders on every card, button and chip, hard 4px offset shadows, flat loud fills in signal yellow, rec pink, volt blue, mint and orange, and heavy uppercase Archivo display type. The landing is a poster: an 88px uppercase headline beside a tilted live-call card with a yellow whisper sticker and a stamped 'Discovery 72' score, over a black marquee. The live call is a cockpit in which whisper cue cards are yellow stickers that tilt and peel off with a 'Used' tick, criterion bars stamp with a hard shadow when evidence lands and stay hatched while provisional, and an orange stripe marks objections. The persona library is the best-realised trading-card idea: an industry colour block, a flat avatar, difficulty stamps (Easy, Hard, Brutal), objection badges and a dashed 'Build a persona' card that opens the wizard, grouped into sections with counts. The wizard is six steps with a live persona card that fills and flashes yellow on each update. The debrief opens with a verdict band (a 120px grade block, a rotated score stamp, a goal sticker) and 'Replay this line' quote chips that flash the transcript. Night Shift dark mode keeps live calls legible. For the fund, a model router gives one dropdown per function, cue and score chips show latency and cost, and the wizard button reads 'Generate with GPT'. Against today's blue-and-slate look it is a clear, shareable difference.
reviews.no_case: Closest cut of the five. Neo-brutalism is loud and playful, and the brief asks for modern, sleek and serious software; enterprise buyers in F2, such as training firms and call centres, may read ink borders, stickers and stamps as consumer or indie rather than serious. Hard shadows and 3px borders on every element add noise, which hurts the long debrief and the dense rubric table the proposal itself admits. Loud colours force ink-only text, so contrast rules are strict and easy to break in contributed components. 'Built with Codex' and 'Reviewed with Codex' badges could imply a partnership with OpenAI and need brand-terms review that the proposal does not address. Its look is cutting-edge indie more than cutting-edge AI, which is the diagnosis the brief names. D (6.0) and E (6.5) are self-scored, and the proposal admits brilliance rests on latency and grader accuracy the UI cannot fix.

reviews.yes_case: Pocket Coach Studio is the most practical of the five for a rep who practises between meetings. It is a dark-first, installable PWA with a four-tab bottom bar (Practice, Library, Progress, Team) and a raised Start call button in the centre, and every primary action sits in the bottom 40 percent of a 390px screen. It uses Vaul bottom sheets for the talk track, rubric, persona detail, filters and coach history, and a Serwist offline cache so the library opens in a dead spot. Amber means the coach is speaking, a rule that keeps the coach visible in every state. On the phone the rubric collapses to a single five-segment strip with hollow segments for provisional scores that firm up on the next turn, coach cues float 12px above the dock and fade after eight seconds unless tapped, and End and grade needs a press-and-hold to avoid mis-taps. The library is a faceted grid with a detail sheet, duplicate-and-edit and a Contribute sheet that prefills a persona file and opens a pull request. The wizard offers four entry paths (paste a call, paste a job or ICP, import a URL, describe it in a sentence) before the stepper, which is the easiest first step of the five for a new user. Desktop reuses the same components in three columns, so the phone design does not fork the product. Model names appear on each AI surface: the hero, the coach card (cue model), the debrief (graded by) and the wizard (generated by). Against today's app, which squeezes End and grade into a chat screen, it gives coaching a surface of its own.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive of the five. A bottom tab bar, sheets and a dark dashboard are a conventional mobile pattern, and the proposal's own self-scores (A 8, C 7) and its warning that a dark coloured UI can drift back into a generic AI dashboard say the same. Mobile is the lead lens, but most practice happens at a desk, so the desktop call is a reused three-column layout rather than a designed cockpit, and the brief's core live coaching is visually the least ambitious here. The offline library, haptics and hold-to-end depend on platform behaviour the proposal admits is weak: iOS has no Vibration API, and a backgrounded PWA can drop audio when a phone locks, which would end a call mid-practice. Persona scale is the smallest of the five (150-plus across about 25 industries), and Team is a secondary, solo-hidden surface. Vaul is a separate dependency that shadcn's default has moved away from, so contributors will carry its upkeep.

reviews.yes_case: Live Coach Studio looks and works like a call cockpit, not a chat app, on one shadcn/ui system whose Radix parts are copied into the repo so contributors can read and change them. Geist handles UI and headings, and Geist Mono handles timers, scores, timestamps and token counts so numbers do not jitter. A collapsible sidebar (icons only at 1024px) holds Practice, Library, New persona, Progress, Team and Settings. A Cmd+K palette jumps to any persona, scenario or past call, and existing routes keep working so README deep links survive. On the live call, focus mode hides the chrome and three lanes carry the work. The transcript sits left with speaker names and turns. The centre holds one amber coach cue at a time (a next best question, or an objection alert with its trigger quote printed beneath it) and a six-segment talk-track bar. The right lane is a live rubric where each criterion starts as a hatched provisional fill and turns solid only when a transcript quote confirms it. Coach modes are Silent, Light and Full, and if the coach times out the lane says 'Coach paused' and the call carries on. The debrief is a two-column scorecard with a call timeline, one tick per turn coloured by criterion, that you click to jump to that moment. Every quote links back to its turn with a rationale. The library has 15 sales-job tabs matching the brief, faceted filters for difficulty, call type and objection type, and 120 personas, with a review checklist for stereotyping that matters for insurance, mortgage and auto. The wizard runs four steps (Source, Draft, Shape, Dry run), and every drafted field links to the sentence it came from with a violet provenance chip showing model and token count. Against today's app, it swaps four stat tiles and a dropdown for trends by criterion, a calibration chart that sets AI scores against manager scores, and a team view the data model already supports. For reps, the coaching is visible and evidence-linked. For the OpenAI fund, every debrief footer reads 'Graded by GPT-4.1-mini' with turns, tokens and latency, a Models page lists which OpenAI model runs grading, coaching, the wizard and the Realtime engine, and the contributor path (AGENTS.md, a Contribute button that opens a prefilled YAML PR, and a Codex-powered PR review action) maps directly onto the program's named uses: PR review, maintainer automation and release notes.
reviews.no_case: The look is the risk the proposal names itself. shadcn plus Tremor blocks is the most common admin-dashboard kit, and Geist, amber and tonal surfaces may not stop it reading as a default template, which fails the 'unlike a default template' test. The analytics push into places a rep does not need them, so the product risks feeling like a BI tool with a call attached: the team and progress pages are dense and chart-led. The coach is visual only, with a 2-second cue target that is looser than the 1.5 seconds the other proposals set. At launch the library is 120 personas with 80 carrying a Draft badge, which is the first thing a reviewer sees. The XL effort also puts the Prisma-backed team view in Phase 3, so the manager surface the brief asks for arrives last.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Call Studio is the most committed look in the set: a dark-first product (canvas #05070B, surfaces #0C1322) on Geist, with glow kept to active elements only, so the one lit thing on screen is the thing that is live. The landing is a dark Aurora hero with an Animated Beam drawing one path from Persona voice to Live coach to Rubric, with the models named on the beam, so a reviewer understands the mechanism in seconds. The live call is a focus-mode, three-zone cockpit. The left rail holds an overall circular progress ring and five criterion bars that tween on each hit, plus a Tracing Beam talk-track rail that lights steps as they are covered. The centre is a persona orb that reacts to speech, and the transcript highlights the words that count toward a criterion. The right rail is an Animated List of dismissible coach cue cards labelled Next question, Objection, Pricing, Talk track or Pace. The coach is a separate text channel that reads the transcript after each rep turn and never touches the persona, with Silent, Whisper and Heads-up intensity. The debrief replaces the long scroll with a replay timeline across the whole call. Markers for coach cues (cyan), objections (amber) and score jumps (emerald) are each playable, and every criterion's evidence jumps to that spot. The progress page is a bento of Number Ticker stats, a score-trend area chart over a goal band, a radar of this week against last month, and a 'Next three drills' list, so numbers turn into a plan. The library is a facet rail and a Bento grid of persona cards with spotlight hover. The wizard is a five-step stepper with source chips and an Animated Beam from sources into the draft. Against today's white SaaS page and a chat window with no feedback during the call, it shows its mechanism, and it handles motion responsibly, with pauses under reduced motion and when the tab is hidden and a WebGL cap on phones. For the fund, mono chips read 'coach gpt-4.1-mini' on each cue and 'grade gpt-4.1-mini' on each criterion with latency, Settings takes an OpenAI-compatible base URL and key, and 'Contribute a persona' opens a draft PR, so OpenAI use is on screen rather than buried in code.
reviews.no_case: The motion-rich look is most exposed to the template critique it cannot fully avoid. Magic UI and Aceternity are the default vocabulary of AI start-up landing pages, and the proposal itself warns that overuse would make the app read as a template again. The copy-in components each need a licence check, and the proposal leaves open that a Magic UI component may force a Tailwind 4 move, which would reopen the stack it says it is keeping. The cue depends on a second model call per rep turn at a 1.5-second target the proposal has not measured, and it scores its own live coaching at 5.4 because the coach channel does not exist yet. The OpenAI Realtime path is missing (voice runs on ElevenLabs), so the Realtime showcase is a promise, not a feature. Dark-first is also the hardest theme for dense rubric tables, and sending reports to a separate Paper theme means keeping two themes accessible.

reviews.yes_case: Loud Dial is the most memorable proposal here, and it is committed across all nine screens rather than on the landing alone. Daylight mode sits on a paper-coloured page (#FFF6E0) with 3px ink borders on every control and card, hard 4px offset shadows that collapse when a button is pressed, and flat yellow, pink, mint, blue and orange fills. Uppercase Archivo display type sits over Inter for transcripts and JetBrains Mono for timers and scores. The landing is a poster: an uppercase headline, a tilted live-call card stamped 'Discovery 72', a black marquee and three sticker cards. The library reads like a deck of trading cards. Each persona has an industry-coloured block, a flat geometric avatar, a difficulty stamp (Easy, Hard, Brutal), up to three objection badges and a Practice button. Personas are sorted into grouped sections with counts such as 'SDR cold calls (48)', with a dashed 'Build a persona' card that opens the wizard. The proposal covers the brief's 15 sales jobs with 200 or more seeded personas. On the live call, the 260px talk-track ledger ticks as steps are covered. The transcript is one column with small-caps speaker labels and mono timestamps. Coaching arrives as a yellow whisper card that tilts, lives for about ten seconds and peels off when marked Used, and that tick is logged as adherence. Criterion bars stamp when evidence lands and stay hatched until a quote confirms them, next to a talk-ratio meter and a coach latency chip. The debrief opens with a verdict band (a 120px letter tile, a rotated score stamp, a goal sticker) and a 'Practise again' CTA. The progress page shows KPI tiles, a criterion heat grid and a levels ladder (Explorer, Closer, Objection Hunter) that makes practice feel like progression. Against today's dropdown and four plain tiles, reps get objects they want to collect and use. For the fund, each cue and score carries a model chip with latency and cost in cents, Settings has a model router with one dropdown per function, 'Generate with GPT' drives the wizard, and community PRs carry a 'Reviewed with Codex' badge that makes contribution visible. The wizard is six steps that fill a persona card field by field, and export is a persona file for a community PR.
reviews.no_case: Neo-brutalism reads as playful and consumer-grade to the enterprise buyers and call-centre procurement teams the F2 case depends on. The proposal admits the risk and mitigates it with a second, calmer reading mode, which is a second design language to maintain. Hard ink borders and offset shadows on every element add noise to long transcripts and debriefs, and this is the look a reviewer is most likely to call trendy rather than cutting edge. Whisper cards that depend on a 1.5-second model call can go stale in a fast call, and the 'Used' tick needs a tap mid-call, which is awkward in voice mode. The Codex story is thinner than it sounds: the in-app 'Contribute a persona' is said to draft the file 'with Codex CLI', a developer tool a deployed app does not normally call. Loud fills need ink text throughout, and keeping AA contrast across nine screens plus a dark Night Shift theme is a continuous audit, not a one-time pass.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is a calm, keyboard-first call cockpit built on React Aria Components. Every control (Dialog, Tabs, Table, Meter, TagGroup, NumberField, Tree, Toast) gets focus, ARIA, RTL and keyboard behaviour before any styling, and Tailwind 3 drives states through data attributes. It looks like a well-made pro tool: a warm neutral canvas (#F6F7F9), white surfaces, 1px hairlines, 10px control radius, Inter for UI and transcript with tabular numerals on timers, Sora only for display headings, and a dark call-mode console (#0B1220) for the live screen, plus a compact or comfortable density switch. The landing swaps generic feature cards for a captioned 20-second loop of the cockpit with one quiet cue, and a 'Try a 60-second roleplay' button that needs no sign-in. The app is a top bar (Practice, Library, Dashboard, Team for managers, and Cmd/Ctrl+K), and practice runs as a visible three-step path: Brief, Call, Debrief. In the call, the transcript sits beside a coach panel. One-glance cues of 12 words or fewer land in a polite live region and never steal focus, with Full, Captions and Off modes. Rubric meters update only at turn boundaries with text values and trend arrows, using the same rubric as the debrief so live and final scores compare directly. The library is a 260px facet rail (industry tree, sales job, objection TagGroup, Easy/Medium/Hard, persona language) with a live 'N personas match' count. A GridList opens a dialog that plays the opening line, and filters live in the URL so a view can be shared. The AI wizard is a five-step dialog where every AI-filled field carries an 'AI draft' badge and must be confirmed before saving. Against today's dropdown of three scenarios and a blurry orb, it turns the call, the library and the debrief into structured surfaces with one rubric throughout. For the OpenAI fund, the landing names the stack, Settings shows which model runs each role with per-call token counts, calls read 'Powered by OpenAI Realtime' when that engine is selected, and debriefs read 'Graded by' plus the model. Its accessibility gates (axe checks, forced-colors and reduced-motion projects in CI) are a real quality claim that a reviewer can test.
reviews.no_case: It plays it safe. Calm neutral surfaces, Inter, blue primary buttons and a light default sit close to the enterprise SaaS look the brief calls generic.
