The proposal admits it skipped Spectrum 2 because pure calm 'reads as enterprise-generic', then added a dark mode to compensate. The 'quiet coach' is thin for a coaching product: cues are short text cards with no spoken or headset cue and no emphasis beyond compliance warnings. The library launches with 12 sales jobs against the brief's 15 (SaaS, real estate, retail and customer success are missing) and 120 personas. The proposal's own self-scores (live coaching 5.3, library 5.2) say it meets the baseline and no more. Its strongest work, accessibility and i18n, delays the visible change: Phase 1 swaps controls and tokens and adds tooling, so the live call does not change until Phase 2. The 1.5-second cue target is unmeasured, and the Codex story is a CONTRIBUTING note plus a planned PR review rather than a named program hook.

reviews.yes_case: Editorial Ledger is the calmest and most typographically disciplined proposal: a paper background (#F6F4EF) with ink text and ink buttons, hairline rules in place of cards and shadows, a 12-column grid, a Newsreader serif for headlines, Inter for UI and JetBrains Mono for timers and scores. One vermilion signal colour is reserved for coach cues, objection alerts and the End and grade button. The landing is a real annotated transcript excerpt beside a 'Start a practice call' button, so the product shows itself rather than describing itself. The live call holds the strongest single idea in the set. Each coaching note is a margin note pinned to the transcript line that triggered it, so the rep can see why it appeared. Cues slide in from the margin in 160ms, and there is at most one per turn. Around the transcript sit a talk-track ledger with ticks, a rubric panel where criteria show as thin bars with 'est.' numbers and deltas until the debrief grader replaces them with quoted evidence (the debrief lists which numbers changed), and next-best-question chips. The debrief reads as a report: a 120px serif score, one plain sentence on goal status, numbered strengths and gaps linked to transcript lines, a criteria ledger with a 1-to-5 segmented scale, and verbatim quotes with line numbers. The grader and models move into a colophon instead of a warning banner. The library is a facet rail with counts, removable filter chips and filters written to the URL so a view can be shared, plus a preview drawer that shows the buyer brief and rubric weights before a rep starts. Against today's blue buttons and long vertical scroll, it feels like a serious editorial tool. For the fund, the colophon names every OpenAI model on each screen that uses one, AGENTS.md describes the persona schema for Codex, Codex reviews each persona pull request alongside the schema lint, and the contributor path maps onto the program's ChatGPT Pro with Codex and API-credit benefits.
reviews.no_case: Austerity is the risk the proposal names. A paper-first, serif-led design reads as a publication or reading app rather than cutting-edge AI tech, and the brief's category A asks for 'modern, sleek, cutting edge', which this does not chase. Its own self-scores (D 6, E 5.5, F1 4) say it is a baseline product on the needs that matter, and an editorial look is harder to sell as SaaS. The live call also splits into two design languages, because the proposal moves it to a night theme. The library is thin where the brief is demanding: 60 polished personas ship first with the rest as community drafts, and the proposal claims 200 personas across 20 sales jobs but lists only 15, so the every-sales-job need is only partly met. The Base UI default rests on a single vendor-blog citation, and Base UI is younger than Radix, which the proposal itself flags with a possible React Aria fallback.

reviews.yes_case: Loud Dial Neo-Brutal is a whole-app system, not a restyle. One token set on :root drives every screen: 3px ink borders, 4px hard offset shadows, five flat loud fills (signal yellow, rec pink, mint, volt blue, orange) and Archivo display type. The landing page becomes a poster hero that shows the product working, and the top bar becomes four chunky tabs with a Cmd+K persona search. Starting a call swaps the bar for a red rec strip with timer and End and grade. In the live room a whisper cue sits on a tilted yellow card that peels off when marked Used, an orange objection stripe runs across the transcript, and five criterion bars stamp when a transcript quote confirms the evidence. Debriefs open on a verdict band with the grade in a 120px yellow block and quote chips that jump to and flash the matching transcript line. The library is a trading-card grid of 200+ personas across the 15 sales jobs, filterable by job, industry, difficulty, objection type and voice, with a dashed Build a persona tile that opens a six-step wizard. The wizard accepts all five source types the brief names, streams fields into a live persona card, runs a 60-second test call, and exports a PR-ready file. It beats today's app on every axis the brief names: it looks like a product, it coaches during the call, and it makes the library browsable. A calm paper reading mode keeps dense transcripts legible, a dark Night Shift handles live calls, and shadcn/Radix parts give contributors accessible primitives. For the Codex fund, each model is named on its chip (voice, coach, grader, debrief), Contribute a persona drafts the file with Codex CLI, community PRs carry a Reviewed with Codex badge, and the migration keeps Tailwind 3 and the current routes so it can ship in phases.
reviews.no_case: Loud neo-brutalism is the most polarising choice in the batch, and enterprise buyers may read it as playful rather than serious. Hard borders and 4px shadows on every control, chip and card add heavy visual weight to dense debriefs and transcripts, and the proposal's own risk list admits the 200-persona seed is a content lift where weak objection sets would make the library look thin.

reviews.yes_case: Editorial Ledger is the calm, premium option. It is a paper-and-ink app on a 12-column Swiss grid, with Newsreader for display, Inter for UI and JetBrains Mono for every score, timer and timestamp. One vermilion signal colour appears only on coach cues, objection alerts and End and grade, and there are no cards or shadows, only 1px hairline rules, so the product reads like a well-made printed report. The live call switches to a night theme, so 'live' is signalled by a state change rather than decoration. Coaching sits in the margin, pinned to the transcript line that caused it. A talk-track ledger ticks down the left, and a rubric-in-motion panel on the right shows six criteria as thin bars with est. marks and deltas, which the debrief grader replaces with quoted evidence at End and grade. The debrief is a two-level report: a serif score numeral and an 'Evidence: 9 of 9 claims quoted' line first, then numbered strengths and gaps linked to transcript lines, a criteria ledger with weights and expandable quotes, and a colophon. The library is a faceted catalogue of 200 personas with a preview drawer that shows rubric weights before the rep starts, and the wizard cites the input snippet behind every generated field, with weight sliders that must total 100 and an Export as PR path. A manager heatmap and coaching queue expose org data the model already holds. It beats today's app by making every score traceable to evidence, which is what a sales manager pays for. For the Codex fund, OpenAI models are named in the colophon of every screen that uses them, an AGENTS.md lets Codex review persona PRs against the schema, and the phased, flag-gated migration keeps every existing route alive, which suits an open-source core with real users.
reviews.no_case: It is the quietest of the three. Hairlines with no cards, one signal colour and serif display on only three screens could read as a polished docs site rather than a cutting-edge AI product, so the first screenshot may undersell the coaching. The 1.5-second cue target also has a fallback to post-turn coaching that the proposal itself says drops D to baseline, and the Base UI default claim is third-party and unverified.

reviews.yes_case: Switchboard Console is the most distinctive proposal on the table. The live room is a dark phosphor call console, and debriefs, library and dashboard use a light paper mode. It uses a patch-panel metaphor that no other sales-training app has: talk-track steps are jacks that light as they are hit, and persona selection draws a patch cord from the persona card to the console. The live call is a three-zone cockpit: a talk-track patch panel on the left, a centre column with an oscilloscope driven by real audio level and a teleprinter transcript with mono timestamps and CALLER and YOU tags, and a right-hand Coach column with an amber whisper ticker above five rubric LEDs labelled live estimate, unverified. Each LED shows its evidence on hover, and the debrief reuses the same evidence objects, so a live cue, a live LED and the final quote share one trail. The debrief is a paper receipt with an LED score ring, a radar of five criteria with a dashed overlay for the previous attempt, and a timeline with score-change markers that replay that moment. The library is the most ambitious in the batch: 300+ seeded personas across 30+ jobs, faceted filters with live counts, source badges (Built-in, Community, Mine), and a dense table toggle. The wizard is conversational, with numbered question cards that accept keys 1 to 4, a streaming build log and a live persona card, and it ends in a 2-minute test call and a PR export. For the Codex fund it has a very explicit OpenAI story: a Model switchboard tray names the model behind each job and shows live cost per call in mono, which is exactly what a fund reviewer wants to see. It beats today's app because the screen itself becomes a coaching instrument rather than a chat window with a hidden drawer.
reviews.no_case: The live coach is throttled to one cue every 20 seconds and targets arrival under 2 seconds, which is looser than the brief's 1.5-second bar. With that cap most turns get no whisper, so the real-time coaching the brief asks for is thin. The phosphor glow and scanlines on the live stage risk legibility and reading as a gimmick, and the one-to-two-week Tailwind 4 migration estimate is optimistic for a total redesign. Model names such as gpt-realtime-1.5 also need checking before they go into the UI.

reviews.yes_case: Ambient Orb Call Room treats the live call as a call, not a chat. The full-viewport canvas centres an audio-reactive GLSL orb at about 44vh, driven by the speaker's level, with a halo of five rubric arcs around it, one per criterion. Arc length is coverage and colour is the score band, so a rep reads their rubric shape at a glance without opening a panel. A mono timer and a Your turn or Their turn pill sit above. Below the orb a single whisper card in Instrument Serif italic appears, is read once and fades after six seconds. An objection turns the halo coral and adds a one-line pivot card. Chrome fades after three seconds without pointer activity, and the bottom rail (mute, text, talk-track dots, End and grade) returns on movement. The same visual language runs across the product: the orb is the brand mark, the persona avatar on library cards with a 3-second voice preview, and the debrief header. The library is a sectioned catalogue with View all (n) links per sales job, facet checkboxes with counts, and a sheet with the full persona brief. The wizard is a co-pilot split view in which a persona card fills field by field, each field carries a source chip that highlights its input span, and it ends in a 60-second test call and a duplicate check against the nearest library entry. For the Codex fund, every screen carries a model provenance line, the coach and grader models are named, settings show estimated cost per call, and a How this repo uses Codex page documents the PR review and release workflows the program funds. It beats today's app because the call room is a distinct product moment, and the mobile call is the same room scaled, with thumb-zone controls and a Vaul transcript sheet.
reviews.no_case: It doubles down on the orb the brief names as part of the generic look, and the orb is the centre of every screen while the proposal admits dark-first can read as generic AI. The transcript lives in a drag-up sheet under fading chrome, so a rep cannot read the persona's words while being coached, which weakens the evidence trail. The seed library is the smallest in the batch: 120 personas across 14 jobs, with no explicit SaaS job, against a brief that names SaaS and asks for every sales job.

reviews.yes_case: Pocket Coach Studio is the mobile-first, installable version of the product. The phone is the primary surface: a four-item bottom tab bar (Practice, Library, Progress, Team) with a raised Start call button in the centre, one primary action per screen in the bottom 40%, and Vaul bottom sheets for the talk track, rubric, persona detail, filters and coach history. The live call on a 390px phone is thumb-first: a 52px top bar with persona, mono timer and state pill, a five-segment rubric strip, an auto-scrolling transcript, and a floating amber coach card with a Why chip to the exact line that triggered it. The dock holds four 56px round buttons and a press-and-hold End and grade, and the keyboard lifts the dock in text mode. Desktop reuses the same components in a three-column layout with a persona card, turn transcript, live rubric rail and coach feed. The library gets 150+ seeded personas across about 25 industries, with facets for role, industry, difficulty, objection, channel and language, Seed and Community tags, and a detail sheet with a Duplicate and edit action. The wizard has four entry paths (paste a call, paste a job or ICP, import a URL, describe it in a sentence), source-quote chips on every generated field, and a 60-second test call from the same card. As a PWA with a Serwist offline cache for the library, reps can browse personas without signal. For the Codex fund the OpenAI story is clear: model chips on the hero, a coach card naming its cue model, a graded-by line on each debrief, and a Models table in the README. Contributors get a prefilled pull request from each persona card, and an AGENTS.md lets Codex CLI add a persona and run the schema tests. It beats today's app because a rep can run a full coached call from a phone, which the current chat screen with its small End button does not support well.
reviews.no_case: It is the most generic look of the five. Dark-first with indigo and amber accents on Geist and sheets sits close to the default SaaS-dashboard look the brief diagnoses, and the proposal's own risk list says the look can drift back to that. Its lens is a phone-first interaction model rather than a visual identity, so distinctiveness is the weakest score in the batch, and its named wizard inputs leave out CRM notes, one of the five sources the brief requires.

reviews.yes_case: A dark phosphor call console for live practice, with paper-white pages for reading and printing afterwards. The live call is a three-zone cockpit. The left 240px holds a talk-track patch panel with six jacks that light as each step is hit. The centre has a canvas oscilloscope showing real audio level and a teleprinter transcript with mono timestamps and CALLER and YOU tags. The right 300px holds a Coach column: an amber whisper ticker that lands one typed cue (OBJECTION, ASK, NEXT STEP or TIME) within about two seconds of the rep's last line, above five rubric LED bars labelled 'live estimate, unverified'. Hovering an LED shows the quote behind it, and the debrief reuses those same evidence objects, so the cue, the LED and the final quote share one trail. The library is a faceted board of 300-plus personas across 30-plus jobs, with cmdk search, difficulty LEDs, objection tags and source badges (Built-in, Community, Mine). The wizard is a numbered conversational build that drafts a schema-valid persona and a rubric whose weights total 100, then offers a 2-minute test call before saving or exporting a PR file. A Model switchboard tray names the OpenAI model behind each job and shows live cost per call, which is the most visible OpenAI usage of the five. It beats today's app, which is a three-item dropdown, a chat-bubble transcript with no coaching and a card scroll after the call, by making coaching and scoring visible while the rep is talking. It also supplies the identity the brief says is missing, a memorable AI-coaching look, while keeping glow on live numbers only so body text stays legible.
reviews.no_case: The retro-terminal costume is the risk: phosphor glow and scanlines can tip into themed cosplay, two full themes double QA on a volunteer repo, and a 300-persona seed list is a content mountain that will look padded if review slips. The one-cue-per-20-seconds cap can also go silent during a fast objection exchange, which is exactly when a rep needs a whisper.

reviews.yes_case: A live-call cockpit built around a copilot rail, on a light product with a dark stage for the call. On desktop the call is a speaker-labelled transcript on the left, where rep lines carry rubric chips such as 'Discovery +4', and a 360px rail on the right. The rail holds a live score strip (overall estimate and five criterion bars with deltas, labelled 'Live estimate'), a talk-track stepper that ticks as steps are hit, and at most three cue cards. Each cue is typed as objection, next question, whisper or guardrail and cites the turn and rubric criterion it came from. 'Use line' drops a suggested phrase into the composer for the rep to send; nothing is auto-sent, and the persona never receives cue text, so it stays in character. Outside the call the product is a browsable catalogue: a 240px facet rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection, call type, pack source) with live counts, and 200-plus JSON persona packs across 18 job families, each section with a View all link. The five-step wizard shows the generated JSON beside the form, runs a dry-run chat, and requires weights totalling 100 before a pack can be saved or sent as a PR. The debrief has a sticky score ring with a grader-source chip, evidence chips that highlight the exact transcript line, and a 'Retry from turn 8' button that branches practice from the missed objection. It beats today's app because coaching and scoring happen during the call, the library replaces a three-option dropdown, and each AI step names its model. Its gates are measurable (p50 cue latency under about 2 seconds, cue precision on 30 scripted calls), and the phases ship the rail behind a flag, which is realistic for a small open-source team.
reviews.no_case: It is the most familiar look of the five: a light SaaS dashboard with a blue primary and the existing ink, a copilot rail that Gong and Balto already made normal, and a 360px rail that squeezes the transcript at 1280px wide. A judge looking for a cutting-edge identity will see a tidy refresh of the default SaaS look the brief criticises, not a new point of view, and nine screens plus a rail and a wizard is a large surface for a volunteer repo.

reviews.yes_case: A Swiss-grid, paper-and-ink application: a 12-column, 1200px grid, hairline rules instead of cards and shadows, a Newsreader serif for titles, Inter for UI with tabular numerals, and JetBrains Mono for scores and timers. Primary buttons are ink, and the one signal colour, vermilion, marks coach cues, objection alerts and End and grade. The live call is the single place it switches to a night theme, so 'live' reads through a state change rather than decoration. The call room has three columns. A 280px talk-track ledger shows ticks, with the current step in signal colour. The centre is one column of turns with small-caps speaker labels, mono timestamps and a rule marking the rep's lines, and coach cues sit in the margin, pinned to the exact line that caused them. A 300px rubric-in-motion panel shows six criteria as thin bars with provisional 'est.' numbers and deltas, and next-best-question chips sit above the composer. The library is a 240px facet rail with counts and removable chips that write to the URL, feeding a three-column grid of persona cards with objection chips and difficulty ticks. The four-step wizard cites the input line for every generated field, and its weight sliders must total 100. The debrief reads like a report on paper: a 120px serif score numeral, a plain goal sentence, and each criterion linked to verbatim quotes with line numbers. It beats today's app because each cue sits beside the words that caused it, live scores are clearly marked provisional until the grader replaces them, and the system has a voice and grid contributors can follow. The staged migration keeps existing routes redirecting, voice and text both keep working, and the OpenAI models are named in a colophon on each screen that uses them.
reviews.no_case: Swiss restraint is the risk: it can read as sober and academic, a magazine skin on a sales tool, rather than the cutting-edge AI product the brief asks for. Its live-coaching claim also rests on margin cues that drop to post-turn when latency misses the target, so the D score depends on a latency result that has not been measured, and the 200-persona library is a content lift the proposal itself calls the bottleneck.

reviews.yes_case: A dark-first, thumb-first progressive web app where the phone is the primary surface and desktop reuses the same components in a three-column layout. The bottom tab bar holds Practice, Library, Progress and Team, with a raised Start call button in the centre, and every primary action sits in the bottom 40 per cent of a 390px screen. During a call the screen shows a persona card with state (Speaking, Listening, Your turn), a segmented rubric rail of five criteria that fill as the rep hits them, with hollow segments for provisional scores, and a single amber whisper card floating above a four-button dock (mute, text, talk track, coach history). 'End and grade' sits behind a press-and-hold. Each cue carries a 'Why' chip that opens the exact transcript line, and the debrief timeline lets the rep tap a coach-cue marker to jump to the moment that triggered it. The library is a grid of persona cards with initials avatars, difficulty bars and objection chips, filtered by a bottom sheet on mobile and a facet rail on desktop. A detail sheet offers Practice and Duplicate and edit, and a Contribute sheet opens a prefilled pull request. The wizard offers four entry paths, cites the source line for each generated field, and runs a 60-second test call before saving. It beats today's app because practice works on a train, the library works offline through a service worker, and the coach stays visible on a phone instead of hiding behind a small End button in a chat layout. Model names appear as chips on every AI surface, with a cost panel showing tokens per call.
reviews.no_case: It has the least distinctive look of the five: a dark canvas with indigo buttons and amber coaching is close to the generic AI dashboard the brief warns about. The mobile-first framing also makes the desktop team and progress views read as an afterthought, since they are described as the same components in three columns. The PWA carries the risk the proposal names, because a locked iPhone can drop audio and end a call mid-practice, and Vaul adds an upkeep burden on top of Radix.

reviews.yes_case: A FaceTime-style voice room in which the orb is the product's identity and the centrepiece of every call. On a dark canvas the orb sits at about 44 per cent of the viewport height, rendered as a custom GLSL shader that breathes with the speaker's audio level, with five rubric arcs around it as a halo: arc length is coverage, and colour is the score band. A whisper card in Instrument Serif italic appears above the controls, reads once and fades after six seconds. An objection turns the halo coral and adds a one-line pivot card. Chrome dissolves after three seconds without pointer or touch, leaving the orb, the timer and 64px mute and End and grade controls, while a drag-up Vaul sheet holds the transcript and talk track. Live estimates show as a dashed halo, and the full grader replaces it with a solid halo at End and grade. Across the product the orb becomes the brand mark, the persona avatar and the debrief header, and the library groups personas into sections per sales job with 3-second voice previews. It beats today's chat-app call by making the conversation feel like a call, not a chat thread, and by moving coaching and live score into the orb's own space rather than a drawer. For a voice-first AI product it is the most distinctive and modern concept of the five, and it reads as cutting-edge in motion.
reviews.no_case: Coaching is the thinnest of the five: one whisper card, five arcs and chrome that fades away leave little room for cue types, a queue, evidence or a 'why' link, and the proposer's own D self-score of 5.4 admits it sits at baseline. It also keeps an orb at the centre, which the brief's diagnosis of a blurry orb calls part of the generic look, and it has the fewest seeded personas, 120 across 14 jobs, against the brief's large-library requirement.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: a dark 'call console' for the live stage (phosphor green on near-black, LED meters, an oscilloscope trace, jack-style talk-track ports) with a light 'paper' mode for the debrief, library, dashboard and print. It is built on shadcn/ui (Base UI), Tailwind v4 tokens and IBM Plex. How it looks and works: the top bar holds Board, Patch, Log and Team plus a command palette, and the flow Board to Patch to Call to Ticket to Log carries the next action forward (the weakest criterion on Log pre-selects a Board filter). In the live cockpit, talk-track jacks light as each step is hit, an oscilloscope and teleprinter transcript sit in the centre, and an amber whisper ticker lands within about two seconds of the rep's last line with a typed tag (OBJECTION, ASK, NEXT STEP). Five LED rubric bars are labelled 'live estimate, unverified' and show their evidence on hover; the debrief reuses the same evidence objects. The library has a faceted rail (job, industry, a 1-5 difficulty control, objection chips), a command-palette search with counts, and source badges. The wizard uses numbered 1/4 question cards with keyboard keys, a source tray (job description, URL, CRM note, ICP, transcript), a streaming build log, a live persona card, rubric weights that total 100, a 2-minute test call before save, and Export as PR. Why it beats today's app: it turns a chat screen and a three-item dropdown into a cockpit where cues and scores move during the call, and it replaces the blurry orb with a real signal display. OpenAI fund angle: a Model switchboard tray names gpt-realtime for voice and gpt-4.1-mini for coaching, grading and the wizard, with live cost per call in mono, so a reviewer can see efficient API use directly; PR templates and Codex review on persona-schema changes match the Codex for Open Source uses. It is the strongest combined answer in this batch to the whole-app, live-coaching and library requirements.
reviews.no_case: The phosphor-and-patch-cord theme is a costume, and some reviewers will read retro terminal styling as nostalgia rather than cutting edge. Glow and scanlines hurt legibility on the live stage, which the proposal admits. Running two full themes (console and paper) doubles QA and can make the product look like two apps. 300+ seeded personas at launch is a content-review burden a volunteer repo will not hold; thin entries will make the library look padded. The 'Base UI became shadcn's default in July 2026' claim is only partly checked: the shadcn docs now lead with the Base UI variant, but the date is unverified. Phase 1 promises a Tailwind 3 to 4 move, a shadcn init, new tokens and a rebuilt shell in 1-2 weeks, which is optimistic for an XL redesign. The model-switchboard and Codex claims must be true for this repo or they will hurt credibility with the fund.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: a dark-first mobile PWA with a four-tab bottom bar (Practice, Library, Progress, Team) and a raised centre Start call button. The same components lay out as a three-column desktop cockpit. How it looks and works: 390px screens with 16px gutters, every primary action in the bottom 40 percent, and an 88px call dock with four 56px round buttons (mute, text, talk track, coach history) plus a press-and-hold End and grade so nobody ends a call by accident. Secondary panels (talk track, rubric, persona detail, filters, coach history) are bottom sheets, so the rep never leaves the call. Live coaching: at most one amber whisper card at a time above the dock, typed as next-best question, objection alert or talk-track step, with a Why chip that opens the exact transcript line. The rubric strip fills segment by segment and shows hollow provisional scores until the next turn confirms them. The debrief timeline markers jump to transcript lines. The library has a filter sheet (role, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel, language), cards with objection chip and difficulty bar, and an offline cache so it opens on a train. The wizard has four entry paths (paste a call, paste a job or ICP, import a URL, describe it in a sentence), and every generated field carries a source-quote chip. Why it beats today's app: it fixes the screen where a rep is most likely to be on a phone and puts coaching on a glanceable surface. OpenAI fund angle: every AI surface names its model ('cue: gpt-4.1-mini', 'graded by', 'generated by'), the README has a Models table, a cost panel shows tokens per call, and AGENTS.md lets Codex CLI add a persona and run schema tests. The Vaul pin is a real choice: the shadcn base drawer now uses Base UI (checked on ui.shadcn.com), so this path is deliberate and carries an upgrade burden.
reviews.no_case: Indigo on near-black with amber accents is the look of a dozen AI dashboards, and the proposal itself warns it may drift back to generic. Mobile-first makes the desktop an afterthought: the same components in three columns is not a designed desktop, and most reviewers will open the repo on a laptop. Tailwind 3 is kept and classes are swapped screen by screen, so the total redesign arrives in pieces and old and new looks coexist for a long time. Pinning Vaul means maintaining a dependency the shadcn default has left, which adds upgrade work for open-source contributors. A backgrounded PWA can drop audio when the phone locks, which can end a call mid-practice, and iOS has no vibration cue for coaching; the proposal flags both and does not solve them. The wizard drops CRM notes as a source even though the brief names it, and 150 personas is a smaller library than the brief's 'large' catalogue.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: a FaceTime-style call room where a single breathing orb carries the conversation. The live call is a full-viewport canvas: a shader orb at about 44vh, surrounded by a five-arc rubric halo (arc length is coverage, colour is the score band), a Geist Mono timer with a Your turn or Their turn pill, and one whisper card in Instrument Serif italic that fades after six seconds. The chrome (rail and tabs) dissolves after three seconds, leaving the orb, timer and controls, and a drag-up sheet holds the transcript. How it looks and works: a calm dark canvas with one glowing element, so the page never reads as a dashboard. The same orb is the persona avatar in the library, the pre-call preview and the debrief header, so the brand is a single object. The library has sections per sales job with 'View all (n)' links and orb-tinted cards with a three-second voice preview, so a rep can hear a persona before practising. The wizard is a co-pilot split view in which a persona card fills field by field, each field with a source chip back to the pasted line. Why it beats today's app: it replaces a chat screen and a blurry gradient card with a voice-first room that coaches inside the orb's space, and it is the most visually distinctive of the five. It also makes OpenAI Realtime a natural fit, including an optional second Realtime session that whispers only to the rep through headphones. OpenAI fund angle: model provenance lines on each screen (coach gpt-4.1-mini, grader selectable, wizard via Structured Outputs), cost per call in Settings, and a How this repo uses Codex page that says plainly that selection is at OpenAI's discretion and shows real usage rather than promising it.
reviews.no_case: The orb is the most common AI-voice visual, and the brief already names the orb as part of the generic look; a sharper shader does not change the category signal. Chrome that fades after three seconds can hide controls, so a rep who glances down mid-call may lose the End button unless the hold-to-reveal works perfectly. The live halo shows coverage arcs, not per-criterion evidence, and 'next-best question' is not a named cue type, so specific guidance depends on the whisper card. The library is 120 personas across 14 jobs, thinner than the brief's full list of sales jobs. WebGL on low-end phones and a second Realtime audio session for headphone whispers are two heavy features for a volunteer repo. Keeping Tailwind 3 means the token system is retrofitted rather than native. The proposer self-scored live coaching at 5.4, which is only baseline by its own estimate.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: a live-call cockpit built around a copilot rail, a 360px panel beside a speaker-labelled transcript with a live score strip, a talk-track stepper, a stack of up to three cue cards and a Whisper, Text only or Off switch. How it looks and works: a light default for library, briefing, debrief and dashboard, and a dark stage for the live call. Every cue carries a colour, an icon and a text label, so colour is never the only signal. 'Use line' drops the exact phrase into the composer for the rep to read and send; nothing auto-sends. The debrief's 'Retry from turn 8' branches the call from the missed objection, so a grade becomes practice. Each score has an evidence chip that highlights its transcript line. The library holds 200+ personas as JSON packs, faceted by role, industry, difficulty, objection type, call type and pack source. The five-step wizard has a sum-to-100 rubric editor, a dry-run chat and a JSON preview showing the exact file that would become a pull request. Why it beats today's app: it is the most complete answer to the coaching requirement, the pattern sales managers already know from Gong and Balto, and the cheapest to ship because it reuses the existing tokens and routes. OpenAI fund angle: every model has a visible job ('Voice: gpt-realtime', 'Coach: gpt-4.1-mini', 'Graded', 'Generated with'), a Models page accepts any OpenAI-compatible base URL, and it claims Codex maintainer use only if true.
reviews.no_case: This is a restyle in a new layout. The canvas, primary blue (#1D4ED8) and ink (#071827) are today's brand tokens, so users see the same product with a better rail and a font swap, which falls short of the brief's total UI change and its demand that nothing look like a template. The copilot rail is a copy of the category norm, so it does not win on distinctiveness, and the proposal admits its rail design came from competitor write-ups rather than screens. Nine screens plus a rail and a five-step wizard is a large surface for a volunteer repo, and the proposal concedes the team view may slip. Cue cards every eight seconds with a cap of three in a 360px rail can feel busy in a fast call, and on phones the rail becomes a bottom sheet that can cover the call. Its model-visibility claims are conditional on being true, which is honest but weakens the pitch to reviewers.

reviews.yes_case: What it is: a curriculum-first trainer. The left rail has Learn (assigned paths and the next drill), Library, Practice, Progress and Team, and the library's front door is an ordered catalogue of paths plus about 150 persona packs. How it looks and works: a warm paper canvas for library, progress and team, a dark night cockpit only for the live call, and violet marking every AI feature, so a rep can tell at a glance which parts are coached. In the live cockpit, five-dot criterion ratings move and flash once per turn under a 'live estimate' label, and violet cue chips under the rep's last sentence name the next question. A right tray holds the objection alert and the talk-track stepper. The debrief has a score ring with a pass-threshold marker, a moment timeline coloured by criterion, quotes with jump-to-transcript links, 'Replay this moment' (a 90-second drill from a weak turn), a 'Better line' rewrite, and a certified or not-yet state. The manager view has a roster with certification status and weakest criterion and an assign-drill form with due date and pass threshold. Why it beats today's app: it turns one scenario dropdown into a programme a sales manager can run, which is what enterprise buyers pay for, and it keeps the rubric evidence intact. OpenAI fund angle: a smaller GPT model produces live cues, GPT-4.1-mini grades and drives the wizard, Codex is the contributor engine through AGENTS.md, and CI uses Codex to review pack PRs.
reviews.no_case: The LMS lens pulls the product toward admin and certification features the brief did not request, and the landing and library lead with paths so the live coach becomes the second story. A 25-second cue rate limit with 12-second expiry is too slow for in-call coaching, and a cue that lands after the rep has moved on feels stale, which the proposal itself lists as a risk. Violet on warm paper with a night theme is a generic enterprise-AI palette, and the paper canvas makes the library look more like a document than a product. Certification gates and manager assignment need real org data and roles, so the most sellable part is the least buildable in an open-source repo. Tailwind 3 is kept, so the system underneath barely changes. The five-dot rating scale is harder to read at a glance than the segmented meters other tools use.

reviews.yes_case: It is a whole-app redesign on one system. A persistent left sidebar groups Practice (pre-call, live call), Library (personas, scenarios, New with AI), Progress (dashboard, history), Team (org only) and Settings. It uses a Catalyst-style layout rebuilt from MIT parts (shadcn/ui, cmdk, Motion, Recharts), so the repo can carry it under its MIT licence. The landing page opens with the live cockpit running as a looping SVG demo, so the first screen shows the product doing the thing it claims instead of feature cards. During a call the app enters focus mode: a dark three-zone cockpit with the persona and talk-track ticks on the left, a presence ring with state pill (Listening, Persona speaking, Your turn) and speaker-turn transcript in the centre, and a coach rail on the right with up to three cue cards (whisper, objection alert), rubric meters that only turn 'covered' when a quote backs them, and a pace gauge. When the LLM grader fails, the rail shows a grey Heuristic badge rather than a fake score. The debrief has a moment timeline, a provenance badge (LLM graded or Heuristic estimate) and Replay this moment. The library is a job-family shelf and grid with a CI-checked badge on each pack, and the wizard shows a provenance chip on every drafted field and runs a 60-second test call before save. Each screen in the brief has a concrete answer where today's app has a dropdown, a chat feed or four numbers. It keeps Tailwind 3, so the migration is incremental. For the OpenAI fund it makes contribution the front door: a wizard output becomes a schema-valid pack, and the plan names a Codex review step on persona PRs, which is the use the Codex for Open Source program asks to see.
reviews.no_case: The look is the least differentiated part. Catalyst-style sidebars with shadcn parts are the most common React SaaS stack, so without the bespoke cue cards and presence ring it can read as a well-made template. The live coaching score (5.6) and the library score (5.3) are both conditional on per-turn scoring shipping and on about 100 human-reviewed personas that do not exist yet. The Codex PR review is a plan, not a running workflow, and the dark cockpit plus light pages doubles QA. Effort is rated XL.

reviews.yes_case: It is a copy-in design system: Untitled UI React primitives are copied into the repo on React Aria components, so buttons, comboboxes, dialogs, menus and tables ship with keyboard and screen-reader behaviour already built in. The palette is tokenised (ink, brand blue, coach teal, positive green, caution amber, with the danger red reserved for End call) and works in light and dark. The live call sits on a dark, low-glare stage in both modes: talk-track progress on a 260px left column, the persona header and speaker-turn transcript in the centre, and a coach rail with a 'Next best question' card, up to two stacked cue cards (Objection, Missed item, Good move) and a live rubric panel. Live scores carry a 'Provisional' tag, and evidence dots jump to the exact turn. On mobile, cues and the rubric move into a bottom sheet, the composer uses 16px input to stop iOS zoom, and tap targets are 44px. The library has a sticky left facet rail with counts for role, industry, difficulty, objection type and source, removable filter chips, a 'Recommended for your role' row, and a preview drawer with brief, talk track and rubric weights. The wizard is a four-step stepper with source tabs, evidence chips that point at the source sentence, a live persona preview and a 60-second test call before saving or exporting a contribution file. Old routes redirect, and each phase ships behind a flag. Against today's chat-feed call screen and three-item dropdown, this is a clear step up in every area the brief names, and the typography (Sora headings, tabular numerals on every score) gives a serious, professional tone for a training product.
reviews.no_case: The look is the proposal's own weak point: its uniqueness self-score is 5, and Untitled UI is widely used, so reviewers may see a polished template rather than cutting-edge AI. The copy-in licence is unverified, and the Tailwind 3 to 4 move touches globals.css and the config across every screen. Scores D and E are only at baseline (5.3 and 5.4), and the Codex angle depends on conditions the proposal has not met yet.

reviews.yes_case: It is the most distinctive proposal here, and it is built around the live call. The call becomes an instrument: a coach-intensity knob (Off, Hints, Full) that visibly sets how often the coach speaks, six talk-track step keys that latch when the grader marks a step covered, a rubric rack of five channel strips whose LEDs move after each rep turn with a one-line evidence quote on tap, a 12-LED voice-level ring for the caller, and a cue strip with green, amber and red states plus a Coach me key on demand. Status is always LED colour plus glyph plus text, so it does not rely on colour alone, and mono numerals keep timers and scores from jittering during a call. The coach runs in its own model call, so the persona never breaks character. The debrief and library share the same tokens on a calmer bone surface, so dense reading and filtering stay easy to scan. Compared with today's chat app and hidden talk-track drawer, the rep gets a glanceable console that coaches and scores during the call, and the knob answers the usual complaint that coaching is either absent or noisy. It is also the look most likely to be remembered in a demo, which matters for an open-source project competing for attention in a crowded category. The phased plan keeps a working demo live at each step.
reviews.no_case: The hardware metaphor can read as novelty, and the proposal admits this but has not yet run the five-rep test it asks for. The look is split into a dark console for the call and a bone paper surface elsewhere, which is two systems rather than the single coherent look the brief asks for. Custom knobs, LED rings and step keys need keyboard and screen-reader support that the proposal has not shown, and the cue quality rests on a labelled eval set that does not exist yet. Its live-coaching score (5.3) therefore depends on work still to be done, and it is XL effort with nine screens to rebuild.

reviews.yes_case: One design system (Radix Themes 3 with Radix primitives) gives accessible defaults for focus, ARIA and keyboard behaviour, and the migration is phased: wrap the app in one Theme (teal accent, slate gray, medium radius), rebuild pre-call, debrief and dashboard first, then the live cockpit, then the JSON library and wizard, and remove Tailwind last. The live coach rail uses tentative and confirmed rubric bars, so the live score never overstates. Each whisper cites the transcript line it reacted to, and the debrief shows which model graded the call, with latency and cost. The dark stage for the call and the landing hero is the one deliberate design move. Radix components are standard and well documented, which makes this the easiest codebase for outside contributors to learn, and its accessibility posture is the strongest in the set.
reviews.no_case: It is the self-admitted default-Radix risk. Radix Themes is a clean default, and the light surfaces with teal accents will read like a well-made template, with the dark stage as the only distinctive element. Keeping Tailwind until the last phase means a long period of two CSS systems and preflight clashes. Its own SaaS viability score (F1 4) is among the lowest, and the D and E scores (5.4 and 5.2) add little beyond the two proposals that advance.

reviews.yes_case: The skin engine is a distinctive and sensible idea. Each sales job gets a data-theme scoped to its own subtree, while the reserved cue, objection, live and AI colours stay fixed across every skin, so amber always means coach and rose always means objection. Skins are validated for contrast in CI, so a contributor can submit one as a pull request with a live contrast checker. Signal, the dark default, suits a live cockpit, and Ledger (light) and Contrast (AAA) are first-class. The manager view pins to light for dense data. Attribution to OpenAI is textual and modest, which is honest. The white-label skin and persona-pack route is a real channel for training firms and call centres (F2 6).
reviews.no_case: Skins recolour the chrome; they do not add coaching or scoring. The proposal's own numbers say the layout alone is about 4.5, and D clears 5 only if a coach lane ships. Per-job skins multiply QA (capped at eight at launch), and the glass header and mesh-gradient backdrop look dated next to current product design. The stack pins Tailwind 3 and daisyUI 4 to avoid a mixed build, so it is the least modern stack in the set. The novelty is a theme engine, which is a means to the product, not the product itself.

reviews.yes_case: Copilot Rail Studio is a dark live-call cockpit built around a copilot rail. The transcript is speaker-labelled rows, not chat bubbles, and each rep line carries rubric chips such as 'Discovery +4'. A 360px right rail holds a live score strip (overall estimate and five criterion bars with deltas, each labelled Live estimate), a talk-track stepper that ticks as steps are covered, and up to three cue cards in four types (objection, next question, whisper, guardrail). Each cue has an icon and a text label, so colour is never the only signal. 'Use line' drops the suggested phrase into the composer for the rep to send; nothing auto-sends. The persona never receives cue text, so it stays in character. The debrief is a two-pane scorecard with a sticky score ring, a goal chip (Met, Partly, Not met), a grader-source chip, a moment strip, and evidence chips that highlight the exact transcript line. 'Retry from turn 8' branches the call from the missed objection, so the grade becomes practice. The library is a faceted catalogue (role, industry, difficulty, objection, call type, pack source) of 200+ JSON packs across about 18 job families, with a 'Start here for your role' row and a New persona button that opens the wizard. The five-step wizard accepts a job description, an allowlisted product URL, CRM notes, an ICP or a pasted call. Every generated field is schema-validated and editable, the JSON pack sits beside the form, and a dry run comes before save or export-as-PR. Against today's app it swaps a chat screen for a coaching cockpit, a three-item dropdown for a catalogue, and a long scroll for a navigable scorecard. Each OpenAI job is named on screen (voice, coach, grading, wizard), which answers the fund brief directly. It is the strongest of the five on the brief's first two non-negotiables, with visible and legible coaching and a real library.
reviews.no_case: It is the safest look of the five. A copilot rail beside a transcript is the Gong and Balto pattern, so distinctiveness is middling and a reviewer could read it as a well-made enterprise tool rather than cutting-edge tech. Its own research found no real live-coaching screens on Mobbin, so the rail is grounded in vendor write-ups. Nine screens, a five-step wizard, 200 launch personas and a Tailwind 4 migration is a very large load for a volunteer-maintained repo, and the 2-second cue target and cue precision are unproven until 30 scripted calls pass.

reviews.yes_case: Ambient Orb Call Room is a voice-first, FaceTime-style call room. The live call is a full-viewport canvas with a shader-driven orb about 44vh tall (audio-reactive, replacing the blurry gradient), a five-arc rubric halo where arc length is coverage and colour is the score band, a Geist Mono timer, and a Your turn / Their turn pill. Chrome fades to nothing after 3 seconds without pointer or touch, and a single whisper in Instrument Serif italic rises, dwells 6 seconds and leaves. An objection turns the halo coral and adds a one-line pivot card. Everything else is one step away: a drag-up transcript sheet and a bottom rail with mute, text, talk-track dots and End and grade. The same orb is the logo, the persona avatar and the debrief header, so the product reads as one system. Navigation is five destinations behind a 64px rail that collapses during a call, and Cmd-K opens the library and wizard from anywhere. The library is grouped by sales job with View all (n) links and 3-up cards that carry a 3-second voice preview, which suits a voice product. The wizard is a split co-pilot view where a persona card fills field by field, and each field has a source chip that highlights its source span. Each screen carries a model provenance line, so the OpenAI stack is visible. Against today's app it swaps a chat screen and a blurry orb for a distinctive, calm call room. It is the most cutting-edge look on the table and the best answer to the brief's unique-design criterion.
reviews.no_case: The coaching surface is thin for a coaching product. The chrome disappears after 3 seconds, the transcript hides behind a sheet, the rubric halo shows arcs and colours but no per-criterion numbers, and the talk track shrinks to dots, so a rep who looks away misses the cue and the pivot. The proposer's own self-score for live coaching is 5.4. The glowing shader is also the identity, which costs performance on low-end phones and risks reading as generic AI.

reviews.yes_case: Call Cockpit Curriculum turns the product into a training system, not just a practice tool. The library is the front door: a left rail with saved filters and Paths (ordered curricula), faceted chips for role, industry, difficulty and objection, and about 150 persona cards across about 20 industries with temperament meters and Start and Assign buttons. The live call is a three-zone desktop cockpit on a night background. A live rubric panel holds five criteria, each with a five-dot rating and a moving meter labelled live estimate. The transcript shows violet cue chips under the rep's last line. A right tray holds the next-best question, an amber objection alert and a talk-track stepper. Cues follow a priority (objection, then missed discovery, then the next talk-track step), and a coach switch (Silent, Whisper, Tough buyer) sits on the briefing card and in the cockpit. The debrief has a pass-threshold score ring, a moment timeline, five-dot criteria with quotes that jump to transcript lines, Replay this moment (a 90-second drill from a weak turn), and a Better line rewrite. Progress shows a criterion-by-week heatmap and certification progress. The manager view has a roster, a rep drawer with supervisor notes, and an assign-drill form with due date and pass threshold, which speaks to the entity buyers (sales orgs and call centres) the brief names. The Codex angle is concrete: Codex reviews pack PRs in CI, and AGENTS.md lets contributors scaffold packs. Against today's app it replaces a dropdown with paths and a catalogue, a chat screen with a coached cockpit, and a flat list with a certification story.
reviews.no_case: Modern is its soft spot. The LMS framing (paths, certification gates, dot ratings, roster tables) reads as enterprise training software, and its distinctiveness lives in the information architecture rather than the look. The one-cue-per-25-seconds cap is slow for a live call, and the Tough buyer coach mode is not specified. Scope is XL across nine screens plus Paths, certifications and a team view, and the Codex claim is a plan, not current usage.

reviews.yes_case: Warm Rehearsal treats a hard sales call as something to rehearse calmly. The canvas is warm paper (#FAF6F0) with terracotta primary, Fraunces headlines and Inter for UI, and the blurry orb becomes a breathing presence ring that scales with the persona's voice level. The flow is built around the rep's state: a 60-second warm-up ring (6-second inhale, 6-second exhale) and a 1-to-5 confidence check before the call, then a debrief that shows confidence before and after next to the score, so the product measures nerves as well as skill. Live, one honey-coloured whisper card at a time (14 words or fewer, with a Why expander) fades after eight seconds, plum objection alerts appear, a six-step talk-track ribbon checks off as steps are covered, and thin live-read bars show trend arrows. Pause and breathe costs no score. The debrief opens with one takeaway sentence, a grade ring, a single next-rep focus, and quote chips that replay the exact transcript line. The library is about 150 personas across 20 jobs with a temperature bar (Warm, Warm-hot, Hot) and Built-in, Community and Mine tabs. The four-step wizard takes five sources, drafts a persona, scenario and weighted rubric with a reason per weight, runs a 30-second dry run and exports a PR file. Against today's app it swaps a dropdown for a catalogue and a cold-call card for a rehearsal room. Nothing else in the field pairs a pre-call warm-up with coaching, so it has the most distinctive identity of the five. The OpenAI story is strong: a model lab that accepts any OpenAI-compatible base URL, Realtime as a voice option, and Codex-run PR review on persona files and release notes.
reviews.no_case: Calm reads as soft, and the proposal's own risk list cites buyers who call calm-first AI roleplay too agreeable, which is a credibility problem with sales managers and reviewers. Live numbers are hidden behind a toggle by default, and one whisper per 20 seconds under-delivers on the first non-negotiable. The palette and serif headings look more like a journal app than cutting-edge AI, which pulls the modern score down. Tailwind 4 touches every screen, and the Radix or Base UI question is unverified by its own admission.

reviews.yes_case: Fluent Live Coach is one enterprise design system done carefully: @fluentui/react-components v9 with FluentProvider, Griffel tokens and Fluent icons replacing Tailwind and the custom classes. The look is Teams-adjacent but tuned, with a custom teal brand ramp, a violet coach accent kept away from score colours, and a dark call stage in both themes so coaching colours read clearly. Navigation is a top bar (Practice, Library, Progress, Team for managers) with breadcrumbs that show the practice path (Library, Briefing, Live, Debrief), and a Cmd+K palette. The live call hides nav and shows a persona avatar with speaking ring, timer, mic level and a transcript with beat tags such as 'Pricing: not yet'. The coach rail has live rubric bars with change arrows, talk-track progress, one violet whisper at a time and an amber objection alert with a suggested reply, and Hold Space opens the full coach. The coach runs as a separate call per turn and returns per-criterion deltas, talk-track state, at most one whisper and objection flags. Live scores are marked provisional, a large score change must cite a quote, and if the coach fails the UI drops to scores only and says so. The library offers a card grid or DataGrid list, four-plus facets and contributor credit lines; the four-step wizard links each generated trait to its source sentence and ends with a 90-second test drive. For enterprise buyers Fluent reads as familiar and safe, and the fund angle is clear: AGENTS.md, Codex-drafted persona PRs, release-note automation and a per-session cost estimate. Against today's app it adds coaching to mobile and moves End behind a menu to prevent accidental ends.
reviews.no_case: It looks like Microsoft's default, so distinctiveness is low and a Teams-like skin does not deliver the cutting edge the brief asks for. The proposal itself flags the risk of reading as Microsoft or Teams. The library never states a persona count, so 'large' is unproven. The Phase 1 estimate (S) for replacing Tailwind and every custom class across all screens is too small, and the 'seed #0F766E' brand ramp does not map directly to Fluent's createLightTheme, which takes a full 16-step brand ramp. The React 19 peer range and the token values are unverified by its own admission.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Coach is a total rebuild on Ant Design 5 plus Ant Design X, the AI-native component layer. The library is a light, browsable catalogue: a 12-job by 10-industry grid of 120 personas (10 per cell, 2 to 3 objection tags each), so every filter combination returns something, plus a coverage map that shows empty cells and invites contributions. The wizard streams its own build as a visible ThoughtChain ('Read product page', 'Extracted 4 objections', 'Drafted persona'), each node expanding to its source quote, and it emits the same schema-valid file that hand-written personas use. The live call is a dark cockpit: a transcript as Bubble components with rep right and persona left, a 360px right column that stays open with the current cue, a ThoughtChain explaining why that cue fired, three next-best-question Prompts, an amber objection alert when triggered, and five provisional rubric bars. Every cue opens to the exact transcript line and reasoning behind it, so the rep can check the coach before trusting it. The debrief is a scorecard with a moment-replay timeline, a percentile line ('higher than 62% of past attempts at this persona') and criterion cards with linked quotes. Every AI output carries a provenance chip naming the model and prompt version. Why it beats today's app: the live screen today is a chat window with no coach, and the scenario choice is a three-item dropdown. Here the coach is a first-class visible system, the library is a real catalogue, and the wizard shows its work. The OpenAI showcase is concrete: OpenAI Realtime as the default voice transport with ElevenLabs kept as an adapter, a Settings panel that picks the grader, coach and wizard models, an AGENTS.md at the repo root, and Codex in PR review and release notes. The cue-with-receipts and the visible agent run are the features a rep, a reviewer or a Codex grant panel would remember.
reviews.no_case: Default Ant Design looks like enterprise admin software, and the proposal itself says the Look score depends on a real token and design pass that has not happened yet. Running antd CSS-in-JS alongside Tailwind preflight during migration is a known source of style clashes, and React 19 with Next 15 compatibility for antd 5 and @ant-design/x is unverified. A heavy component library on the live route strains the bundle budget, and the plan leans on lazy loading to contain it. Coaching quality is a prompt and latency problem, not a layout problem: a beautiful ThoughtChain over weak cues fails criterion D, and the proposal never shows a measured coach latency. The 120-persona set is a content project with no cost or staffing plan. F2 is self-scored 4, which is honest; training companies and call centres will not pay for a skin on a component kit.

reviews.yes_case: Live Desk Cockpit is a Catalyst-pattern app shell rebuilt from MIT parts (shadcn/ui on Radix, cmdk, Motion, Recharts) on the existing Tailwind 3 setup, so no new licence review is needed and the migration is incremental. The persistent left sidebar groups Practice (pre-call and live call), Library, Progress, Team (org only) and Settings, with Cmd-K to jump to any persona or start a call, and it collapses to icons on tablets and to a four-item bottom bar on phones. The library is organised by job family as horizontal shelves with See all and a grid toggle, a left filter rail covering role, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel and length with counts, and cards marked CI-checked when a pack passes schema and rubric-sum checks; the launch target is 120 personas and 60 scenarios. The wizard is one prompt box with source chips (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP, pasted call), then numbered clarifying choice cards with Skip, a persona-scenario-rubric-voice stepper, provenance chips that point to the source sentence behind each field, a 60-second test call, and a save or open-PR action. The live call is a dark cockpit: an SVG presence ring with a state pill (Listening, Persona speaking, Your turn), a transcript with objection chips, a coach rail with up to three cards (whisper cue, objection alert), rubric meters that only mark a criterion covered when a quote backs it, and a pace gauge. The debrief shares the same criteria with a Replay this moment action, and the landing hero is the live cockpit itself running as a loop, not a stock illustration. Why it beats today's app: a dropdown and a chat screen with no feedback become a product where coaching and scoring are the centre of the screen. The OpenAI showcase is visible: a models chip row in the cockpit, a Settings > Models page showing each model's job and per-call cost, OpenAI Realtime selectable beside ElevenLabs, and a Codex-in-PR-review workflow that checks persona schema and rubric weights and posts a review comment.
reviews.no_case: Catalyst is a well-known pattern, so the shell reads as fashionable rather than distinctive, and a judge could find the look more polished than original. The proposal dropped Catalyst code for licence reasons, which means the team has to build and polish its own AppShell, and that work is not free. The dark cockpit with light library, debrief and dashboard means two visual languages and double the QA, and the dark text contrast for amber and teal is flagged but not yet checked. Scores D and E are self-scored as conditional on per-turn scoring shipping and on at least 100 reviewed personas, so without them this is a nicer shell over the same thin engine. Per-turn structured scoring adds latency and API spend on every turn, and the sidebar plus two right rails plus a call bar is dense for a rep on a phone, where the mobile call is only partly settled.

reviews.yes_case: Call Record Console turns practice into records. Five objects (Persona, Scenario, Call Record, Rubric, Member) share one record-page header, a Path stage bar and a tab set, so a rep moves from a persona to its calls to its rubric with the same mental model a sales team already uses in its CRM. The dark-first console is calm enough for a live call, with a 56px icon rail (Home, Library, Practice, Records, Progress, Team), a breadcrumb trail, a Cmd-K palette and an engine chip that names the coach and grader models. The persona library is the deepest of the five: a facet rail (sales job, industry, difficulty, objection type, call type, source) with live counts, saved-view tabs such as 'Ramp new hires' and 'Pricing pushback', a sortable table with a card toggle, and a persona record page with six tabs (Overview, Behavior, Objections, Script, Rubric, History) and a primary Practice button. It is planned at 120 personas across 24 sales jobs and 15 industries, one JSON file each, so contributors add personas by pull request. The five-step wizard is prompt-first: one input takes a URL, job description, CRM export, ICP or pasted call, every generated field carries a provenance chip, and a 60-second dry run gates Save or Export as a PR-ready file. The live console has a Path bar that fills as the rep hits talk-track stages, rubric bars pinned to transcript lines as teal markers, inline coach lines in amber, and a coach channel that drops cues arriving after about 2.5 seconds rather than showing them late. Live numbers carry a 'live estimate' label until the grade replaces them. Why it beats today's app: the three-item dropdown and the single long debrief scroll become a navigable record system, and the planned CRM-activity sync to Salesforce or HubSpot gives training companies and BPOs (F2) a reason to pay. OpenAI shows up where it acts: a Coach chip on the console, a Graded by footer on each debrief, a per-session token and cost panel, Realtime as an adapter beside ElevenLabs, and a Codex CLI task that drafts and validates persona files.
reviews.no_case: Lightning is Salesforce's pattern, and even without the logo, a highlights header, Path bar and related lists read as a CRM. A reviewer could judge it as enterprise software rather than cutting-edge AI voice coaching, and the proposal's own risk section warns that density can drift into clutter. Tremor is a dashboard kit whose future is uncertain (the proposal cites a third-party report of a Vercel deal) and whose Tailwind 3 compatibility is unconfirmed, so one of the six dependencies may not survive. The 2.5-second coach budget is a hope, not a measured figure, and criterion D depends on it. CRM sync is planned, not built, so the F2 value is partly promise. The 80-persona launch floor is still a content project with no staffing plan, and the 'Path' and 'record page' metaphor will feel heavy to a rep who wants a 90-second warm-up.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Skins Console makes the theme the spine of the product. Each sales job (SDR cold call, AE discovery, insurance, solar and so on) is a daisyUI skin scoped to that persona's subtree, so the cold-call practice carries an orange primary and the insurance one an indigo, while reserved semantic tokens (amber for coach cues, rose for objections, teal for live and listening states, violet for AI output) never change across skins, so amber always means coach. Users switch Signal (dark), Ledger (light) or Contrast (AAA), the manager view is pinned to dense Ledger, and community skins ship as schema-checked theme files in a pull request. The live call is a cockpit: a skin-tinted orb with a 'Your turn' pill, a chat transcript with JetBrains Mono timestamps, one amber whisper card (press 1 to accept, 2 to dismiss, collapsing to a chip after 12 seconds), five rubric rings with delta arrows that tick after each turn, a six-segment talk-track bar, and a rose objection alert with a one-line suggested reply. The debrief has a horizontal moments timeline where each marker scrolls the transcript to its line, and an 'Estimated: keyword fallback' chip replaces today's yellow banner. The OpenAI story is visible and modest: a model strip names which model does coaching, grading and wizard drafting, and a developer drawer shows a realtime-style event log that contributors can watch. The stack stays on Tailwind 3 and daisyUI 4, so the migration is the smallest of the five (effort L), and the look is the most distinctive of the set (C self-scored 8). Why it beats today's app: the blurry orb and four generic feature cards go, replaced by a live product preview and a skin gallery that show the product rather than describe it.
reviews.no_case: Per-job skins are a clever gimmick that may fragment a product the brief wants to feel like one coherent system, and every new skin is another QA surface that needs contrast checks. The library is 60-plus personas at launch, which is below the 'large, open-source level' bar in the brief, and E is self-scored as conditional on seeded content. daisyUI 4 is a theme and component layer on Tailwind 3; it does not change the app's structure, so the interaction model is largely today's plus additions. Coaching is conditional on a coach lane that has not shipped, and the proposal itself says the layout alone is about 4.5 on D. Community skins risk looking like brand impersonation without tight validation of names. Business value for F2 is thin, because a call centre buys outcomes and persona packs, not a skin.

reviews.yes_case: Quiet Coach Console is a crisp, conventional, conversion-minded SaaS redesign built on the Untitled UI React copy-in kit, with React Aria accessibility underneath and Tailwind v4.3 tokens in CSS @theme. The chrome is light (canvas #F8FAFC, white surfaces, one brand blue) with a dark live stage in both modes. The top nav is Practice, Library, Create, Progress and Team, with Settings in the avatar menu; Practice runs pre-call, live call and debrief as one flow with a step bar; Create is the AI persona wizard, also opened from the library empty state. The library has a left sticky facet rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection type, source, channel) with counts and removable chips, a 'Recommended for your role' row above a three-column grid, and persona cards with an initials tile, difficulty dot, top objection and Preview and Practice buttons. The live call is a three-column console: a talk-track stepper that ticks steps off while the caller is still talking, a speaker-turn transcript with an SVG voice meter, a 'Next best question' card, up to two typed cue cards (Objection, Missed item, Good move) with dismiss, and rubric meters tagged Provisional with evidence dots that jump to the turn. Coach level (Silent, Light cues, Full coaching) is a setting. The debrief is a scorecard with criteria cards, evidence quotes and a 'Practice next' card linking to a library persona for the weakest criterion. Why it beats today's app: a dropdown and a collapsed talk track become a coach console with a rubric that moves during the call. The OpenAI showcase is practical: each surface names the model doing the work and its per-call cost, Settings lets users bring their own key, and a Codex CLI route adds a persona.
reviews.no_case: The proposal admits the look is generic: Untitled UI is widely used, category C is self-scored 5, and the author is relying on the bespoke coach rail and rubric meter to rescue the design. A reviewer will see a template, which is the opposite of the brief's cutting-edge bar. Licence terms for copy-in Untitled UI inside an MIT repo are unverified, and the Base UI fallback would mean building the whole look in-house. Moving from Tailwind 3 to v4.3 churns globals.css and tailwind.config.ts across every screen, and the phase plan is about a week before any visible progress. F1 is self-scored 6.5 for F2 and 4 for F1 because SaaS is crowded. The conversion-first hero and the 'Create' top-level nav put sign-up ahead of the live practice experience, and the persona library is described as a full open-source catalogue with no launch count.

reviews.yes_case: Call Cockpit Curriculum is a whole-app redesign with two modes. Light mode is a curriculum-first Library: a slim left rail (Learn, Library, Practice, Progress, Team), ordered Paths with certification gates and manager-assigned drills, a faceted catalogue of about 150 personas across roughly 20 industries, filters for role, industry, difficulty and objection type, and a source-first AI wizard (Source, Persona, Scenario and rubric, Dry run) that saves privately or proposes a pack. Dark mode is the live cockpit: a 300px rubric rail with five criteria as 1-5 dots and moving meters labelled live estimate, a transcript with violet cue chips under the rep's last line naming the exact next question, an amber objection alert, a talk-track stepper and a composer. A second, cheaper coach stream returns one cue per turn chosen by priority and rate-limited to one per 25 seconds, while the persona stays in character. Today the app is a chat window with a three-item dropdown and no feedback until the call ends, so this beats it on the brief's first two needs and on the basic shape of a sales-training product. The Codex pitch is concrete: AGENTS.md, a persona-pack scaffold, Codex CLI to draft and validate packs, and Codex-run PR review in CI. The phased migration keeps today's chat as a fallback behind a flag, which makes it buildable in steps. Business read: F2 is strong because paths, assignments and certification match how training firms and call centres buy; F1 is a fair 6.
reviews.no_case: XL scope: nine screens, a wizard, a cockpit, a pack system and a roughly 150-persona content load. The proposal's own risk list concedes that persona quality varies by contributor and that the library cannot claim scale without human review. The scores are self-reported, and the Look 8 is a claim, not a demonstrated design. Criterion D depends entirely on cue latency under 2 to 3 seconds, which the proposal assumes rather than shows. Paths, certification gates and assignments add LMS machinery the brief did not ask for, and the Team view can only ship as a read-only MVP, so the F2 enterprise story is partly promised. Five dots on a 300px rail in a dark cockpit risks density on a laptop. The Codex fund case leans on Codex reviewing persona PRs, which is plausible but not built.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Coach rebuilds the product on Ant Design X, the AI-native layer over antd 5, so the coaching surfaces are first-class components rather than hand-rolled cards. The live cockpit is always dark (darkAlgorithm scoped to its subtree) and reads as a real call console: the transcript is a Bubble list with small coach tags under rep lines ('Good: asked budget', 'Missed: next step'), a 360px right column that stays open with the current cue, next-best questions as Prompts, an amber objection alert, and five provisional rubric bars that lock at debrief. Every cue opens to the exact transcript line and to a ThoughtChain of why it fired, so a rep can check the coach before trusting it. This is the clearest answer in the set to the brief's need for evidence-backed coaching. The library is light and filterable (sales job, industry, difficulty, objection tags) with a coverage map that shows 12 sales jobs by 10 industries, 10 personas per cell, and marks empty cells as help wanted, a contributor hook no other proposal has. The wizard streams its own build as a ThoughtChain ('Read product page', 'Extracted 4 objections', 'Drafted rubric'), with each node expanding to its source quote. The OpenAI case is the strongest of the five: Realtime as the default voice transport with ElevenLabs kept as an adapter, a settings panel choosing the grader, coach and wizard models, a provenance chip on every AI output naming the model and prompt version, Codex CLI for PR review and release notes, and a public grader-eval page as stretch. Against today's chat app with no coaching, this is a different product.
reviews.no_case: Default antd is the look problem. The proposal admits it reads as enterprise admin and that the Look score depends on a token and design pass that is not specified. Ant Design's CSS-in-JS and Tailwind preflight will fight during migration, and React 19 and Next 15 compatibility is unverified. Making Realtime the default voice path is a pipeline change that could slow the core launch. The self-scored F2 of 4 is fair: an enterprise sales-org buyer will see a console that looks like an admin tool. Coaching quality depends on the prompt and cue latency, which no layout can rescue.

reviews.yes_case: Call Record Console treats each call, persona, scenario, rubric and member as a record in an original dark console, borrowing Lightning's structure without its logo or blue chrome. Every record has the same header and tabs, and a Path bar of talk-track stages (Open, Diagnose, Qualify, Handle objection, Close) fills as the rep reaches each stage, the same component before, during and after the call. The live console has a persona rail with buyer state and a Geist Mono timer, a transcript timeline where rubric hits pin as teal markers and coach lines sit inline in amber, and a right panel with a whisper cue, a next-question chip, an objection alert, the Path tracker and a rubric meter whose bars link to evidence lines. Coach mode is Silent, Whisper or Full, and cues older than about 2.5 seconds are dropped rather than shown late. The debrief is honest: if the heuristic grader ran, an Estimate chip replaces the letter grade, and a footer names the grader model and rubric version. The proposal also finds a real defect in the repo, where the keyword fallback can show an F at 50 percent, and it fixes that in scoring as well as UI. The library is 120 personas across 24 sales jobs and 15 industries, with saved views and a six-tab persona record page. The wizard is five steps with a source snippet on every field, a 60-second dry run, and export as a PR-ready file. Codex fits through a JSON-schema CI validator and a Codex CLI task that drafts and validates persona files. Business read: F2 at 7 is fair given BPO and training-company demand; F1 is a 6.
reviews.no_case: Records, related lists, a Path bar, a transcript timeline and a utility panel can pile into the CRM clutter the proposal itself warns about. The 'cap at three panels' rule is a promise, not a layout. Five objects and six persona tabs ask a rep to learn a sales-ops mental model before they can practise. Dark-first with a light print mode doubles the contrast work. The Tremor recommendation rests on an unverified claim that it is joining Vercel, and the Lightning borrowing is close enough to invite trade-dress questions. The CRM-sync roadmap pulls the product toward being a sales tool in its own right, which is a bigger product than the brief needs. Distinctiveness is middling because the metaphor is familiar to anyone who has used a CRM.

reviews.yes_case: Warm Rehearsal is the most distinctive proposal in the set. The app becomes a practice room: a warm paper canvas with Fraunces display type and Inter for UI, a breathing presence ring that follows the persona's voice level and replaces the blurry orb, a 60-second warm-up before every call, and a confidence check before and after so growth is visible. The library is about 150 JSON personas across 20 jobs, filtered by job, industry, temperature (Warm, Warm-hot, Hot) and objection, and the Hot tier pushes back rather than agreeing. Live, the coach gives one whispered cue at a time, 14 words or fewer, with a Why tap and a Quiet mode, in a right rail with a six-step talk-track ribbon and five criterion bars with trend arrows. The debrief opens with one takeaway sentence and one next-rep focus instead of five equal cards, and tapping a quote replays that exact transcript line. The wizard takes five sources, drafts a persona, scenario and weighted rubric, runs a 30-second dry run, and exports a persona as a pull request.
