Shadcn, Geist, hairline cards, a violet primary and a dark hero with a looping demo look like the default SaaS template the brief names as the problem. The swipe deck is a feature bolted onto that look rather than an idea that shapes it, and its two-mood split (dark for live, light for everything else) has no unifying concept behind it. Nothing in it would make a reviewer stop scrolling the README.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit and Drill Feed pairs a dark instrument cockpit for live calls with a vertical snap feed of 30-second objection drills as the front door. A drill card puts one objection on screen, gives 20 seconds to answer while a ring fills, and returns five scores and one quoted line in under five seconds. Then it swipes to the next, which makes practice a daily habit and a shareable clip. The live cockpit has a persona instrument with an SVG voice ring driven by real audio level, state chips such as Skeptical or Price-sensitive, a six-step talk-track rail, a speaker-labelled transcript with inline coach markers, and a right panel with one amber cue, a coral objection alert with two suggested replies, five live rubric bars that flash plus 4 or minus 4, and a next-question card. The coach runs as a sidecar returning zod-validated JSON. Every cue must quote a transcript line, cues are rate-limited to one per 20 seconds and held while the rep speaks, and if the coach fails the screen shows Coach offline while the call continues. Personas are YAML files published with a JSON Schema, about 150 across 16 job families, each with a 30-second drill variant, and Remix turns any persona into a PR-ready file. The wizard uses structured outputs against that schema and marks every generated field with its source. The OpenAI story is the most candid of the five, flagging that the Codex fund terms are discretionary. Against today's three-item dropdown and blurry orb, a daily drill is a stronger reason to return than a library alone.
reviews.no_case: It is two products stapled together. The proposal admits the feed cannot carry coaching depth, so the cockpit still has to carry the core, and the feed is a funnel layered on top. Its own self-scores (D 5.5, E 5.4) sit at or below baseline, and E falls short below about 60 reviewed personas, which a volunteer open-source project will not produce quickly. It also stays on Tailwind 3 for the migration, and the TikTok-style feed is the toy-like risk its own text flags for enterprise sales buyers.

reviews.yes_case: Flight Deck Cockpit makes the whole app one instrument panel. Flights and debriefs default to a dark cockpit, browsing defaults to daylight, and both come from one CSS token file, so every screen shares one grammar of tape gauges, status lamps and tabular telemetry. Pre-flight is a checklist of status lamps (mic level, persona loaded, goal read, talk track reviewed), and Start flight stays locked until mic and goal are green. In the live call, six rubric tape gauges move after every turn with weights and tallies (Discovery 3 of 10). An On course lamp and a JetBrains Mono timer sit in the top bar, and a right-hand cue stack shows at most two coach cues, each with a Use line button that drops the phrase into the input. The coach is a separate grader call. It never speaks as the persona, returns rubric deltas plus at most one cue quoting the transcript, is throttled to one cue per 20 seconds, expires cues after 8 seconds, and falls back to an amber Estimate lamp so a heuristic score is never mistaken for a graded one. The debrief is a black-box replay: outcome stamp, score ring, a timeline with score-over-time curve and event markers. Scrubbing or pressing play rewinds the gauges to match, and each evidence chip seeks to the second the quote was said. The library uses faceted rails with counts, a cmdk palette and 'flown N times' social proof. The wizard streams persona fields into a live preview with confidence chips, requires a test flight before saving, and exports PR-ready JSON validated by the same zod schema CI uses. Against today's three-item dropdown, blurry orb and silent call, this is a complete product system, not a reskin. The OpenAI story is visible: each flight's report names the model behind each job (GPT-4.1-mini for grading and cues, Structured Outputs for the wizard, Realtime as a selectable voice engine) with a per-flight cost estimate, and AGENTS.md plus Codex-reviewed persona and rubric PRs give the fund a concrete maintainer workflow.
reviews.no_case: The metaphor is the main risk: a dark instrument panel with Fly, Pre-flight, Black box and End and grade can read as a gimmick to HR and enterprise buyers. The library spec is also the weakest part of its E case. It names no seeded persona count, and its facet examples omit recruiting, retail, real estate and auto even though the brief names them. Its own D and E self-scores are both 6.5, which holds only if the sidecar and the library ship as designed.

reviews.yes_case: Swipe-to-Rehearse Coach Studio is dark-first for the live call and light everywhere else. A violet AI colour is reserved for anything the model wrote, so reps always know what came from the model. The live call has three zones: a left rail of talk-track steps that tick as the coach detects them, a centre transcript with speaker labels, mono timestamps and a waveform header, and a right coach panel with stacked rubric meters that move with delta chips while the rep is still talking, plus one whisper card. The whisper card lands within about two seconds of the rep's turn and says what to ask next, and an objection alert banner appears on a trap. The coach is a separate model stream, so the persona stays in character and never sees coaching. If coach latency spikes, the call carries on and scoring simply lags. Live meters are labelled 'live estimate', and the debrief re-grades with the heavier model and is the authoritative grade. It has a score ring, a call timeline whose coloured markers jump to the exact transcript line, criterion accordions with evidence quotes, and a 'Biggest miss' card that offers to play the fixed line in the AI voice. The library is a sticky filter rail with a three-column grid of persona cards showing objection chips and difficulty meters. Its launch target is 150-plus personas across 20-plus sales jobs, including insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, auto, medical devices, B2B procurement, recruiting, retail, customer success and collections, each with an objection pack. Swipe (right to run, left to skip, up to save) is an opt-in drill mode, so the grid stays the serious default. The four-step wizard takes any source, shows a provenance badge on generated fields, estimates cost before generating, runs a dry run before saving, and exports the same JSON file format as the library, so AI-drafted personas can return upstream as contributions. A model strip names each role's model and per-call cost, and a bring-your-own-key page makes the OpenAI stack inspectable for fund reviewers. Against today's dropdown and blurred orb, it is the most complete answer to the brief's persona-library requirement of the five.
reviews.no_case: Swipe is a motif that can read as a dating app to enterprise buyers, which undercuts the serious-training positioning even as an opt-in mode. Once swipe is demoted, the core is a well-made but conventional card grid, sheet and cockpit, so it is the least memorable of the top three. It also gives no self-scores, so its 2-second cue latency and 150-persona claims are targets it has not shown it can meet.

reviews.yes_case: Pipeline Rehearsal Console makes the home screen a board of the rep's real deal stages. Each card shows its last rehearsal score and a Rehearse button, and any practice call, pre-built or wizard-made, can attach to a deal. Stages generalize by job, with aging buckets for collections, screen-to-offer for recruiting and renewal windows for customer success, so it is not a sales-only metaphor. Practice is grounded in the actual work. The pre-call briefing shows a deal card with the last call summary and 'fix next time' items pulled from the last debrief, and a Rehearse tomorrow's call button appears when a calendar event links to a deal. The live call is a three-column cockpit on the dark canvas. A left rail shows done, now and next talk-track steps and the goal. The centre transcript runs in three lanes (persona teal, rep neutral, coach violet between turns). A right rail holds a provisional rubric ring, five criterion rows marked provisional with 1-to-5 chips, and a Next best question card. Coach cues have types (next question, objection alert with a suggested bridge, talk-track step complete, pace or filler warning), each with a Why expander. The persona never sees coach text, and the latency target is under 1.5 seconds. The debrief has a scannable top band, a Moments timeline that jumps the transcript, criteria with quotes, and a CTA that generates a drill aimed at the weakest criterion. The library is about 180 personas across 14 job families and 16 industries, with a pipeline-stage filter. The wizard has four steps, 'What we read' chips that show what was extracted, a Show schema toggle, rubric sliders that must total 100, and redaction before sending. Against today's dropdown and silent call, it ties practice to the deals reps actually work, and the OpenAI model stack with per-call cost sits on the landing page and in every debrief footer.
reviews.no_case: It turns the home screen into a sales kanban, so a training tool for an open-source project starts to look like a lightweight CRM, and collections, recruiting and CS only get bolted-on lanes. Most screens default to light with Sora and Inter kept, so it reads as less cutting-edge than the cockpit proposals. Its L effort is optimistic for nine screens, a kanban and a Tailwind v3 to v4 move, and its D and E self-scores of 6.0 clear baseline only if the 1.5-second latency and 180-persona targets hold.

reviews.yes_case: Open Practice Hub is a Hugging Face-style community hub for call practice. The top bar has Practice, Library, Create persona and Progress, plus a GitHub stars pill and Fork. The hero says 'Practice the call before it counts' and is followed by task chips for SDR cold call, AE discovery, insurance, mortgage, solar, home services and collections, and a Trending personas row. The library is a three-column card grid. Each card has a monogram ring with a hue hashed from the name, a difficulty bar, objection tags, stars, forks and an author handle. Clicking opens a right-side model card with what the persona tests, rubric weights, a 30-second sample, a fork tree showing lineage, and Start practice, Fork and Star buttons. That makes the library a contributor ecosystem, which is what an open-source fund reviewer looks for, rather than a static dropdown. The wizard reads a job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP or a pasted call. It asks up to three follow-ups that cite source lines, plays a 20-second cold open in the persona's voice while the form fills, and publishes as Save privately, Share to team, or Open PR with the persona file prefilled. The live call is three zones. A left rail of talk-track steps checks off as they are covered. The centre has a persona presence orb with a speaking state and a speaker-labelled transcript. The right coach column has six rubric meters that tick with deltas such as +6 Pricing, one amber whisper cue, and a rose objection alert with a suggested bridge line. Coach intensity (Quiet, Standard, Strict) and a per-minute cost meter sit in the bar, and the coach is isolated from the persona's realtime context. Against today's dropdown and chat-like call, it adds a visible contributor path and social proof while keeping the rubric discipline.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive look of the top five: a flat hairline system with an indigo primary that reads as a well-made Hugging Face clone, not cutting-edge AI coaching. Its persona and coach numbers are soft (120-plus personas, and a roughly 2-second cue latency it says to spike before committing to), and it gives no self-scores, so it has the thinnest evidence for the coaching bar of any proposal that reached the top three.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit and Drill Feed pairs a dark-first live cockpit with a TikTok-style 30-second objection feed as the front door. Each feed card runs one 30-second objection. The rep answers for 20 seconds while a ring fills linearly, then sees five scores and one quoted line in under five seconds before swiping to the next objection. That is a daily habit short enough to repeat, and each result is shareable as a clip, which gives it a retention advantage over today's app, where a full call gets no feedback until grading. The cockpit is the depth layer. A 240px left panel holds a persona with an SVG voice ring driven by real audio level, state chips such as Skeptical or Price-sensitive, a timer and a six-step talk-track rail. The centre has a speaker-labelled transcript with inline coach markers. A 320px right panel holds one amber whisper cue, a coral objection alert with two suggested replies, five live rubric bars that flash +4 or -4, and a next-question card. Every cue must quote a transcript line, is rate-limited to one per 20 seconds, and is suppressed while the rep is speaking. Live scores are labelled 'live est.' and replaced by the evidence-backed grade afterward, and a 'Coach offline' status keeps the call going if the sidecar fails. The persona library is schema-first: about 150 personas across 16 job families, each with a 30-second drill variant, published as JSON Schema under /personas so contributors add one by pull request. The Codex plan is concrete (AGENTS.md, Codex review on persona and rubric PRs, Codex-drafted release notes, Codex Security scans of auth and MFA). It also says plainly that OpenAI's grant is discretionary and to verify the amount before applying, which a fund reviewer will trust.
reviews.no_case: Its own self-scores sit right at the bar on the two basic needs (D 5.5 and E 5.4), and E falls short below about 60 reviewed personas. It admits that nine screens, a feed, a wizard and two voice providers is too much for one release. A TikTok-style feed at the front door also risks reading as a toy to enterprise buyers, so its most novel idea is the one most likely to be cut in practice.

reviews.yes_case: Flight Deck Cockpit runs each practice call as a flight, with three screens that share one instrument grammar. Pre-flight is a briefing: status lamps for mic level, persona loaded and goal read, a mission card that maps success criteria to rubric weights, objection cards with a prep answer, and talk-track phases that tick off live. Start flight stays disabled until mic and goal are green. In the live HUD, a dark panel holds the flight log (timestamped, speaker-tagged turns) in the centre, six rubric tape gauges on the left that move after every rep turn with tallies such as Discovery 3 of 10, and at most two coach cue cards on the right. Cues come from fixed categories (objection, next question, talk-track phase, forbidden early claim such as price), each with evidence quotes, and one tap on Use line drops the suggested phrase into the input. The debrief is a black box: an outcome stamp (Goal achieved, Partial, Missed), a score ring, and a timeline of the whole call with a score curve and event markers. Scrub or press play and the transcript, audio and gauges rewind together, and each evidence chip seeks to the exact second. A Next flight card gives one drill. The library is faceted (role, industry, difficulty, objection type, mode) with 'flown N times' social proof. The five-step wizard (Source, Persona, Scenario, Rubric, Test flight) streams fields with confidence chips through OpenAI Structured Outputs against the same zod schema CI uses, never saves before a test flight, and exports PR-ready JSON. Against today's chat app with no feedback and a three-item dropdown, this is a complete whole-app system with a clear identity and a daylight mode for browsing. The OpenAI story is concrete: each flight shows which model handled grading and coaching, with a per-flight cost estimate, Realtime is a selectable voice engine, and a /contribute page plus AGENTS.md give contributors and Codex CLI a clear path. An amber Estimate lamp marks heuristic fallback scores so they are never mistaken for graded ones.
reviews.no_case: The persona library is never sized: 'a large open persona set' is not a number, and the brief asks for a visible catalogue spanning every sales job, so the E score of 6.5 is asserted rather than shown. The 20-second cue throttle silences most of a fast call, which weakens the real-time coaching the brief makes non-negotiable. The mobile End and grade long-press is a hidden control that screen-reader and motor-impaired users cannot easily reach. Dark cockpit contrast is an admitted risk, and an XL build across five phases is a lot to land.

reviews.yes_case: Broadcast Desk treats every practice call as a live broadcast. On the live screen a dark stage shows the persona as an audio-reactive ring, with captions as a lower third, a talk-track segment bar and a mono timer. A 360px right rail is a coach feed of typed cues with glyphs (amber nudge, rose objection alert, violet next question, green praise). Each cue links to the transcript quote it reacted to, and any cue can be pinned. A left strip holds a five-criterion scoreboard with provisional bars and green or rose delta chips. The coach runs out of band from the persona: at most one cue every two turns, never while the persona is speaking in voice mode, aiming for a cue within 1.5 seconds of the rep's turn ending. After the call, the debrief is replay-first. A segmented score ring has one arc per criterion. A timeline shows auto-marked moments such as 'Best moment', 'Missed fee question' and 'Strongest close', each playable and exportable as a 1200x630 moment card. Criterion rows with quotes jump the replay to the matching timestamp. Landing, library, wizard, pre-call and dashboard use light surfaces, so enterprise screens stay calm. The persona library is the most specific in the set: 150 or more personas across 20 or more sales jobs (insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, auto, medical devices, B2B procurement, recruiting, collections, customer success), three difficulty levels, tagged objections, a 'Hear them' 10-second voice sample on every card, a 'Good first persona' tag, and collections such as 'Insurance renewals'. The wizard drafts from a job description, URL, CRM notes, ICP or pasted call, shows provenance per field, and requires a 60-second test drive before saving. It treats source text as data, so a pasted page cannot rewrite a persona's rules. Against today's blank dropdown and chat screen, the rep gets a stage that reacts during the call and a replay worth sharing. A Model rack names the model behind each role, and voice can be OpenAI Realtime.
reviews.no_case: Stream and overlay language (broadcast, pinned cues, shareable moment cards) is the riskiest look in the set for enterprise sales leaders. The coach feed is still a chat-style list, which is the very diagnosis the brief used against today's live screen. A 150-persona library with a 10-second voice sample for each is a heavy content and audio-generation load with no budget shown, and the 1.5-second cue target rests on a coach pipeline that does not exist yet. XL effort across nine screens plus a new coach pipeline is a lot for one open-source release.

reviews.yes_case: Patch Bay Console makes the live call an instrument. On a dark graphite chassis, the live console has three columns. Left: a talk-track sequencer of six step keys that latch when the grader marks a step covered. Centre: a caller window with a 12-LED voice-level ring, a state LED ('Dana speaking' or 'Your turn'), the last four turns and the full transcript on scroll. Right: a rubric rack of five channel strips, each with a coverage meter and a covered, partial or missed LED that moves after every rep turn, plus a one-line evidence quote on tap. A cue strip along the bottom shows one colour-coded cue (green on track, amber next question, red objection), a 'Coach me' key and a hint counter. A labelled coach-intensity knob (Off, Hints, Full) sets how often the coach speaks, and keys 1 to 6 jump to step keys. The coach runs in its own call, so the persona never breaks character, and every status is LED colour plus glyph plus text. The rest of the app keeps the same tokens on a calmer bone surface, so reading and filtering stay easy. The debrief is a two-pane evidence view: each quote chip scrolls and blinks the matching transcript line, and a model ledger shows which model graded, token counts and estimated cost. The library targets about 240 personas across roughly 20 industries and 12 job families, with a five-position LED difficulty dial, multi-select filters kept in the URL, saved presets and a detail drawer. A four-step wizard (Source, Persona, Rubric, Dry run) drafts persona and rubric weights from a URL, document, CRM notes or a pasted call, then runs a 60-second dry run before save. Against a dropdown of three scenarios and a blurry orb, this console gives feedback while the call happens. It is the most distinctive of the five, and the OpenAI story is visible: bring-your-own key for any OpenAI-compatible base URL, gpt-4.1-mini as default, and a Realtime voice toggle, so credit use shows on screen.
reviews.no_case: The hardware look is a novelty bet for sales buyers, and knobs, LED chases and channel strips need custom keyboard and screen-reader work that the proposal leaves for later testing. The first release ships only 60 reviewed personas against a 240 target, so the library is thin at launch. The proposal also says Codex already runs PR review and release notes in this repo. It does not: the repo has no AGENTS.md, no workflow files and no Codex reference outside the brief, and an OpenAI fund reviewer would check that first.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Room Mission Control is a dark telemetry console for practising live calls, with a light theme designed at equal weight rather than inverted. The live call has three zones. A left rail carries the call clock, a talk-ratio gauge that turns coral after 20 seconds above 70 percent, a words-per-minute gauge, a tone bar, and rubric meters that stay tentative until a verbatim quote confirms them. The centre is a speaker-lane transcript with per-turn waveforms, a composer and a persistent End and grade. The right rail is a coach rail that shows one amber whisper at a time, coral objection chips, checkpoints that tick off, and the next question as ghost text. Coaching and scoring come from a separate coach channel, so the persona never breaks character, and each event type renders in only one place. Reps can mute the coach or rate a cue as useful or noisy to tune it. The debrief replays the call: a score ring with a 'calibrated' badge, a full-call waveform with evidence ticks coloured by criterion, and criterion cards whose quotes jump to timestamps. The library launches with 150 to 200 personas across 12 to 15 job families, with multi-select facets shared through the URL. The wizard takes a URL, a document, a transcript or a form, cites the source line for every drafted field, and stress-tests the draft with three simulated calls before save. Against a chat app with no feedback, the live screen becomes a cockpit. On the OpenAI side, Realtime over WebRTC is the showcased default voice, GPT-4.1 mini handles persona text, coaching, grading and the wizard, and a model-stack strip on each call shows which model did what, with latency and cost.
reviews.no_case: The coach runs on rolling windows 'roughly every 8 to 12 seconds' yet promises a cue within two seconds of the rep's turn ending, and the proposal never reconciles the two, which undercuts the live coaching the brief needs. Dark telemetry sits close to the trading terminal the proposal itself warns about, so its distinctiveness is middling next to the more unusual cockpits. A 150 to 200 persona launch sits against its own 'persona quality beats quantity' risk, leaving the content burden unresolved, and the migration churn of Base UI and Tailwind v4 is flagged but not costed.

reviews.yes_case: Radix Coach Stage is the most buildable redesign. One Radix Themes system (teal accent, slate grays, medium radius) gives every screen the same focus, keyboard and ARIA behaviour, and custom work shrinks to a documented set of coach patterns. The landing hero and live call sit on a dark stage surface with a faint teal tint and solid panels. Library, pre-call, debrief, progress and team sit on a light slate background with hairline borders in place of soft shadows. Sora display headings keep the brand, and Geist Mono tabular numerals keep timers and scores from jittering. The live call has three columns: persona avatar, state chip and voice ring; a transcript with speaker lanes and inline tags for objections, pricing and next steps; and a coach rail with one whisper card that cites the exact transcript line it reacted to, a talk-track stepper, and a rubric meter whose tentative and confirmed bars keep the live score from overstating the evidence. The debrief has an accordion of criteria with bar, weight, rationale and quotes, each with 'jump to line' and 'play audio', plus a sticky transcript and a 'Next drill' card. The library is a faceted rail (sales job, industry, difficulty, objection, channel) with counts over roughly 120 seeded personas stored as zod-validated JSON. The wizard (Source, Extract, Shape, Dry run) streams fields with evidence and confidence chips and publishes locally or opens a prefilled PR. The OpenAI case is explicit and honest: Realtime is a named voice option, a Models page shows per-call cost, a Grader Lab compares rubric agreement, and a 'Reviewed with Codex' badge appears only once Codex review actually runs. Against today's template look, it gives a coherent system that measures and coaches the call.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive of the five, by its own admission: the default Radix look is close to the default-template look the brief already rejects, and the dark stage and voice ring are the only things separating it. Its persona library is about 120 personas, and the proposal says the realised library score stays under baseline until seed content ships, so the E fit is weak. For a brief asking for cutting-edge and unique, it reads as competent and safe.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit and Drill Feed is a whole-app redesign on shadcn/ui with Geist type and a dark ink-950 instrument-panel palette, where signal teal marks only live state and coral marks only objection alerts. The core is a three-column live call: a left persona panel with an audio-driven SVG voice ring, a Geist Mono timer and a talk-track rail; a centre speaker-labelled transcript; and a right column with one amber whisper cue, a coral objection alert with two suggested replies, and five live rubric bars that flash +4 or -4. Coaching runs in a sidecar model call so the persona never breaks character, every cue must quote a transcript line, and cues are rate-limited to one per 20 seconds. A 30-second objection drill feed sits on top as the daily habit and shareable clip, backed by a schema-first library of about 150 personas across 16 job families and a four-step AI wizard that returns validated JSON and cites its sources. Against today's chat window, three-item dropdown and blurry orb, this turns practice into an instrument panel with real coaching, a real library, and Codex work inside the repo (AGENTS.md, Codex review on persona and rubric PRs), which maps directly onto the fund's PR-review criteria. It also keeps existing route paths and sizes each migration phase realistically.
reviews.no_case: The scope is XL: nine screens, a feed, a wizard and two voice providers, which the proposal itself admits is too much for one release, so the cockpit could slip behind the feed. A TikTok-style drill feed may read as a toy to enterprise buyers. The 150-persona claim depends on a content review pipeline that does not exist yet, and the coaching score depends on p95 cue latency under two seconds, which is untested. The fund dollar figure is unresolved by the proposal's own note.

reviews.yes_case: Pipeline Rehearsal Console turns the app into a sales-native workspace. The home is a pipeline board of deal stages, each card carries a Rehearse button, and the pre-call briefing shows the company, last call summary and a fix-next-time list pulled from the last debrief. The live call is a three-column coached cockpit: a talk-track stepper with done, now and next, a persona presence card, a three-lane transcript with coach markers between turns, and a provisional rubric rail with five 1-to-5 chips that the debrief later confirms with quotes. Cues are typed (next question, objection alert, talk-track step complete, pace or filler warning), capped at one per 20 seconds, and each has a Why expander. The library is a faceted set of about 180 personas across 14 job families and 16 industries, and the wizard uses the same zod schema as its structured output, with a What we read chip list that shows what was extracted and a server-side URL allowlist. Against today's app, it answers the rep's real question, what am I walking into tomorrow, and it labels every live score provisional, with a Heuristic estimate chip when the grader fails.
reviews.no_case: This is the weakest look of the five. It keeps Sora and Inter, uses a blue primary and a light canvas, which repeats the template feel the brief diagnosed as the problem. Mixing a dark live call with light pipeline, library and dashboard screens risks an incoherent system. The pipeline home is a large scope bet that pulls an open-source trainer toward CRM territory, and it depends on imported deal data, with CRM connectors left to paid or contributor work, so most reps would meet an empty board at first. The 180-persona library is a content job with no review budget described.

reviews.yes_case: Open Practice Hub reframes the app as a community hub in the Hugging Face mould: task chips across the top, trending-first sorting, one-line cards with author credit and usage counts, and a right-side model card for every persona showing what it tests, its rubric weights, a 30-second sample, fork lineage, and Start practice, Fork and Star buttons. The look is light by default with a dark call route, an indigo primary and a flat monogram system. The call screen has a dark control bar, persona-labelled transcript bubbles, six live rubric meters that tick with deltas such as +6 Pricing, an amber whisper cue and a rose objection alert with a bridge line. The wizard reads a job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP or pasted call, asks up to three follow-ups, cites source lines, runs a dry run, then saves privately, shares to a team, or opens a PR. It also takes a sound position that rep leaderboards are opt-in and measure improvement, which suits team buyers. For reviewers, the fork-and-star loop is an obvious open-source contribution path that today's three-item dropdown lacks.
reviews.no_case: Putting community sharing and popularity ahead of the rep's own practice means the trainer may read as a marketplace with a call screen attached. The look is a Hugging Face-style light template on Sora and Inter, the least cutting edge of the five. The live coaching column has less evidence and budget detail than its rivals, the launch library is only a 120-persona target, and the proposal gives no self-scores, so its business and Codex case is the vaguest. Pass-rate leaderboards depend on opt-in anonymised results that will not exist at launch.

reviews.yes_case: Practice Graph Studio is a GitHub-native redesign. The top bar mirrors a repo header, every persona is a versioned file with a schema check, and the Source tab shows the file with an Edit as PR action, so contributing and practising use the same surfaces. The look is dark-first with a calm Geist and Geist Mono system and signal teal for passing and live state. A 52-week practice graph shades each day by score band rather than volume, so a streak means improvement. The live cockpit has a 56px control bar, a two-lane transcript, and a rubric panel whose bars fill as criteria are covered and turn solid only when the grader confirms them. A single whisper cue auto-dismisses after eight seconds and links to the exact transcript line. The wizard builds a persona card where every field shows its source line, runs a 60-second test call, and opens a PR diff, with a Codex review comment planned before Open PR. Against today's dropdown and generic gradient hero, it gives reviewers a concrete open-source story: a product-true live call, a browsable catalogue of versioned files, and a visible contribution path on every screen.
reviews.no_case: The launch library is a 60-persona floor, well below the 120 to 180 that rival proposals promise, so it may fall short of the brief's large-library bar for every sales job. The dark developer-tool look is a real risk for sales buyers, as the proposal concedes. The contribution graph can still reward volume unless its quality guard works. PR-based persona submission assumes GitHub literacy that most reps and sales managers lack, and the Codex review of persona PRs is still planned rather than shipped. The Tailwind v4 move carries a reported Radix Select background problem that must be tested before merge.

reviews.yes_case: Keynote Bento is a full bento-grid system: a light canvas with white hairline tiles for pre-call, debrief, progress and team, and one dark stage for the live call and the hero. It runs on shadcn/ui with Geist display type at 56 to 88px and spring motion. The live call keeps the rep's eyes on the caller: a stage on the left with an orb whose ring shows listening, thinking and speaking, a talk-time meter and two caption lines, and a bento rail on the right with a whisper tile, next-question tile, objection tile, talk-track progress and live rubric deltas such as +4, each tied to a transcript quote. Coach levels are Off, Whisper and Full, with a target of about two seconds. The persona library is the broadest in the group: 150 personas across 25 job families, a natural-language search box, facets for rep job, buyer role, industry, difficulty and objection type, and a Build with AI tile that leads into a four-step wizard with a 60-second dry run. Against today's dropdown and four feature cards, the debrief becomes a scannable score timeline with cues, and a team surface finally appears that reuses the same bento components.
reviews.no_case: Bento grids are now a familiar pattern, so the look is polished but not distinctive. Its white tiles and signal-blue actions sit close to the default SaaS look the brief criticises. The proposal's own estimate drops from 5.2 to about 4.6 if only the built-in personas ship, and the 150-persona seed is a large content job with uneven quality. Dense tiles at 390 pixels risk overflow, which the proposal flags. Its Base UI claim rests on sources that disagree about Radix support. It also keeps a react-three-fiber orb on the live stage, which adds weight on phones.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Skins gives each sales job its own colour and keeps the coaching colours fixed. SDR cold calls wear spark orange, insurance and mortgage wear harbour indigo, and home services and solar wear verdant lime. A skin scopes to its subtree with data-theme, so the job's briefing card, library cards and debrief top band all pick up the colour. Whatever the skin, amber always means coach, rose always means objection, teal always means live and violet always means AI, so a skin can never make a warning look decorative. The live call is a focus mode: the header collapses to a skin dot, a mono timer and End. A whisper card slides in and collapses to a chip after 12 seconds, and rubric rings tick with delta badges. Against today's blue template with a blurry orb and a three-item dropdown, each job now has a visible home in a faceted library grouped by job. Community skins are theme files checked in CI, so a first contribution is a small pull request, and a Make a skin page with a live contrast checker makes that approachable. A developer drawer with a realtime-style event log is a visible OpenAI integration that contributors can watch.
reviews.no_case: The headline idea is cosmetic by design: skins recolour surfaces, chrome and the orb. The proposal's own live-coaching score is 5.3 and falls below 5 without a coach lane that does not exist yet. Staying on Tailwind 3 and daisyUI 4 defers the modern stack, so the build ships a smaller change than the look promises. Eight launch skins, each needing contrast and layout QA, plus community skins that must be vetted for brand names, multiply the test and moderation surface for a feature reps will notice far less than the call itself. The library score of 5.5 also depends on seeded content the proposal admits is weeks of curation.

reviews.yes_case: Radix Coach Stage is the most buildable redesign in the set. One Radix Themes setup (teal accent, slate gray, medium radius) with Radix primitives gives every dialog, tab, toast and form accessible focus and keyboard behaviour without custom code, and Tailwind goes away once the last screen moves. Library, debrief, progress and team are light, calm and well typeset. The live call and landing hero switch to a dark stage with a voice ring driven by audio level. The coach rail shows one whisper at a time, and each whisper quotes the transcript line it reacted to, so a rep can check the coach. Rubric bars move from tentative to confirmed, and a Coach level control (Off, Light, Full) sits in the pre-call briefing. The debrief is an accordion of criteria with quotes, a warning callout when the heuristic grader ran, and a model receipt with grader model, latency and cost. The wizard has four steps: streamed field cards carry evidence and a confidence chip, rubric sliders total 100, and a 90-second dry run precedes publish or a prefilled PR. Against today's app, a template with no coaching or team surface, this is a system a contributor can read in an afternoon. For the fund, Settings > Models, a Grader Lab that accepts eval cases and an AGENTS.md give Codex CLI contributors a real way in, and the proposal does not claim Codex review until it runs.
reviews.no_case: The author's own risk is the verdict: a default Radix look is what reviewers read as a template, and the dark stage and voice ring are the only moves that separate it from one. Radix Themes has no coaching HUD, score ring or persona dossier, so most distinctive screens are custom builds on primitives, which erodes the low-debt pitch. The migration runs Tailwind 3 and Radix Themes CSS side by side through several phases, with preflight and token clashes to diff screen by screen. The self-scored C is 7 and the coach and library scores sit near 5, so it meets the baseline on the needs without clearly exceeding it.

reviews.yes_case: Patch Bay Console is built from physical-feeling controls, and the live call is where the metaphor earns its keep. Six talk-track step keys latch when the grader marks a step covered. The caller window carries a 12-LED voice-level ring and the last four turns. A rubric rack of five channel strips shows covered, partial or missed LEDs, each with a one-line evidence quote on tap. A cue strip shows the current cue in colour plus glyph plus text, with a Coach me key and a hint counter. A three-position Off, Hints, Full knob sets how often the coach speaks, so the rep can change how much help they get without leaving the call. Stop red is reserved for End and grade. The debrief uses quote chips that scroll and blink the matching transcript line, plus a model ledger naming the grader model, tokens and estimated cost. Library cards show LED difficulty and a Contribute key that exports persona JSON as a pull request. Against today's app, a chat window with a hidden talk-track drawer, this is a glanceable instrument, and it is the most distinctive of the five. The fund story is concrete: BYO key accepts any OpenAI-compatible base URL with a Realtime voice toggle, so usage is visible and cheap to try.
reviews.no_case: Knobs, LED ladders and bezels can read as a costume to enterprise buyers and to reps who take thirty calls a day, and the proposal concedes the risk. Custom controls, including the rotary knob, step keys and weight sliders, need keyboard and screen-reader support built and tested by hand, and the in-repo instrument kit becomes a product the maintainers must keep alive. Coaching is unproven: cues stay off by default until a labelled eval set exists, so the coach knob has little to gate at launch. The library shrinks from 240 personas to 60 at first release, and the live console waits for a stable grader, coach and labelled eval set, so the signature screen depends on work not yet done.

reviews.yes_case: Mission Control treats the call as an instrument panel. The left rail shows the call clock, a talk-ratio gauge that turns coral after 20 seconds above 70 percent, a words-per-minute gauge, a tone bar, and five rubric meters that stay tentative until a verbatim quote confirms them. The centre is a speaker-lane transcript with a waveform under each turn and a composer. The right rail holds one amber whisper cue at a time, coral objection chips and checkpoints that tick off. The coach is a separate GPT-4.1 mini channel that emits typed events (cue, objection, checkpoint, talk-ratio alert, rubric evidence). Each type renders in exactly one place, so the persona never breaks character and the rep can tell at a glance what kind of signal arrived. Reps can mute the coach or rate a cue useful or noisy, which tunes it in real use. The light theme is designed at equal weight for scorecards and the library. The debrief replays the audio with evidence ticks that play their moment. Against today's chat screen with no feedback and four number tiles, it adds a progress story with a 12-week heatmap and skill radar, and a team view with a roster and criterion heatmap. For the fund, a model-stack strip on every call shows which model handled voice, coaching and grading, with latency and cost, so reviewers see real API use inside the product. AGENTS.md and Codex review of gallery snapshots give Codex a real job.
reviews.no_case: Dark telemetry is now a common look for AI products and can feel like a trading terminal to new reps, a risk the proposal names but does not resolve. The scope is XL and stacks Tailwind 4, Base UI, a custom canvas waveform, Realtime over WebRTC and ElevenLabs behind one adapter all at once. That is a lot for an open-source project and leaves little slack if one layer slips. The talk-ratio and WPM gauges plus waveforms add dense chrome to a screen that already has a transcript, a cue rail and a rubric, so the cockpit risks overwhelming the call it is meant to coach. The live coach channel does not exist yet, so the 5.8 coaching score is a promise, and the proposal itself says latency and cue noise are unproven.

reviews.yes_case: Broadcast Desk makes a practice call feel like a live show. The live call is a stage: an audio-reactive persona ring, captions on a lower third, a talk-track segment bar and a mono timer. A 360px coach chat rail streams typed cues (nudge, objection alert, next question, praise), each with a glyph and a 'why' link to the exact transcript line. A left strip holds the five rubric scores as provisional bars that tick with green or rose deltas, and the rest of the app stays light and calm. After the call the debrief is replay-first: a timeline with coach markers and auto-clips such as 'Best moment' and 'Missed fee question', each playable and exportable as a 1200x630 moment card. Every quote in the criterion rows jumps the replay to its timestamp. In the library each persona card has a 10-second 'Hear them' voice sample, so a rep judges a persona by how it sounds before choosing it, and collections such as 'Insurance renewals' give 150-plus personas a path. The wizard shows provenance chips on each drafted field and gates saving behind a 60-second test drive. It beats today's app, which has a chat thread with nothing reacting until grading, a three-item dropdown and four stat tiles. For the OpenAI fund it names each model's job in a Model rack, makes Realtime a selectable voice, and gives Codex a real loop: a Codex CLI review on each persona PR, plus release notes.
reviews.no_case: The stream metaphor can read as gamey to sales leaders, the buyers the F2 case depends on, and the proposal itself flags this. Shareable clips and moment cards put recordings of real calls into circulation. The manager 'Import a real call' transcript upload brings in customer conversations, yet the proposal names redaction but not consent. It is XL: a new coach pipeline, 150 reviewed personas, a TTS sample for every persona, PNG export and an audio timeline all arrive before the core is proven. The 6.0 scores for coaching and library are conditional on content and a coach channel that do not exist yet. Voice whispers are deferred, so in voice mode the coach reaches the rep only through the screen at launch.

reviews.yes_case: Broadcast Desk turns each practice call into a live show. The persona sits in a centre stage ring that pulses with input and output audio levels, live captions run as a lower third, and a 360px coach rail on the right streams typed cues like chat messages. Each cue pairs a glyph and colour with a type (nudge, objection alert, next question, praise), carries a 'why' link that jumps to the transcript quote that triggered it, and can be pinned. A 240px left strip shows the rubric as five live, provisional criterion bars with green or rose delta chips, so the rep sees how they are doing while still talking. When a criterion jumps or drops, a marker lands on the replay timeline and a clip is queued. The debrief is replay-first: a timeline across the whole call with coach markers and three auto-clips (Best moment, Missed fee question, Strongest close), a score ring, a radar and bars where every evidence quote seeks the replay, and a 1200x630 moment card that exports as a PNG with names redactable. Outside the live call the look is a calm light surface with a 64px icon rail (Library, Practice, Progress, Team). The persona library is a browsable catalog of 150 or more personas across 20 or more sales jobs, the same jobs the brief names, with a facet rail (sales job, industry, difficulty bars, objection type, voice or text), a three-column card grid, and a 'Hear them' ten-second voice sample on every card so a rep can judge a persona before choosing it. The AI wizard takes all five sources the brief lists (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP, pasted call), fills persona fields with provenance chips, proposes rubric weights and a talk track, and requires a 60-second live test-drive call before Save to library; drafts carry a draft badge until a reviewer verifies them. The team view adds a manager table, a coaching queue, and a split view of call replay plus supervisor notes, which the data model already supports but the UI never shows. Against today's app (chat box, side drawer, three-item dropdown, four stat tiles, blurry orb) this is a full system with new tokens for both modes, a new shell, and a coach channel kept separate from the persona so the character never breaks. For the Codex fund it makes OpenAI visible on purpose: a Model rack on the landing page and in Settings names each role (GPT-4.1 family for coaching and grading, the wizard, Realtime as a real voice option beside ElevenLabs), each call shows token counts and an estimated cost, and Codex CLI reviews persona pull requests and drafts release notes. The shareable moment card also gives the project a natural launch artifact for the application.
reviews.no_case: The broadcast metaphor is the main risk: 'stage', 'clips' and a coach chat that streams like a Twitch overlay may read as gamey to the sales leaders who are the F2 buyers, and the proposal says so itself. Its own self-scores put live coaching (D 6.0) and the library (E 6.0) only at baseline, the 150-persona claim depends on reviewed content that does not exist yet, and nine screens plus a latency-sensitive coach pipeline and a Radix to Base UI swap make the XL scope heavy for an open-source project.

reviews.yes_case: Flight Deck Cockpit turns every rep into a flight on a dark instrument panel. The dark cockpit is the default on the live and debrief screens. A 240px left HUD rail shows six rubric tape gauges that move after every rep turn, each with weight and tally (for example Discovery 3 of 10), plus talk-track phase ticks. The centre is a compact persona instrument (orb or waveform) above a flight-log transcript with timestamps and speaker tags. The top bar carries a mono timer, an On course status lamp, a mode toggle, mute and End and grade. A right HUD stacks at most two coach cue cards, each with a Use line button that drops the suggested phrase into the input in one tap, and a Dismiss. Cues come from fixed categories (objection, next question, talk-track phase, forbidden early claim such as price), quote the transcript line they came from, expire after eight seconds, and are throttled to one per 20 seconds. The live numbers and the final grade use the same rubric so they cannot silently disagree, and if the grader falls back to heuristics an amber Estimate lamp says so. On a 390px phone the HUD becomes a pill-gauge strip, the coach cue is a bottom sheet with a one-tap Use line, and End and grade is a long-press so the call cannot end by accident. The debrief is a black box: an outcome stamp, a score ring, a whole-call timeline with event markers, and a press-play replay where the rubric gauges rewind in step with the transcript and, in voice mode, the waveform, so each evidence chip seeks the exact second a quote was said. Pre-flight is a checklist of status lamps (mic level, persona loaded, goal read, talk track reviewed) that must go green before Start flight enables, a clearer briefing than today's collapsed talk track. The library is a faceted rail with counts (role, industry, difficulty, objection type, mode) feeding a card grid with usage counts ('flown N times'), with Create with AI as the first tile. The five-step wizard (Source with File, URL, Notes and Transcript tabs plus an ICP form; Persona; Scenario; Rubric with weights summing to 100; Test flight) streams fields into a live preview with confidence chips, never saves without a two-minute text test flight, and exports a PR-ready JSON. The system is a total redesign: a Tailwind v4 token file with both themes on :root, shadcn components copied into the repo for contributors and Codex agents to edit, a slim icon rail, and a daylight mode for browsing so the library is not stuck in the dark. The OpenAI story is concrete: each flight's report card names the model behind each job (GPT-4.1-mini for grading and cues, Structured Outputs for the wizard, Realtime as a selectable voice engine), shows a cost estimate, and Settings lets a maintainer swap any slot to another OpenAI-compatible model. An AGENTS.md at the repo root tells Codex CLI how to run tests and add a persona, and Codex handles persona and rubric PR review, release notes and scorecard fixtures. Against today's chat app, which gives no feedback until the end, this changes the interaction model and has the most memorable visual identity of the five.
reviews.no_case: The persona library is under-specified. The proposal says only 'seeded with a large open persona set', never states a count, and names four roles and six industries, leaving out auto, real estate, retail and recruiting even though the brief requires every sales job; the E self-score of 6.5 is generous for a library described that loosely. The cockpit metaphor carries the same gimmick risk as any instrument-panel theme in an enterprise sales tool, and a dark default on the two screens reps see most is a hard sell in a daylight sales office.

reviews.yes_case: Swipe-to-Rehearse Coach Studio is a dark-first live call with a light, grid-first product everywhere else, built on shadcn/ui, Tailwind v4, React 19 and Geist. The live call is a three-zone cockpit: a left rail with talk-track steps that tick live and the goal; a centre transcript with speaker labels, mono timestamps and a waveform header showing who is speaking; and a right coach panel with stacked rubric meters whose delta chips are labelled 'live estimate', a single whisper card about two seconds after your turn that names the next question to ask, and an objection alert banner when the persona raises price or a competitor. The coach runs as a separate model stream, so the persona never sees coaching and never breaks character. A quiet mode turns it off, a cost-per-call ticker sits in the footer, an 'Ask the coach' box takes mid-call questions, and a talk-to-listen ratio meter shows whether the rep is doing most of the talking. On a 390px phone the coach is a bottom sheet with three snap points: peek shows one whisper and eight rubric dots, half shows the full whisper and alert, full shows the meters. The call dock holds a large mic, a Coach toggle and a hold-to-end control, and the screen stays awake during a call. The persona library is a sticky filter rail with saved filter sets for sales job (SDR cold call, AE discovery, CS renewal, collections, recruiting), industry (insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, auto, medical devices, B2B procurement, retail, SaaS), difficulty, objection and mode. The default is a three-column grid with a monogram avatar, objection chips, a one-line hook and minutes per card, and a Grid or Deck toggle. Deck mode is an opt-in 90-second drill where right runs, left skips and up saves, so the swipe idea stays without making the whole library feel like a dating app. Clicking a card opens a sheet with the persona, talk track and rubric before you start, and Duplicate to edit forks it into a contributor file. The AI wizard is four steps: Source (any of job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP or pasted call, with role chips), Persona, Scenario (talk track, rubric weights totalling 100, scripted replies) and Dry run. It has a side chat for edits such as 'make them more skeptical about price', a cost estimate before generation, a schema validation checklist and a provenance badge on AI-written fields, and it exports the same file format as the library so drafts can go back upstream as pull requests. Against today's app, which tells the rep nothing until the debrief and offers a three-item dropdown and a blank form, every surface changes. For OpenAI, a model strip on the landing page and in the live call names the Realtime voice, the coach, the grader and the wizard with per-call cost; Settings gets a bring-your-own-key page; and Codex runs in the repo's own workflows (PR review, persona-file validation, release notes), documented in CONTRIBUTING and tied to the Codex for Open Source criteria.
reviews.no_case: It is the safest of the five and the least distinctive. With the swipe deck set aside as an opt-in drill, the rest is a well-made modern SaaS layout (cards, rails, sheets, a grid) that could belong to any AI sales tool, and the brief's C criterion asks for more than polish. The live coaching stops at a whisper card and meters, and the proposal has no self-scores at all, so its business case (F1, F2, F3) is never argued in the document.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit and Drill Feed is a dark-first control room with one idea the others lack: a 30-second objection drill as a daily habit. The front door is a full-height vertical snap feed where each card is one objection: a 30-second persona objection, a 20-second recorded answer with a ring that fills as you speak, then five scores and one quoted line that land in under five seconds, and you swipe on. Each persona has a 30-second drill variant, so the feed draws from the same library as the roughly 150 seeded personas across 16 job families. The rest is the cockpit: the live call is a three-column instrument panel with a persona panel and SVG voice ring on the left, a speaker-labelled transcript with inline coach markers in the middle, and on the right one amber whisper cue, a coral objection alert with two suggested replies, five live rubric bars that flash +4 or -4 when a discovery question lands, and a next-question card. The coach is a sidecar that returns zod-validated JSON, must quote a transcript line for every cue, is rate-limited to one cue per 20 seconds, and stays quiet while the rep speaks; if the coach fails, the cockpit shows Coach offline and the call goes on. The debrief is a replayable timeline with a score sparkline and turn markers, criteria as expandable rows whose evidence quotes seek the timeline, a next-drill card, and a print stylesheet forced to light so the existing Print button stays useful. Progress is a streak heatmap, a rubric radar, objection-mastery bars and a Next up card. The manager view is a sortable roster with a review queue, a criteria heatmap and supervisor notes, built on TanStack Table. The wizard has an entry screen with four cards (paste a call or notes, import from a URL, describe a buyer, start blank), four accordion steps that collapse to one-line summaries, dials for skepticism, talkativeness, budget authority and time pressure, a 30-second test drill before save, and an export to YAML or an opened pull request that is never auto-submitted. Against today's blurred orb, chat screen and three-item dropdown, this is a complete system where the feed is the shareable front door and the cockpit is the depth. For OpenAI, the landing page and cockpit ribbon name the voice, grading, coach and wizard models with per-call cost; Realtime is added as a provider beside ElevenLabs; AGENTS.md tells Codex CLI how to test and add personas; Codex reviews persona and rubric pull requests, drafts release notes, and scans the auth and MFA code with Codex Security, which is one of the real Codex for Open Source benefits.
reviews.no_case: It is the most trend-driven of the five. A TikTok-style 30-second feed as the front door can read as a toy to enterprise buyers, and the proposal admits the feed cannot carry coaching depth, so the cockpit has to do all the real work. It stays on Tailwind 3 for the migration, self-scores live coaching (5.5) and the persona library (5.4) at or below baseline, and says the library only works if at least 100 personas are reviewed, which does not exist yet.

reviews.yes_case: Pipeline Rehearsal Console makes the home screen a kanban of the rep's real deal stages, so practice is organised around the deals they actually work. Each deal card shows its last rehearsal score and a Rehearse button, and a Rehearse tomorrow's call hero appears when a calendar event links to a deal. The pre-call briefing is deal-aware: a deal card with the last call summary and 'fix next time' items from the last debrief, a persona brief with what they want, three likely objections and three must-hit points, and a briefing card with a stacked rubric-weight bar, a talk-track checklist, a mic meter and a Start call button. The live call has three columns: a left stepper of talk-track steps (done, now, next), the goal and an audio-reactive persona presence card; a centre transcript in three lanes (persona in teal, rep neutral, coach cues in violet between turns); and a right rubric rail where five criteria show 1-to-5 chips, each score tagged provisional, with a Next best question card and a cue budget of one per 20 seconds. Cue types include next question, objection alert with a hint such as 'acknowledge then value', talk-track complete, and pace or filler warnings, and each has a Why expander that shows its evidence. The debrief has a grade ring with the numeric score first, a Moments timeline of coach cues and score changes that scrubs the transcript, criteria cards with the quote that moved each score, a drill button that generates a persona aimed at the weakest criterion, and a team percentile line. The library is about 180 seeded personas across 14 job families and 16 industries, with facets for job, industry, difficulty, objection, channel and length. The wizard is the clearest demonstration of AI grounding in the set: 'What we read' chips show the facts the model pulled from a job posting or URL, rubric sliders must total 100, a Show schema toggle reveals the structured-output JSON, and a two-minute test call comes before saving. The manager view is a pipeline board with rep cards per stage, a coverage matrix and a radar with Self, Manager and Peer toggles, plus Assign practice from call, which turns a real call into a rep's drill. It is a distinctive product idea that connects practice to revenue. For OpenAI, the model stack (Realtime voice, gpt-4.1-mini coach and grader, structured-output wizard) appears with per-call cost on the landing page and debrief footer, and an 'Add persona with Codex' button copies a prompt for the Codex CLI, with a 'Reviewed with Codex' badge that appears only if the repo really uses Codex for PR review.
reviews.no_case: The kanban home is the most CRM-like first screen of the five and reads like the default-SaaS look the brief's own diagnosis calls out. It is also the least modern stack: Tailwind v3 through Phases 0 and 1, the same Sora and Inter type as today with JetBrains Mono added, and an effort rating of L, which reads as a smaller programme than the other XL proposals. The deal-stage and job-lane mapping is a lot of product to carry in an open-source core, and the Codex angle depends on a conditional badge rather than a shipped workflow.

reviews.yes_case: Signal Room is a dark-first telemetry console for the live call, with a light theme designed at equal weight rather than inverted, and one token file drives all nine screens (Tailwind v4 with shadcn on Base UI). On a live call the left rail shows a call clock, a talk-ratio gauge that turns coral only after 20 seconds above 70 percent, a words-per-minute gauge, a tone bar, and five rubric meters that stay marked tentative until the grader finds a verbatim quote. The centre is a speaker-lane transcript with per-turn waveforms; the right coach rail shows one amber whisper cue at a time, objection chips and a checkpoint list that ticks off. The persona only talks. A separate coach channel emits typed events, each rendered in exactly one place, so the persona never breaks character and cues do not pile up. Today the live call is a chat with no feedback until the debrief, and this puts coaching and scoring on screen mid-call. The library is 150 to 200 versioned persona files across 12 to 15 sales jobs, with multi-select facets (sales job, industry, difficulty, objection type, call type, voice or text) that live in the URL so a filtered view can be shared, and forks export as PR-ready files. The wizard takes a URL, document, transcript or form, cites the source line behind each drafted field, and runs three simulated calls to flag flat replies before saving. A model-stack strip on every call names which OpenAI model handled voice, coaching and grading, with latency and cost, so the OpenAI use shows in the product itself. Mobile gets a peek-and-expand cue sheet and a thumb-zone End and grade bar, and the phased rollout behind flags keeps every route working during the change.
reviews.no_case: The live-coaching promise does not hold together: the coach runs on rolling windows roughly every 8 to 12 seconds, yet the proposal targets a cue within two seconds of the rep finishing a turn, and the coach backend does not exist yet, so the headline feature is still a plan. Its dark telemetry and glowing gauges are also a look a reviewer has already seen on many AI dashboards.

reviews.yes_case: Flight Deck gives the whole rep journey one grammar: a pre-flight briefing, a live HUD and a black-box debrief, all sharing the same gauges, status lamps and mono telemetry. The dark cockpit owns the live flight and the debrief, and daylight covers landing, library, wizard, logbook and team, so browsing stays readable. Pre-flight is a real checklist: mic level, persona loaded, goal read and talk track reviewed each show a status lamp, and Start flight enables only once the mic and goal are green, so a rep cannot launch a dead call. In flight, six rubric tape gauges move after every rep turn with weight and a running tally (Discovery 3 of 10), talk-track phase ticks advance, and at most two cue cards show, each with a Use line that drops the suggested phrase into the input in one tap. Cues come from fixed categories (objection, next question, talk-track phase, forbidden early claim such as price) with an evidence quote, and throttle to one per 20 seconds, expiring after 8. If the grader falls back to the keyword heuristic, an amber Estimate lamp says so, so a fallback never passes as a graded score. The debrief is a black-box replay: scrub the call and the gauges rewind with the transcript and audio, and evidence chips seek to the exact second. The logbook heatmaps criteria across the last twelve flights, which shows whether a skill is moving rather than four flat numbers. The OpenAI story is concrete: each flight's report card names the model behind grading and cues, the wizard's Structured Outputs and the optional Realtime voice, with a per-flight cost estimate. Phase 0 is a token-only pull request, so reviewers see a colour diff before any feature change.
reviews.no_case: It sets no cue-latency target at all, and its throttle of one cue every 20 seconds is slow enough that a cue can arrive after the moment has passed. Its library is described as a large open persona set with no count, job-family breadth or delivery date, so the self-scored 6.5 on the library is not backed by the text. The cockpit metaphor also carries a gimmick risk with sales leaders.

reviews.yes_case: Patch Bay Console turns the live call into a tactile instrument on a graphite console with bezelled keys. A coach-intensity knob sets how often the coach speaks (Off, Hints, Full), an LED strip shows next-question, objection and on-track states, six talk-track step keys latch as the grader marks each step covered, and every rubric criterion is a channel strip whose meter moves after each rep turn. Status is always LED colour plus glyph plus text, so colour is never the only signal, and the knob uses React Aria's slider keyboard model so it works without a mouse; reduced motion turns every chase and spring into an instant colour change. Debrief and library sit on a calmer bone paper surface on the same tokens, because dense reading suffers under skeuomorphism. It is the most distinct idea in the set: the proposer read three vendor sites and found none that describes a glanceable in-call cue panel, a gap worth testing. The knob gives the rep a real choice about how much help they get, which is a control rather than decoration. The library is a faceted browse (job, industry, five-LED difficulty, objection, channel, built-in or community source) with a path to create a persona, and the wizard drafts persona, objections and rubric weights with a 60-second dry run before save. The OpenAI story is named on the console: Realtime voice, gpt-4.1-mini grading, and a bring-your-own key for any OpenAI-compatible base URL. The migration is phased behind a flag, with a preview page for the instrument kit and a five-rep test of the console before the full look ships.
reviews.no_case: The hardware look stops at the call, so the redesign reads as two visual systems rather than one coherent look across every screen, which the brief asks for. It launches with 60 reviewed personas against a 240 target, which is not the large library the brief needs at launch, and it labels a nine-screen rebuild plus a custom SVG instrument kit as L effort, which is optimistic.

reviews.yes_case: Broadcast Desk makes each practice call a live broadcast. The persona is the stage, a ring that pulses with audio levels, captions sit in a lower third, a segment bar tracks talk-track steps, and a mono timer runs. A right-rail coach feed lists typed cues (nudge, objection alert, next question, praise), each with a glyph and a why link to the transcript quote behind it, and reps can pin or dismiss them. Rules keep it calm: at most one cue every two turns, nothing while the persona is speaking, and every cue must link to a quote. The debrief is replay-first: a full-call timeline shows coach markers and three auto-clips (Best moment, Missed fee question, Strongest close), each playable and exportable as a 1200x630 moment card, and every evidence quote seeks the replay. The manager view has a team table, a coaching queue and an Import a real call button that turns a real transcript into a practice persona, closing the real-call-to-practice loop that competitors pitch. The library is concrete on breadth: 150-plus personas across 20-plus sales jobs, three difficulty levels, tagged objections, named collections such as Insurance renewals and Procurement pushback, and a 10-second Hear them sample on every card. Light is the default for library, wizard, pre-call, dashboard and team, so enterprise screens stay readable in daylight and the stream metaphor is limited to the live and replay screens.
reviews.no_case: The streaming-overlay look (on-air red, clips, a Coach chat feed, a moment-card export) is the gamey style a sales leader is least likely to champion, and the proposal names that risk and then leans into it. Its numbers conflict too: a 1.5-second cue target sits beside its own admitted one-to-two-second coach latency, and 150 generated Hear them voice samples carry TTS cost and licensing questions the proposal never prices.

reviews.yes_case: Swipe-to-Rehearse is the most practical shell in the set. It is light by default for library, progress, team and debrief and dark for the live call, with a 64px icon rail that expands on hover and shadcn components on Tailwind v4 that a contributor can read and PR. The library is a filterable card grid by default, with a sticky facet rail (sales job, industry, difficulty, objection type, mode), saved filter sets, and a side sheet showing the talk track and rubric before a rep starts. Swipe is an opt-in 90-second objection drill (right to run, left to skip, up to save), so the gesture does not get in the way of serious browsing. The live call puts talk-track steps and the goal on the left, a timestamped transcript with a waveform header in the centre, and on the right a coach panel with live rubric meters and delta chips, one whisper card that auto-dismisses, an Ask the coach box and a cost-per-call ticker. The coach is a separate stream, so the persona never sees coaching, and if coaching stalls the call carries on while scoring lags instead of blocking. The debrief's under-the-hood drawer shows the rubric line and the model behind each score, which is strong for trust and for the OpenAI transparency story. The testing plan is the most concrete in the set: Playwright screenshots of all nine screens in light and dark at 390 and 1440 pixels as the regression baseline. A 150-plus persona library across 20-plus sales jobs, and a wizard that accepts any source with a dry run before save, cover the library and wizard needs.
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive design here: Geist, stock shadcn components, a violet AI colour and a conventional library with a Tinder-style layer on top. The swipe deck is the element most likely to make a serious training product look like a dating app, and the rest is what competitors already ship, so a reviewer would not remember it beside the other four.

reviews.yes_case: Practice Graph Studio is a whole-app redesign built like a repo. A dark-first calm cockpit sits under a GitHub-style header (wordmark, MIT badge, star link, Practice, Library, Studio, Progress, Team). Progress is a 52-week practice graph of 12px cells shaded by score band, not raw volume, so a streak means improvement. Personas are versioned files with a Source tab and an Edit as PR action. The live call is glanceable: rubric bars fill as criteria are covered, talk-track steps tick, and at most one whisper cue shows for 8 seconds with a 'why' link to the exact transcript line. The footer shows latency and per-call grader cost. The library launches with 60+ personas covering the brief's jobs (SDR cold call, AE discovery, insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, auto, medical devices, procurement, recruiting, retail, customer success, collections), filtered by role, industry, difficulty, objection type and source. The wizard takes exactly the brief's inputs (job description, product URL, CRM note, ICP, pasted call), labels each generated field with its source line, and Open PR shows a schema-checked diff with a Codex review comment. For the Codex fund it is the strongest case of the five: contributor-native (Good first persona, PR-style submission, Codex reviewing persona PRs), OpenAI models named on the call footer with cost, and an MIT core. It beats today's dropdown and chat screen by making practice history and coaching the story.
reviews.no_case: A GitHub-shaped sales product can read as a developer toy to a sales manager, and the proposal's own risk list concedes a dark cockpit can look like a dev tool. The contribution graph can still reward streaks that buyers see as gamification. Persona-as-PR invites strangers to submit personas that need real safety and bias review, which is a maintainer burden the proposal treats lightly. The 60-persona launch is the smallest library in the set, so 'large' is met only at the low end. The 1.5-second live cue target depends on a streaming grader the repo does not have yet, and the Tailwind 3 to 4 migration is a known breakage risk the proposal flags but does not solve.

reviews.yes_case: Keynote Bento is the most finished-looking proposal: one bento system where light tiles carry the review screens (landing, library, pre-call, debrief, progress, team) and a fixed dark stage holds the live call. The orb's state ring shows listening, thinking and speaking without relying on color, and a talk-time meter shows rep versus caller. The live rail holds a whisper tile, a next-question tile, an objection alert that appears only when triggered, talk-track progress, and a live rubric with delta chips (+4, -2), each tied to a transcript quote. The library is the broadest here: 150 personas across 25 job families, a natural-language 'Describe a buyer' search, facets for rep job, buyer role, industry, difficulty and objection type, job-family sections with View all counts, and a Build with AI tile first in the grid. The four-step wizard streams a persona card field by field, with rubric weight sliders that must total 100 and a 60-second dry run. The debrief timeline marks exactly where a coaching cue changed the call. Model chips, a Realtime-or-ElevenLabs voice choice, and a debrief cost line make the OpenAI stack visible, and a Built with Codex contributing guide fits the fund. Against today's dropdown and chat screen it is the largest visible step up.
reviews.no_case: A bento grid is now a common SaaS template look, so distinctiveness is middling, and the glowing orb and dark stage risk reading as a gimmick if accents are overused, as the proposal itself warns. Coaching latency is budgeted at about 2 seconds, and its own self-score of 5.4 says it exceeds the bar only if latency holds under 2 seconds, so the live experience is at best baseline. Effort is XL: a Tailwind 3 to 4 move touching every class, a Base UI switch the proposal admits rests on sources that disagree about Radix, and 150 personas that need subject-matter review before any of the look reaches users.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence Conversational Studio turns setup and persona building into a conversation: one 48px question per screen (for example 'Who picks up the phone?'), Enter to advance, a summary card that assembles as answers arrive, and a permanent 'Skip all to form' escape. The landing hero is itself a question input, so the product's first move is a wizard step. The live console is calm and private: the persona never sees coaching, a Pulse orb is driven by real audio level with its voice provider labelled, at most two amber cue cards show and dismiss after 8 seconds, and a five-criterion live rubric uses the same weights as the debrief so the numbers match. The library has clean facets (sales job, industry, difficulty dial, objection type, mode), URL-synced filters, and a Build one with AI card at the end of the grid. Model Lab in settings lists each role's model with cost per call and median latency, and a Codex-powered GitHub Action reviews persona PRs against the schema, which is the maintainer automation the fund funds. For a first-time rep or a buyer building a persona it is the most approachable of the five, and it clearly beats the form-filled scenario editor.
reviews.no_case: It runs two interaction languages: one question at a time for setup, then a dense cockpit for live calls. The proposal concedes the one-question rhythm fails mid-call, so the consistency story is weaker. Live coaching is unbuilt: the proposal admits the repo has no coach stream, so its D score of 5.2 is a promise, not a plan that already meets the bar. The Typeform idiom slows expert users who want to build a persona fast. The live call is conventional. The claim that react-hook-form is already in the repo is wrong: package.json lists zod and Next 15 but not react-hook-form, which is a credibility ding. Fifteen jobs at about 10 personas each means the 150-persona target is still a content promise.

reviews.yes_case: Composed Coaching Console is the most AI-native design in the set. A fixed system (dark console, teal signal glyph, hairline depth, Geist) hosts a closed registry of typed blocks, and the grader and coach stream which blocks appear and in what order for each call. A debrief opens on the single moment that cost the deal, criterion cards expand to quotes that jump to the transcript and play audio, and cue cards quote the line that triggered them. Every AI-written element carries a spark glyph and a why chip linking to validated transcript turn IDs, so reps always know what the model wrote and what it rests on. During the call a three-zone console shows a speaker-lane transcript with micro score chips per rep turn, a live rubric strip that tweens as coverage grows, at most two amber cues, and a Blind, Guided, Coached dial that fades scaffolding over time. The wizard uses AI Elements chat beside a persona card that fills field by field with provenance chips, and Save or Open PR exports the same pack file contributors can write by hand. For the Codex fund it has the cleanest model story: Realtime voice as an option, grader model, rubric version and token cost in every debrief footer, and Codex in PR review and release notes. It leaves today's chat screen and blurred orb far behind.
reviews.no_case: Per-call composed layouts add a reliability surface that is hard to QA: schema validation, layout drift across an open-ended set of compositions, and reps who expect predictable scoring from a sales tool. Its own live-coaching score of 6 holds only if cue latency stays under about 1.5 seconds, and the three-cues-per-minute cap makes coaching deliberately sparse.
