The filter rail covers six job families (SDR cold, AE discovery, CS, support, collections, recruiting) with industry carrying the rest, so 'every sales job' is less explicit than in other proposals. The visual language is a tidy dark console rather than a striking look, and an L-sized build stacks a Tailwind v4 migration, AI SDK and AI Elements at once.

reviews.yes_case: Coach's Field Notebook is the most memorable of the set. Paper grain at 3-4 percent, Fraunces headlines, a vermilion Caveat coach voice, and grades that land as tilted ink stamps make each call an open spread: the transcript on ruled paper on the left, and on the right the coach writing margin notes beside the exact line that moved a score. Objections arrive as tilted yellow sticky notes linked to the talk-track step, and a pencil-bar rubric ledger marks provisional deltas until the debrief re-grades. Every debrief number traces to a quote and a transcript line, and a fallback grader state is explained with a retry rather than a yellow banner. The library and dashboards deliberately switch to a crisp grid, so browsing 120 personas stays fast, and the tally-mark logbook with milestone stamps gives a clear reason to return. For the Codex fund it shows OpenAI as the engine: gpt-realtime and gpt-4.1-mini named per role in the footer with latency, a How it uses OpenAI diagram, and settings that let forks swap in any OpenAI-compatible model. It stands apart from every dark SaaS sales tool, which is itself a pitch advantage for an open-source project.
reviews.no_case: The brief asks for modern, sleek and cutting edge, and paper texture, tilt and handwriting read as warm and retro. The proposal's own risk list says it can look twee in an enterprise demo. Caveat handwriting is hard to read at scale, and a text-heavy margin stream is slower to scan mid-call than a glanceable cue, which weakens the live coaching need. The design also breaks its own lens on library and dashboards, so the 'total' system is really two systems. Live coaching and the 120-persona library both depend on a coach stream and a content project that do not exist yet, and some supporting claims, including the Base UI default, come from vendor or third-party blogs rather than primary sources.

reviews.yes_case: Swipe-to-Rehearse Coach Studio is a whole-app redesign on shadcn/ui copy-in components, Tailwind v4 CSS tokens and Geist, with a dark-first live call and a light library, progress and debrief. Desktop gets a 64px icon rail that expands to show labels; mobile gets a four-tab bar with 48px touch targets. The live call is a three-zone cockpit on a dark canvas: a left rail with the goal and talk-track steps that tick as the coach detects them, a centre transcript with speaker labels, mono timestamps and a waveform header, and a right coach panel with live rubric meters that show delta chips marked live estimate. One amber whisper card appears about two seconds after the rep's turn and fades after eight seconds. The coach is a separate model stream, so the persona never sees coaching; a quiet mode turns it off per session, and if coach latency spikes the call keeps going while scoring lags. The library is a faceted grid by default, with job, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode filters over 150-plus personas across 20-plus sales jobs. Each card opens a side sheet with the talk track and rubric. Swipe-to-drill is an opt-in mode, so the serious default stays a grid. The wizard takes exactly the sources the brief names (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP, call transcript), fills a persona card with provenance badges on AI-written fields, shows a cost estimate before generation, runs a dry run, and exports the same JSON file a contributor would open as a PR. Today the app offers a three-item dropdown and a long empty form, and nothing reacts until the call ends; this version makes every turn coached and scored. The OpenAI story is visible: a model strip names each role's model and per-call cost, Realtime is a first-class voice option beside ElevenLabs, a bring-your-own-key page sits in settings, and Codex runs PR review, persona-file validation and release notes, documented in CONTRIBUTING, which covers all three program categories.
reviews.no_case: The swipe lens is the riskiest idea in the set. It shows up in the headline mode, the landing hero, the three-card deck preview and the signature moments, and a sales-training buyer may read a Tinder-style deck as a toy, which the proposal's own risk list concedes. The scope is XL: nine screens, a spring-physics deck, a wizard, a 150-persona library and a motion dependency. Phase 0 promises a token move, shadcn install and replacement of every .card and .btn class in about a week, which is optimistic for a whole-app rewrite. The library is a large authoring job that does not exist yet, and the 1.5-second cue target and per-call cost figures are assumptions with no measured baseline. Live cues are not tied to a quoted transcript line, so a rep cannot check why a cue fired. Codex use is a documented intention in CONTRIBUTING, not a shipped workflow, so the fund pitch rests on plans, and the business and licensing case is left unpriced.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit and Drill Feed is a whole-app redesign with two layers. The core is an instrument-panel live call on a dark canvas: a 240px persona panel with an audio-driven SVG voice ring, state chips such as Skeptical and Price-sensitive, a Geist Mono timer and a six-step talk-track rail; a centre transcript with speaker labels, timestamps and inline coach markers; and a 320px right rail with one amber whisper cue, a coral objection alert with two suggested replies, five rubric bars that flash plus-four or minus-four, and a next-question card. Every cue must quote the transcript line that triggered it, is rate-limited to one per 20 seconds and is held while the rep speaks. A coach-level control (Silent, Whisper, Live cues) sets intensity, and if the coach fails the cockpit shows Coach offline while the call goes on. Voice is OpenAI Realtime beside ElevenLabs. The layer on top is a 30-second objection drill feed: a vertical snap feed where each card is one objection, a ring that fills while you answer, and a score plus one quoted line in under five seconds. That gives the app a daily habit and a shareable clip that a cockpit alone cannot provide. The library is about 150 personas across 16 job families, each with a 30-second drill variant, filters for job, industry, difficulty, objection, mode and length, and a Remix action that forks any persona into a PR-ready YAML draft. The wizard offers four entry cards, dials for skepticism, talkativeness, budget authority and time pressure, a 30-second test drill, and Export YAML or Open PR. Codex maps to all three program categories concretely: AGENTS.md, Codex review on persona and rubric pull requests, Codex-drafted release notes, and Codex Security scans of auth and MFA, with a /docs/codex page and an honest caveat that the program's benefits are discretionary. Against today's dropdown and four-tile dashboard, a rep gets a cockpit that coaches while they talk and a reason to come back tomorrow.
reviews.no_case: The feed is the front door, not a side module: the desktop nav lists Drills first, mobile opens on Drills, and the proposal's own risk section admits a TikTok-style feed can read as a toy to enterprise buyers. For a serious sales-training app that is a credibility problem on the first screen, and the proposal concedes the feed cannot carry coaching depth, so it is a funnel that has to justify itself on top of a cockpit. Scope is XL and the author says it is too much for one release: nine screens, a feed, a wizard, a 20-second recorded-answer capture path and two voice providers. The migration keeps Tailwind 3, so the modern claim is mostly a token-level promise at launch. Its own self-scores for coaching (5.5) and the library (5.4) sit at the baseline and are conditional on measured latency and on 100 reviewed personas, so the proposal does not clear the bar on its own numbers. The wizard entry cards never name a job description as a source, which the brief lists explicitly. The Codex Security line depends on a benefit the proposal itself says is granted at OpenAI's discretion.

reviews.yes_case: Practice Graph Studio makes the app look and behave like a repository a maintainer would be proud of. The top bar mirrors a GitHub header with a wordmark, MIT badge, star link and tabs for Practice, Library, Studio, Progress and Team, and each persona has a Source view showing the file it is stored as. The library has a 240px filter rail with counts for role, industry, difficulty, objection and source (official or community), a three-column grid of cards with a difficulty meter and version tag, and a detail drawer whose Source tab offers Edit as PR. The Studio wizard is a split pane: a chat on the left where you drop a job description, URL, CRM note, ICP or call, and a live persona card on the right where every field carries a provenance chip that highlights the sentence it came from. A 60-second test call comes before save, and Open PR shows the file diff. The live cockpit is calm and dark: a 56px top bar with a Your turn pill, timer, coaching level (Silent, Cues, Full) and End and grade; a two-lane transcript with a tone bar under each persona line; a 320px rubric rail whose criterion bars fill as covered and turn solid only once the grader confirms; a talk-track progress panel; and one cue card at a time that auto-dismisses after eight seconds, with a why link to the exact quote. The debrief reads as a review: a criteria index with weights, evidence quotes with timestamps that jump a replay pane, and a practice queue aimed at the weakest criteria. The progress view's signature is a 52-week practice graph shaded by score band rather than volume, so a streak means improvement. Every call and debrief footer names the Realtime voice model and the gpt-4.1-mini grader, with live cost counters and a per-criterion model attribution. Against today's three-item select and blurry orb, this is a product a contributor can read, fork and change through a pull request.
reviews.no_case: The library launches with a floor of 60 personas, the thinnest of the five against 120-plus, 150 and 180, and the brief names a large, browsable library as a non-negotiable. The coach is not clearly separated from the buyer: the proposal describes one per-turn grader stream feeding cues, scores and the debrief, and never says the persona is kept blind to coaching, which the current app requires. The 1.5-second cue target depends on a streamed grader with no stated fallback number. The Tailwind 3-to-4 migration sits on the critical path, and the proposal itself flags the reported Radix Select transparency problem after v4 upgrades. Its L estimate may understate rebuilding nine screens. Codex is a planned repo action rather than a shipped one, so the fund case is thinner than P40 or P41. The proposal also admits a GitHub-native dark cockpit may read as a developer tool to sales buyers, and a contribution graph can reward showing up over learning even with score-band shading.

reviews.yes_case: Pipeline Rehearsal Console ties practice to the work a rep already does. The home, when signed in, is a kanban of deal stages where each card shows its last rehearsal score and a Rehearse button, and a calendar event linked to a deal surfaces a Rehearse tomorrow's call hero. For non-sales jobs the board becomes lanes: collections aging buckets, recruiting screen-to-offer, renewal windows for customer success. The pre-call briefing answers what am I walking into, with a deal card, fixes from the last debrief, a persona brief with three likely objections and three must-hit points, and a briefing card with a stacked weight bar. The live call has three columns: a talk-track stepper with done, now and next; a transcript in persona, rep and coach lanes; and a provisional rubric rail with 1-to-5 chips and a next-best-question card. The coach runs as a separate channel, the persona never sees its text, cues are budgeted to one per 20 seconds with no more than three high-priority per call, and latency is targeted at 1.5 seconds. The library is the broadest in the set at about 180 personas across 14 job families and 16 industries, with facets for job, industry, difficulty, objection, channel and length, plus a pipeline-stage filter. The wizard shares one zod schema between structured outputs and the saved file, shows What we read chips for extracted facts, and enforces rubric weights that total 100. The migration keeps Tailwind 3, existing routes and data shapes, with additive Prisma tables, so it is the lowest-risk whole-app path. The model stack (Realtime voice, gpt-4.1-mini coach and grader, wizard structured outputs) appears on the landing page and in each debrief footer with cost. Against today's dropdown and four tiles, it gives reps a reason to rehearse before a specific call.
reviews.no_case: This is the most conservative proposal: Sora, Inter and JetBrains Mono on a blue primary, a light canvas by default, Tailwind 3 until phase 3, and hairline borders with no signature motion or new visual identity. Against a brief that says the app does not yet look like cutting-edge AI voice coaching, that is the weakest answer. The pipeline is scope the brief never asked for: the core loop needs deal data or a CSV import, the kanban changes what the app is for, and the proposal's own risk list admits nine screens plus a kanban is a lot. Its Codex story is a conditional badge that appears only if the repo already uses Codex for PR review, plus a button that copies a Codex CLI prompt, so it does the least for the Codex for Open Source criteria. Distinctiveness is low: a deal board beside a live call is a recognisable SaaS layout, and the persona library and wizard look like the default.

reviews.yes_case: Open Practice Hub is a Hugging Face-style community hub for call practice. The top nav has Practice, Library, a primary Create persona button, Progress and Team, plus a GitHub stars pill and Fork. The library has a left facet rail for role, industry, difficulty, objection type and channel, a sort row (Trending, Most forked, New, Highest pass rate), and a three-column grid of persona cards showing a monogram ring, role and industry chips, a difficulty bar, two objection tags, stars, forks and the author handle. Opening a card shows a right-side model card: what it tests, rubric weights, the opening line, a 30-second sample, a fork tree, and Start practice, Fork and Star buttons. The wizard takes a job description, URL, CRM notes, ICP or pasted call as tabs, asks up to three follow-ups, cites the source lines it used, plays a 20-second cold open in the persona's voice during the dry run, and then offers Save privately, Share to team or Open PR with the file prefilled. The live call has a right coach column with six rubric meters that tick with deltas such as +6 Pricing, an amber whisper cue and a coral objection alert with a suggested bridge line. A coach pass fires after each turn or on triggers such as objection keywords, a four-second silence or a missed talk-track step, and intensity runs Quiet, Standard or Strict with a visible per-minute cost. Leaderboards rank personas, scenarios and teams, while individual rep rankings are opt-in and measure improvement rather than absolute score. Against today's three-item select and blurry orb, a rep can browse 120-plus personas by job and industry, fork one they like, and keep the contribution loop inside the open-source repo.
reviews.no_case: It looks like a template: flat-first with 1px hairlines, light by default, Sora and Inter on Tailwind 3, an indigo primary, and a flat-first rule the proposal itself treats as its design language. That misses the brief's bar for modern and cutting edge, and the monogram-ring avatars are a restrained version of the default. The community layer (stars, forks, author handles, pass rates from opt-in anonymised results) needs a shared backend the proposal never specifies, so a self-hosted open-source install would show empty counters and the hub metaphor overpromises. The Hugging Face framing also positions the product as a catalogue of personas rather than a sales-call cockpit. The coach has a trigger-based pass with no latency guarantee, and its live-call target is about 2 seconds with no fallback spec. The Codex story mentions PR review and persona maintenance in one sentence but names no specific repo workflow or file. Per-persona pass rates and rep-level sharing add consent and data-protection work the proposal lists as a risk but never scopes.

reviews.yes_case: Composed Coaching Console is a total redesign on one fixed system: shadcn/ui on Radix, Tailwind v4 tokens in CSS, Geist Sans and Geist Mono, 1px hairlines instead of shadows, a teal signal colour for all AI-made elements and amber reserved for coach cues. Dark is the default for the live console, and a full light set covers the library and debrief. The distinctive idea is that the AI composes each call's coaching and debrief from a closed catalogue of typed blocks (ScoreHero, MomentReplay, CriterionCard, PatternCallout, DrillCTA, plus cue blocks during the call). The model picks order and content but never emits markup, and every block cites transcript turn IDs that must validate. During a call the rail shows one amber cue at a time, the rubric strip fills as coverage grows, and live scores are labelled estimates until the full grader confirms them. The debrief opens on the moment that cost the deal, not a letter grade. Today the live call is a chat app and the debrief is one long scroll of identical cards; this replaces both and keeps the classic fixed-order debrief as fallback. The persona library is one zod-validated data pack per persona, and the wizard exports that same pack file, so it doubles as a contributor on-ramp. For the Codex fund it is the most concrete: a model strip on the landing page, grader model, rubric version and token cost in every debrief footer, a Realtime voice path, and Codex PR review stated in the README.
reviews.no_case: The model-composed layout is the riskiest idea in the set. Block order can drift, screens will be hard to compare across calls, and the fixed-order fallback is an admission the core can fail. Live coaching is self-scored at 6 and depends on a sub-1.5-second coach stream that is not built yet; cue latency decides the whole live-coaching claim. The look (near-black navy, teal, hairlines) is tasteful but close to the generic dark-tech style that Linear-style competitors already own, so it may not stand out. The 150-persona target across 18 industries is a content project the UI cannot solve, and the provenance chips are only as good as the citation validator behind them.

reviews.yes_case: Clay Coach is a warm, tactile console built around a soft-clay 3D persona bust rendered with react-three-fiber, which the repo already depends on. The caller's jaw follows the caller's audio level and the halo changes colour with state: sage when on track, amber the moment an objection lands. Tokens on :root drive a light default and a first-class dark mode. 3D is kept to the character only; scorecards, dashboards and tables stay flat with 1px hairlines, so the playfulness does not reach the data. On a live call the caller sits in the centre, a six-step talk-track rail doubles as the live tracker, rubric bars stay hatched while provisional and turn solid once a transcript quote confirms them, and whisper cues slide in beside the transcript and tuck into a Coach tray afterwards. The coach runs as a separate model channel that reads the transcript but never the persona, so the caller stays in character. The debrief is a clay medallion with percentile phrasing, a radar, sorted criteria rows, and tapping any quote scrubs audio and transcript to that second. The library uses versioned JSON recipes that include an avatar recipe, so contributors add a persona by editing one file with no 3D skills, and the wizard tags each field with its source sentence. Against today's chat app with a blurry orb, it gives the rep a character to practise with and a visible coach. The Model Ledger chip on each AI surface shows model, latency, tokens and cost, which suits the Codex fund's efficiency question, and the /contribute page makes the repo a contributor front door.
reviews.no_case: The clay character is a visual bet. Playful clay can read as unserious to enterprise and call-centre buyers, who are the customers the F2 case depends on. 3D performance on low-end Android and embedded webviews is unproven and forces static stills that dilute the signature moment. The persona library is weakly specified: the proposal names facets and Built-in, Mine and Community tabs but does not commit to the brief's list of sales jobs or seed counts, so E is the thinnest of the five on content. The two-second cue budget depends on a parallel coach channel the proposal does not design in detail, so D is conditional. Calling the clay look distinctive does not make it cutting-edge tech for the brief's C criterion, and the proposal has not been tested with reps.

reviews.yes_case: Coach's Field Notebook is the most distinctive system in the set. It is a warm training notebook: a paper canvas with faint grain, sheet-coloured cards, ink text, blue for the rep's lines, graphite for the caller's, vermilion Caveat handwriting for coach notes in the margin, tilted ink stamps for grades, and a highlighter behind quoted evidence. A live call is an open spread: the transcript on ruled paper with line numbers on the left and the coach margin on the right. Coach notes write themselves in beside the transcript line that triggered them, rubric deltas show as a ledger marked provisional, and an objection raises a tilted sticky note linked to the talk-track step. The persona never sees coach output. The debrief makes every number link to its exact transcript line, and a fallback grade is explained with a retry rather than hidden behind a yellow bar. The library matches the brief's own list job by job: 15 families (SDR cold, AE discovery, SaaS, insurance, mortgage, real estate, solar, home services, auto, medical devices, B2B procurement, recruiting, retail, customer success, collections), 8 or more seeded personas each, as index cards that flip to show talk track and rubric weights. The six-step wizard fills a live index card as the model streams and can save to the library or open a PR. Against today's dropdown and blurry orb, it makes coaching and grading visible and readable. On the Codex fund, models are named in the live footer with latency, the landing page has a How it uses OpenAI diagram, and Settings gives one model per role with OpenAI-compatible overrides, which invites forks, plus AGENTS.md and a Codex skill that drafts persona packs.
reviews.no_case: Paper, grain and handwriting are the opposite of the modern, cutting-edge technology signal the brief asks for, and the proposal's own risk list concedes it can read as retro or twee in an enterprise demo. Handwriting is a legibility cost in dense live use, and the system stacks four type families (serif display, neutral UI, handwriting, mono) on one screen. The lens does not carry into the density the library and team views need, so they fall back to a plain grid. XL effort with a 120-persona seed is a heavy lift for a first redesign, and the D and E self-scores of 5.5 show the proposal does not yet clear the baseline on its own. Its Base UI default claim and competitor weaknesses come from vendor and third-party blogs and are unverified.

reviews.yes_case: Clearcall Coach Console is an accessibility-first redesign built to WCAG AAA: 7:1 body text, 3:1 control edges, 44px targets, 56px live-call controls, no colour-only state, no motion dependence, and one polite live region that announces each cue at most every eight seconds. The canvas is warm clay-paper, light by default, with a dark theme held to the same contrast ratios and violet reserved for the AI coach. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next is the only typeface and text scales to 200 percent without clipping. The live call has three named landmark regions (Transcript, Coach, Controls). Talk-track steps show as Done, Next or Missed with words, criterion rows show points, a bar and a status word, and everything stays tagged Provisional until the grader confirms. Each cue has a type label and a Dismiss button, and an S key reads the score aloud. Against today's app, which gives no feedback during the call and crowds the mobile header, this is designed around screen-reader users, low-vision users and bright offices, with text and an icon for every state. The library covers 15 sales jobs with 120 or more personas, four facets with a filter rail and removable chips, and a 30-second voice preview. The five-step wizard extracts fields with source sentences, validates weights to 100 and ends in a two-minute test call. For the fund and for entity buyers, the AAA gate plus axe-core in CI is a concrete procurement story, and the Model lab that grades the same transcripts with GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-4.1 side by side shows model choices being made.
reviews.no_case: AAA shapes the look toward clean and safe rather than cutting-edge, and the 'modern and sleek' criterion will likely score lower than the other proposals on A and C. The flat, shadowless language is close to the default accessible component look and offers little signature moment beyond the cue rail. Cue cadence for screen-reader users is a guess until blind and low-vision users test it, and the proposal itself says cues should stay opt-in until then. The 15-job, 120-persona library and the wizard are content and engineering work that no UI can deliver on its own. The voice path is not designed in the UI beyond a provider label, and the coach stays text-first, so the live coaching claim is not as strong as the accessibility story.

reviews.yes_case: Cockpit Dark Command Center is a polished, keyboard-first control room on shadcn/ui over Radix. A Cmd-K palette covers navigation, practice by persona name, creation, library filters, call controls and theme, with every command showing its keycap. The surfaces are hairline-bordered near-black with one blue accent and mint for passing scores, and a full light set is held at parity because reps practise in bright offices. The live call is deliberately sparse: transcript in two speaker lanes with inline objection and rubric marks in the centre, a talk-track rail on the left, a single amber whisper cue card with one objection alert on the right, and rubric meters that stay provisional until two turns of evidence exist. The top bar has a presence ring, a mono timer, coach latency and End and grade with a confirm step. The library is a dense keyboard-row table (j, k, Enter, slash) with facets, a preview drawer and a card-grid toggle, replacing a three-item dropdown with a catalogue of 120 or more persona-scenario pairs across eight sales jobs and 20-plus industries, with compliance notes on regulated talk tracks. Debriefs are a split view with a sticky transcript, and provenance chips say whether a model or the heuristic graded each call. The Codex angle is concrete: 'Powered by OpenAI models' text, model names and token costs on screen, a Structured Outputs badge, AGENTS.md for Codex CLI, and a Codex review pass on persona pull requests. It is the most conventional and buildable of the five, with a clear tokens-first migration plan.
reviews.no_case: Linear-style dark command centres are now a familiar genre, and this reads as a well-made SaaS admin tool rather than an AI training product; the proposal's own distinctiveness score of 7 is generous. Cmd-K-first is a power-user pattern that leaves casual reps and touch users dependent on the visible nav and the mobile tab bar. The stack claim that shadcn runs on Tailwind 3 is out of date for the current component set, so the migration and no-churn assumptions need checking. Dense tables and keyboard rows are an odd fit for a sales call, whose core moment is a conversation. The coach stream is not designed in detail, so D is conditional at 6.0, and the 120-persona library is a content job the UI cannot solve alone.

reviews.yes_case: Pipeline Rehearsal Console turns the whole app into a sales-native cockpit. The home is a kanban of deal stages, and each card has a Rehearse button and its last rehearsal score, so practice happens against the deals a rep is actually working. A calendar-linked deal gets a Rehearse tomorrow's call hero. The board is generalized into job-specific lanes (aging buckets for collections, screen-to-offer for recruiting, renewal windows for customer success), so one layout serves every job. Look: a dark-by-default live room (#0B0F17 canvas, #121826 surfaces, violet coach cues, rose objection alerts, teal persona lane) against light #F5F6F8 pages for library, pipeline and progress. Sora headlines, Inter UI text, JetBrains Mono timers and scores, 14px cards, hairline borders, and no heavy shadows. The live call is three columns at 1440px: talk-track stepper and persona presence on the left, a three-lane transcript in the centre with coach cues between turns, and a provisional rubric rail on the right with a score ring, five criterion chips and a Next best question card. Cues are capped at one per 20 seconds, the target is under 1.5 seconds from turn end, and every live score is labelled provisional until the debrief confirms it with the quote that moved it. The debrief has a Moments timeline that scrubs the call. The library is a facet rail (job, industry, difficulty, objection type, channel, length) with live counts, a cmdk search and about 180 persona cards. The wizard takes a job description, product URL, CRM note, ICP or a redacted pasted call, shows 'What we read' chips for extracted facts, requires rubric weights to total 100, runs a two-minute test call, then saves or opens a PR. Today the app has a three-item dropdown, a chat call that reacts to nothing until grading, and no manager surface. This design fixes all three. For OpenAI, a model stack line with per-call cost sits in each debrief footer, and a /contribute page shows maintainer activity, which matches the Codex for Open Source criteria.
reviews.no_case: The pipeline-first premise asks every user, including students and job seekers with no CRM, to start inside a sales kanban. The job-specific lanes fix the labels but not the premise, and the home must be built and tested in five different layouts. It is also the heaviest build of the five (dnd-kit, Recharts, TanStack, AI SDK, react-hook-form, Motion, cmdk, a Tailwind v3 to v4 move and CSV/ICS import) at L effort, and the 180-persona and Codex-badge claims are promises the proposal has not started to deliver.

reviews.yes_case: Practice Graph Studio makes the project look like a repo and makes practice look like a commit log. The top bar mirrors a GitHub header: wordmark with an MIT badge, a star link, and tabs for Practice, Library, Studio, Progress and Team. Each persona is a versioned file. Every card has a Source tab showing that file with an Edit as PR action, and the wizard's Open PR shows the file diff. The signature view is a 52-week practice graph of 12px cells shaded by average score band rather than by how often a rep trained, so a streak means getting better, with a quality guard against volume gaming. Look: a dark canvas (#0A0D12), three surface steps (#11161D, #1A212B) with #263040 hairlines, signal teal #2DD4BF for focus and primary actions, amber #F5B841 for whisper cues, rose #FB7185 for objections, Geist and Geist Mono for UI and numbers, depth from surface steps instead of shadows, and two-letter monogram tiles tinted per industry instead of stock avatars. The live call is a dark cockpit: a 56px top bar with a 'Your turn' pill, a timer that stays visible, a coaching level control (Silent, Cues by default, Full), mute, and End and grade. A two-lane transcript carries tone bars. A 320px right rail holds rubric bars that fill as criteria are covered (dotted while provisional, solid once the grader confirms) and a six-step talk track. Only one cue shows at a time, auto-dismisses after 8 seconds, and links to the exact transcript line behind it. The per-turn grader streams with a target near 1.5 seconds and falls back to post-turn scoring rather than stalling the call. The debrief is a review: an outline index with weights, criterion cards with timestamped quotes that jump a synced replay. Today's chat call shows nothing until grading and its timer clips. This gives a rep glanceable coaching, and it gives the project a contributor path (persona PRs with schema checks, plus planned Codex review) that matches the Codex for Open Source criteria.
reviews.no_case: The GitHub-native look carries the risk the proposal itself names: a repo header, mono type and an IDE-like dark cockpit will read as a developer tool to a sales manager. The library is 60-plus personas at launch, against a brief that asks for a large library across every sales job, so E is the thinnest of the top three. The coach spec has cues and objection alerts but no explicit next-best-question module. The practice graph is only as good as its score-band rule, and the Tailwind v4 migration is a phase-0 risk with a reported Radix Select background bug. The Codex review is a planned action, not a shipped one.

reviews.yes_case: Keynote Bento is a modular, Apple-style system where every screen is a grid of tiles on a light canvas (#F5F5F7, white tiles with #E5E5EA hairlines, 28px radius on desktop and 22px on phones). It uses Geist display type at 56 to 88px on heroes, Geist Mono tabular numerals for timers and scores, and signal blue #2F6BFF for primary actions. A dark stage (#0B0B0F) appears only on the live call and the landing hero, so attention goes to the caller. The landing page has a headline tile ('Practice the call before it counts') with two CTAs, a dark stage tile with a looping mini call, a persona chip strip with job-family counts, and a model tile naming the Realtime voice, gpt-4.1-mini grading and the persona wizard. The library opens with a 'Describe a buyer' search and a Build with AI tile, then a masonry grid of persona tiles grouped by job family. It targets 150 personas across 25 job families, with facets for rep job, buyer role, industry, difficulty and objection type, and each tile credits its contributor. The live call splits 62/38. The left stage has an orb whose ring shows listening, thinking or speaking without relying on colour, a talk-time meter and two caption lines. The right bento rail has a whisper tile (one cue for six seconds), a next-question tile, an objection alert that appears only when triggered, talk-track progress across six steps, and a live rubric with delta chips such as +4 that tap through to the evidence. On phones the score pill sits above the fold, the whisper is a pill, and every control is in the thumb zone. The debrief is also a bento: grade hero, a score timeline with cue markers showing where coaching changed the call, criterion tiles with evidence chips, and a Practice next tile. Against today's three-scenario dropdown, blurry orb and silent chat call, this is a complete visual and interaction reset that shows the product working. It also adds an OpenAI model chip on every surface that uses a model and a cost line per debrief, which is the proof fund reviewers look for.
reviews.no_case: Bento is now the default layout of AI landing pages, so the keynote pitch is a template with better type, and it fails the distinctiveness test the brief sets. The proposal's own numbers are soft: D self-scores 5.4 and E self-scores 5.2, and E falls to about 4.6 without the 150 seeded personas, which is a content job nobody has started. It is XL effort, and phase 0 rewrites every class from Tailwind 3 to 4. The claim that Base UI became shadcn's default in July 2026 rests on one benchmark blog, and the proposal's own sources disagree on whether Radix is still maintained, so the component layer is unverified. Bento density at 390px is a known overflow risk.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence Conversational Studio makes setup and persona creation one question per screen. The landing hero is one input styled as a wizard question ('What do you sell, and who do you call?') with an Enter hint. The persona wizard is seven one-question steps, each with a single answer control (chip grid, text field or drop zone). Enter advances, a step counter shows progress, and a permanent 'Skip all to form' escape stays visible. A summary card on the right assembles itself as answers arrive, so the persona feels built with the user rather than filled in. The review step has editable fields and a generated opening line, a similarity check warns about near-duplicates, and a footer chip names gpt-4.1-mini with structured output. The look is a paper canvas (#F7F6F2) with Geist at 48/52 for questions and near-black ink, and a dark room (#0B0E14) for the call and debrief, where amber is used only for coaching cues and coral only for objections. The library has a 240px facet rail (sales job, industry, difficulty dial, objection type, mode) with filters synced to the URL, 15 sales jobs at about ten personas each, targeting 150-plus, and a last cell that says 'Build one with AI'. The live call is a 7/5 split: a caller orb showing state ('Caller speaking' or 'Your turn') above the last six turns, and a coach rail with six rubric bars, talk-track dots and a cue stack capped at two amber cards, each with 'Say this' and dismiss. A coral bar pins objections, and End and grade needs a two-second hold. The debrief opens with a verdict and a skill radar against the last three calls, then a moment timeline where 'Redo this moment' replays the sixty seconds around the weakest turn. The settings Model Lab lists each role's model with cost per call and median latency from the user's own runs, so the OpenAI stack is visible in use. Against a ten-field scenario form and a chat call, this is more guided, glanceable and replayable.
reviews.no_case: The one-question idea is the only truly distinctive move, and it stops at the live call. The 'total' redesign is therefore two interaction models stitched together: a conversational setup and a dense panel cockpit. The proposal's own self-scores put the basic needs at or under baseline (D 5.2, E 5.4), and it admits the repo has no coach stream yet. The library is about 15 job families with a 150-plus target and no shipped count. Seven one-question steps are slow for a sales enablement lead who already knows the persona, and next-best-question appears only as one sample cue.

reviews.yes_case: Open Practice Hub is a community hub for call practice in the style of Hugging Face Spaces. The top bar carries Practice, Library, a Create persona button and Progress, plus a GitHub stars pill and a Fork button. The landing hero is a split layout: 'Practice the call before it counts' with two CTAs on the left, and a 12-second looping product clip on the right showing a persona card, a rubric meter ticking and one whisper cue. Below it are task chips (SDR cold call, AE discovery, insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, collections) and a Trending personas row. The library has a filter rail (role, industry, difficulty 1 to 5, objection type, channel, license), sort chips for Trending, Most forked, New and Highest pass rate, and cards with a monogram ring, role and industry chips, a difficulty bar, objection tags, stars, forks and the author handle. Opening a card shows a model card with what the persona tests, rubric weights, opening line, a 30-second sample, a fork lineage tree and Start practice, Fork and Star. Each persona is one YAML file validated in CI, so forking copies the file and records lineage. The wizard runs Source, Persona, Scenario, Rubric, Dry run and Publish. An assistant asks up to three follow-ups and cites the source lines it used, a dry run plays a 20-second cold open in the persona's voice, and publish offers Save privately, Share to team or Open PR. The live call has three zones: a talk-track rail, a centre stage with the orb and transcript, and a coach column with six rubric meters that tick with deltas such as +6 Pricing, one amber whisper cue and a rose objection alert with a bridge line. Coaching runs as a separate pass that fires on objection keywords, a four-second silence or a missed talk-track step, returns typed JSON, and never enters the persona's context. Intensity is Quiet, Standard or Strict, and a per-minute cost meter sits in the bar. Against a three-item select and a long form, this makes personas shareable, forkable artifacts and gives contributors a fork, edit, lint and PR path that fits an open-source fund.
reviews.no_case: It is a Hugging Face Spaces page with sales words. Stars, forks, trending and fork trees are community chrome a rep training for a call does not need, and they turn the product into a model marketplace. Leaderboards and pass rates built on opt-in data need a hosted backend that the open-source core does not ship, so the social layer is out of scope for the free tier. The first pass keeps Tailwind 3, so the 'modern' claim rests mostly on palette, and the indigo, green and amber accents look like most 2024 AI SaaS. The coach triggers are clever, but nothing in the proposal shows that the four-second silence rule or the Why expander helps a rep rather than distracts.

reviews.yes_case: Composed Coaching Console is a dark, calm live console in which the AI composes each debrief from a closed set of typed blocks, so every report is personal to the call but always on-brand. On a call, the caller is a Pulse orb whose ring follows real audio level, labelled 'Caller speaking' or 'Your turn'. The last six turns sit in speaker lanes, and each rep turn carries micro score chips such as +3 Discovery. A five-criterion rubric strip tweens as coverage grows. A rail holds talk-track dots, a next-best-question chip and at most two amber whisper cards that quote the exact line that triggered them and dismiss after eight seconds unless pinned. A coral objection bar pins to the top when a persona's objection tag fires. A Blind, Guided, Coached dial stays visible before, during and after the call, so reps can turn scaffolding up or down. The debrief opens on a ScoreHero (grade, skill band from Novice to Advanced, one verdict sentence). The grader then streams a plan that orders MomentReplay (the turn that cost the deal), CriterionCards, PatternCallouts and a DrillCTA for the weakest criterion. Every block cites transcript turn IDs that must validate, with a fixed-order fallback. The library ships about 150 persona packs as JSON or YAML, validated by zod in CI, with filters for job family, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode, personal-best rings, and a dashed Build your own tile first. The wizard takes pasted text, a description or a URL, drafts the persona in chat while a card fills field by field with a provenance chip on every field, runs a 60-second rehearsal, and saves the same pack file that contributors submit. Against today's chat app and three-item select, this is the only proposal where the product changes shape to fit each call. For the fund it is the strongest of the set: every debrief footer names the grader model, rubric version and token cost, and Codex reviews persona PRs and release notes, which is the maintainer-automation workflow the program funds.
reviews.no_case: Generative layout is the riskiest bet in the set. A model that chooses the debrief's block order on every call can make two reps' reports look like different products, which hurts the team view and any side-by-side comparison of calls. The closed catalogue and fixed-order fallback only contain the drift without removing it. Every debrief also gains a composition step with its own latency and token cost, and the L effort label hides a lot of new engineering: block registry, grader plan schema, citation validation, AI Elements, and a Tailwind 4 move in weeks 1 to 2.

reviews.yes_case: Practice Graph Studio is a dark-first sales dojo built like a GitHub repository. The header carries an MIT badge, a star link and tabs for Practice, Library, Studio, Progress and Team, and every persona has a Source view that shows the actual persona file. The landing page leads with a product-true live-call card where criterion bars fill and one whisper cue lands, then a 'Personas are files' band with an Open a persona PR button. The live call is a calm two-lane cockpit: rep and persona lanes with timestamps, a tone bar under persona lines, a waveform scrubber, and a right rail with a five-criterion rubric whose bars stay dotted until the grader confirms them, a six-step talk track, and one cue slot that auto-dismisses after eight seconds with a 'why' link to the exact transcript line. Coaching levels (Silent, Cues, Full) let experienced reps turn coaching down. The best decision is that the debrief reuses the same grader output as the live coach, so a score the rep watched climb cannot contradict the final grade. Progress centres a 52-week practice graph shaded by score band rather than raw volume, so a streak has to mean improvement. The library is a filterable catalogue with counts, an official versus community source filter, a Good first persona label and an Edit as PR action. The wizard is a split pane where each extracted field shows the source sentence that produced it, then a 60-second test call, then Open PR with a file diff. The business model is spelled out: MIT core, paid hosted team analytics and manager queue, and licensing to call-centre and training firms. Against today's dropdown and blurry orb, this reads as a real product with a contributor pipeline built in, and the planned Codex review of persona PRs before merge is a concrete maintainer-automation story for the fund.
reviews.no_case: It reads as a developer tool to the sales buyer it has to win: dark by default, monospace everywhere, and a contribution-graph motif that a sales manager may see as GitHub cosplay. Its own risk list concedes the point. The library starts at 60 seeded personas, the least breadth among the three advanced proposals against a brief that asks for a large library. The Tailwind 3 to 4 migration, with reported transparent dropdown backgrounds, is Phase 0 and gates everything else.

reviews.yes_case: Open Practice Hub is a community hub for call practice that looks like a product catalogue crossed with a model-card registry. The landing page is product-first: a looping 12-second clip of a persona card, a rubric meter ticking and a whisper cue, task chips (SDR cold call, AE discovery, insurance, mortgage, solar, home services, collections), a Trending personas row, and a stat strip with stars, forks and practice-call counts, with a footer naming the Realtime API and GPT-4.1 mini. The library is a three-column card grid with a left rail for role, industry, difficulty 1 to 5, objection type, channel (voice or text) and license, and sort chips for Trending, Most forked, New and Highest pass rate. Opening a persona shows a right-side model card: what it tests, rubric weights, the opening line, a 30-second sample, a fork tree showing who built on whom, and Start practice, Fork and Star buttons. Forking copies the YAML and records lineage, which is a real open-source contribution loop. The call screen is a three-zone control room: talk-track steps that check off on the left, a centre stage with the orb shrunk to a live-state indicator, and a right coach column with six live rubric meters that tick with deltas such as +6 Pricing, an amber whisper cue and a rose objection alert with a suggested bridge line, plus a bottom bar for timer, mute, intensity and End and grade. The coach runs on a rolling transcript with objection, four-second silence and missed-step triggers, and is isolated from the persona's realtime context. Leaderboards rank personas, scenarios and teams, and rep rankings are opt-in and measure improvement, a considered answer to consent and HR risk for team buyers. The wizard reads a job description, URL, CRM notes, ICP or a pasted call, asks up to three follow-ups that cite the source lines it used, runs a dry run, then saves privately, shares to a team or opens a PR. Against today's three-item dropdown, this is a 120-persona library a contributor can grow, and its Codex story (review and lint of persona PRs, a good-first-persona label) is the contributor-maintainer workflow the fund describes.
reviews.no_case: It risks looking like today's app with a new skin: light canvas, hairline cards, an indigo primary, monogram rings and amber stars on shadcn parts, which sits close to the default SaaS look the brief calls generic. The hub vocabulary (trending, forks, stars) leans on community-marketplace behaviour that a call-centre buyer may not care about. It also keeps Tailwind 3 for the first pass, so the modern-stack payoff is deferred.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence Conversational Studio runs two calm registers: paper-coloured pages for landing, library, wizard, progress and team, and a private dark cockpit for the live call and debrief. The landing page opens with a question rather than a feature grid: 'What do you sell, and who do you call?', typed into an input styled as a wizard step, beside an animated call card with a caller orb, a cue typing 'Ask about unit age first' and a rubric bar at 72. Persona creation is one question per screen in 48px Geist, with Enter to advance, a 'Step 3 of 7' counter, source drop zones for PDFs, URLs and pasted text, a summary card that assembles at the right edge as answers arrive, and a 'Skip all to form' escape so power users are never trapped. Structured output is checked against the same zod schema the persona JSON files use, and a similarity check warns about near-duplicates before save, which matters for an open library. The library is a faceted grid with filters synced to the URL (job, industry, difficulty dial, objection type, mode), so a filtered view is a shareable link. It targets about 150 personas across 15 sales jobs, with difficulty pips and a Build one with AI card. The call screen has a pulse orb labelled 'Caller speaking' or 'Your turn', the last six turns, and a coach rail with a six-bar rubric, talk-track dots and at most two amber cues that can be pinned. End and grade needs a two-second hold, which stops accidental endings. The pre-call briefing asks one warm-up question and returns a three-line pre-flight score on the opening before the call starts. The debrief offers Redo this moment, a 60-second role play built around the weakest turn. The migration is incremental and keeps every route live, which makes it the safest path to a shipped redesign.
reviews.no_case: It is two products on two surfaces. The signature idea, one question at a time, covers persona creation, which happens far less often than calls, and the wizard is a slow way to build a persona that a paste-and-extract flow does in one pass, with a skip button that makes the good path optional. The mandatory warm-up and pre-flight score add friction to the most frequent action. The proposal also admits the coaching bar is met only once a coach engine exists, and that its dense cockpit may overwhelm first-time reps.

reviews.yes_case: Keynote Bento is a light bento system for almost every screen: white hairline tiles with 28px radius on a #F5F5F7 canvas, Geist display type at up to about 88px on heroes, and one tile grammar throughout. The landing page is a bento of a headline tile ('Practice the call before it counts' with a 60-second call CTA), a dark stage tile with a looping mini call, a whisper cue and a rubric bar climbing from 58 to 74, a persona-chip strip with job-family counts, a model tile naming Realtime voice, gpt-4.1-mini grading and the wizard, and a contributor tile. The live call moves to a fixed dark stage: a 62 percent left column with a state ring that shows listening, thinking and speaking without relying on colour, a talk-time meter for rep versus caller, and two 22px caption lines. A 38 percent bento rail holds a whisper tile (one cue for six seconds), a next-question tile, an objection tile that appears only when triggered, a six-step talk-track progress tile, and a live rubric whose delta chips (+4, -2) tick under the rep's eyes, each tappable to its evidence line. The debrief is a bento with a grade hero (a 120px letter and a Geist Mono 0 to 100 score), a score timeline that marks exactly where a cue changed the call, strengths and areas tiles, and five criterion tiles with evidence chips. The library is the broadest on paper: 150 personas across 25 job families, with a Build with AI tile first, a facet rail with counts, and tiles tinted by difficulty with a preview drawer that plays a voice sample. The motion system is one spring (stiffness about 260, damping about 28) across tiles, sheets and cues, which is the kind of total, coherent change the brief asks for. Against today's flat cards and gradient orb, this looks like a product built by a design team, and the bento composition will read well as a static README image.
reviews.no_case: The bento grid is now a common template, so coherence is its main asset. The proposal's own risks say the dark glow can read as a gimmick and bento density can overflow at 390px. The wizard is a four-step form with weight sliders, the least differentiated answer to the wizard brief. The Tailwind 3 to 4 rewrite touches every class at XL effort, on top of Base UI, which the proposal itself calls young. It is the most polished-looking option in the set with the least distinctive interaction model, and it has the highest rebuild cost.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence Conversational Studio is a whole-app redesign with two faces. The workspace screens (landing, library, wizard, progress, team) sit on a warm paper background in Geist Sans, and the wizard asks one large question per screen. The live call and the debrief switch to a calm dark cockpit with hairline dividers and Geist Mono numerals. Setup and persona creation are Typeform-style: each screen asks one question such as 'What do you sell, and who do you call?', Enter advances, a step counter shows progress, and a permanent 'Skip all to form' keeps the old ten-field form for people who want it. The library has a 240px faceted rail (sales job, industry, difficulty dial, objection type, voice or text), URL-synced filters, removable chips and a three-column card grid, with 'Build one with AI' as the last tile. The brief's fifteen sales jobs are named packs with about ten personas each. On the live call, a full-bleed dark screen with no nav shows a Pulse orb whose ring follows the caller's audio, the last six transcript turns, and a coach rail with a six-bar live rubric, talk-track dots and at most two amber cue cards that auto-dismiss after eight seconds. A coral objection bar pins to the top, and End and grade needs a two-second hold. The debrief opens with a large mono grade, a six-criterion radar against the last three calls, a moment timeline with a sparkline, and a Redo this moment button that replays the 60 seconds around the weakest turn. It beats today's app because the live screen is a chat app with no feedback and the scenario picker is a three-item dropdown. It also makes the OpenAI story concrete through a Model Lab card showing cost and latency per role, and a Codex-powered action that reviews persona pull requests against the schema.
reviews.no_case: The one-question wizard is slow for a rep who wants to paste a job description and go, and the dense dark cockpit may overwhelm first-time reps. The proposal concedes its live coaching only meets the bar once a coach engine exists, and its own self-score for live coaching is 5.2, so the headline capability is still a promise.

reviews.yes_case: Composed Coaching Console is a dark-by-default coaching console whose layouts are assembled per call from a closed set of typed blocks. Every screen shares one token system (near-black canvas, a teal signal colour reserved for everything the AI generates, amber only for whisper cues, hairline borders instead of shadows, Geist Sans and Geist Mono for numbers) and one component layer (shadcn/ui on Radix, with Vercel AI Elements for chat). During a call the rep sees a transcript timeline with a small score chip on each rep turn, a live rubric strip that tweens as criteria are covered, and a coach rail that shows at most three amber whisper cards a minute. Each card quotes the exact line that triggered it and fades after eight seconds. Coach modes (Blind, Guided, Coached) sit visibly before, during and after the call. After the call the debrief is composed rather than fixed. It opens on the single moment that cost the deal, then criterion cards, pattern callouts and a drill, in an order the grader picks from a closed catalogue. Every block cites transcript turn IDs and the page falls back to a classic fixed-order debrief if the plan fails validation. The library is a faceted catalogue built from persona pack files (about 150 at launch across 18 industries), and the wizard (Source, Draft, Tune, Rehearse) streams a persona card field by field, with a source chip on each value that points at the sentence it came from. It beats today's app because nothing on the current call screen reacts to the rep, the persona form is blank, and every debrief is the same stack of identical cards. The OpenAI story is visible: a model strip on the landing page and a footer on every debrief naming the grader model, rubric version and token cost.
reviews.no_case: The generative debrief is the riskiest idea in the council. Layouts that change from call to call are harder to test, harder to make accessible and easier to read as inconsistent, and the proposal's own fallback concedes the point. Its library names six job families and 18 industries, which is thinner than the brief's list of named sales jobs, and its live coaching still depends on a coach stream that does not exist yet.

reviews.yes_case: Coach's Field Notebook makes every session feel like an open training notebook. The palette is warm paper (#F4EEE1) with a faint grain, ink text, ruled lines on the transcript and talk-track pages, and a vermilion handwritten coach voice in Caveat that appears in the margin beside the exact transcript line that moved a score. Fraunces sets the headlines, Instrument Sans carries UI text and JetBrains Mono carries timers and scores. The live call is an open spread at 1440 pixels: the transcript on the left page, with rep lines in blue ink and caller lines in graphite, and the coach margin on the right page, where notes write themselves in over about 600 milliseconds. A pencil-bar rubric ledger shows provisional deltas per turn, objection sticky notes tilt and link to the matching talk-track step, and the footer names the model and its latency. Scores land as stamps: the debrief grade is a hand-stamped letter, every number links to its transcript line, and the fallback-grader state explains itself with a retry button instead of a bare warning bar. The library is a logbook of index cards with paper tabs for fifteen job families, each card flipping to show its talk track and rubric weights, and the progress page is a tally-mark logbook with milestone stamps. The wizard is a six-step intake that fills an index card line by line as the model streams, ending in a test roleplay and a save or pull request. It beats today's dropdown, blurry orb and single long scroll because it is the most memorable of the five and shows evidence on every page. A lamp-lit dark mode and a clean print view are included.
reviews.no_case: The proposal itself admits modern is a weakness: paper texture and handwriting can read as retro or twee, and an enterprise buyer may take it for a toy. It is also the most expensive. It is XL effort over about nine weeks, the Tailwind v4 move touches every screen, and the 120-persona seed is a content project on top of the UI work.

reviews.yes_case: Clearcall Coach Console is an accessibility-first whole-app system built on React Aria Components and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next. It has AAA contrast (7:1 body text), 44-pixel minimum targets, 56-pixel live-call controls and an axe-core wcag2aaa gate in CI. Its look is a warm off-white canvas with ink text, a violet accent reserved for AI coaching, flat 2-pixel borders with no shadows, and a dark mode that also meets AAA and honours forced colours. The live call has three named landmark regions: Transcript on the left at about 60 percent width, the persona status and controls in the centre header, and a 320-pixel coach rail on the right. The rail stacks talk-track steps marked Done, Next or Missed, a provisional rubric meter with points, a bar and a status word, and one cue card at a time with a type label (Ask, Objection, Next question) and a Dismiss button. Screen readers get one polite announcement per cue, no more often than every eight seconds, and pressing S reads the full score aloud. The debrief leads with a grade as large text (62 out of 100, Needs practice), then strengths and improvements as equal lists, then criterion accordions whose evidence chips jump to the transcript line. The library is organised into job packs with four facets shown as both a filter rail and removable chips, a 30-second voice preview on each card, and about 120 personas at full seed. The wizard runs source, extract, persona, rubric and a two-minute test call, and every extracted field carries its source sentence. It beats today's app, whose chat-bubble layout clips the timer and crowds the End button, and whose scenario picker is three items. It gives every rep a legible coach and an honest score, and an accessibility record that counts in procurement (F2).
reviews.no_case: It is the least distinctive of the five. The flat, high-contrast system is competent and calm but could be any well-built enterprise tool, and its modern signal is weak against a brief that asks for cutting edge. The proposal's own risk list says AAA gates will cost it points on look, and the cue cadence is a guess until blind and low-vision users test it.

reviews.yes_case: Clay Coach is a warm, tactile whole-app redesign built around a soft-clay 3D caller. The caller is a parametric clay bust rendered with react-three-fiber, whose jaw follows the caller's audio level and whose halo changes colour with state: cobalt while the caller speaks, sage on track, amber the moment an objection lands. The rest of the app stays flat and precise. Scorecards, the progress dashboard and the team table use hairline rules, tabular mono numbers and cobalt data marks, so the playfulness lives only on the persona and the call. Light is the default, and dark is first-class for dim rooms and screen-share. On the live call, a centre console shows the caller bust, speaker-lane captions and a six-step talk-track tracker on the left. The right rail shows five rubric bars that hatch while provisional and lock solid when a transcript quote confirms them, and coach cues slide in beside the transcript under a Coach switch set to On, Quiet or Off. Mobile puts the caller in the top third and cues into a bottom sheet with swipe to dismiss. The debrief is a two-column scorecard: a clay medallion grade with percentile phrasing, a rubric radar, criteria rows whose evidence quotes scrub the audio to the exact second, and a coach-cue timeline that shows which cues were followed. The library is faceted by role, industry, difficulty, objection, mode and source (built-in, mine, community), with a New persona card as the first tile that opens the wizard. The wizard accepts all five inputs the brief names (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP and pasted call) and tags every generated field with its source sentence. Every AI surface carries a Model Ledger chip with model, latency and cost per call, and a contribute page lets people add a persona by editing one recipe file. It beats today's app, which is a chat screen with no feedback, a select-box library and a single-scroll debrief.
reviews.no_case: The soft-clay 3D caller is the biggest gamble. Playful 3D can read as unserious to call-centre and enterprise buyers, the F2 market this proposal wants, and the 3D pipeline (build-time busts, one WebGL canvas, still fallbacks for low-power devices) is more work than the rest of the design. The proposal also never states a persona count or names the fifteen sales jobs, so its library is right in shape and unproven in content.

reviews.yes_case: Keynote Bento is one Apple-style system across every screen. Light pages (library, pre-call, debrief, progress, team) use a #F5F5F7 canvas with white bento tiles, hairline borders, 28px radii and a soft two-layer shadow, with Geist display type at keynote scale and spring physics that reflow tiles. The live call becomes a fixed dark stage: the left 62 percent holds a state-ringed orb (listening, thinking, speaking, readable without colour), a talk-time meter and two 22px caption lines, while a right-hand bento rail shows a six-second whisper cue, a next-question tile, an objection alert that appears only when triggered, six-step talk-track progress and a live rubric with +4 style deltas that tap through to the evidence quote. The debrief becomes a grade hero, a score timeline that marks the exact turn a cue changed the call, criterion tiles with evidence chips that jump to the transcript, and a dark Practice-next tile. The library is a 150-persona, 25-job-family catalogue with a facet rail (rep job, buyer role, industry, difficulty, objection type) and counts, persona tiles tinted by difficulty with three objection tags, a preview drawer that plays a voice sample, and a Build with AI tile first in each grid. The AI wizard is four guided steps (Source, Persona, Rubric, Test call) with a streaming persona card, rubric sliders that must total 100, a 60-second dry run and an Export-as-contribution action that opens a PR template. Against today's three-item dropdown, chat-style live call and four-number dashboard, it covers every must-have in the brief and makes the OpenAI stack visible: a model strip on the landing page, the grader, token and cost line on each debrief, and Realtime voice as a first-class path beside ElevenLabs. The migration is staged (tokens and Tailwind v4 first, then shell and landing, then the live cockpit behind a flag), so it ships in pieces.
reviews.no_case: It is the most familiar look of the five: bento tiles and a glossy dark stage are now a common template, and its own self-scores (coaching 5.4, library 5.2) show it only just reaches the baseline. The 150-persona launch is an unstarted content job and the roughly 2-second cue latency it depends on is unproven.

reviews.yes_case: Composed Coaching Console is a fixed, branded design system in which the AI assembles each call's coaching and debrief from a closed catalogue of typed blocks. The model chooses which blocks appear and in what order, but it never emits markup, so every layout stays on brand, accessible and inside the registry. Debrief blocks include ScoreHero (Mono grade and skill band), MomentReplay (the turning point with timestamp), CriterionCard (score, one-line reason, expandable quotes), PatternCallout and DrillCTA, and every block must cite transcript turn IDs that validate against the transcript, with a classic fixed-order debrief as fallback. The look is a dark coaching console by default (#0A0E14 canvas, #111821 surfaces, hairlines instead of shadows), with teal reserved for AI-generated content marked by a spark glyph so the rep always knows what the model wrote, amber only for whisper cues, and a light theme for library, progress and a print-friendly debrief. The live call is a three-zone console: a speaker-lane transcript timeline with per-turn micro score chips (for example +3 Discovery), a persona header with a temperament meter and objection tag, a live five-criterion rubric strip that tweens as coverage grows, a right-hand coach rail with at most two cue cards that dismiss after eight seconds, and a waveform driven by real mic level. A visible Blind, Guided and Coached dial fades scaffolding over time, which turns coaching into a learning curve rather than a permanent crutch. The wizard is a chat (AI Elements) that fills a persona card field by field with a source chip on every field, then Tune presets and a 60-second Rehearse step before Save as persona pack. Against today's chat-bubble call and dropdown of three scenarios, it is the most distinctive answer to the brief, and the OpenAI story is built in: model names and token cost in every debrief footer, a Realtime voice path, and a Codex-powered Action that reviews persona pull requests against the schema, which is the PR-review automation the Codex programme funds.
reviews.no_case: The AI-composed layout is the riskiest idea in the set: block sequences can drift and make debriefs read as inconsistent, the sub-1.5-second cue latency it needs is untested, and the launch covers only six job families, short of the brief's 'every sales job' bar.

reviews.yes_case: Clearcall is a high-contrast, screen-reader-first coaching console on a warm paper canvas (#F7F7F4), with ink text at about 17 to 18.7 to 1 contrast, violet reserved for AI coach output, and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next as the single typeface. Controls are flat, with 2px solid borders and 44 to 56px targets, no blurred orbs, no drop shadows and no motion beyond a 150ms cue slide-in. Dark mode and forced-colours support come from the same token set. The live call has three named landmarks (Transcript, Coach, Controls). The transcript takes about 60 percent of the width on the left. The 320px coach rail stacks talk-track steps labelled Done, Next or Missed, a provisional rubric meter per criterion with points, a bar and a status word, and one cue card with a type label (Ask, Objection, Next question) and a Dismiss button. The rep sees the next move and the live score as text and icon, never colour alone, and the S key reads the score aloud. The debrief leads with the grade as large text (62/100, Needs practice), with evidence chips such as 'Line 4' that jump to the matching transcript line and deltas written in words. Progress shows a criterion-by-week table, and every chart has a view-as-table toggle. The library is a three-column card grid under pack headers (for example SDR cold calls (18)), with four facets as both a filter rail and removable chips. The wizard extracts product, buyer, objections and price band from a URL, job posting, CRM note or pasted call, shows the source sentence for each field, and exports a persona file for a pull request. Against today's dropdown and chat bubbles, it becomes a console that a rep, a screen-reader user or a procurement reviewer can all use, with a model receipt (model, tokens, cost) on every debrief and a Model Lab that grades the same transcripts with GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-4.1 side by side.
reviews.no_case: It is the least exciting look of the five: flat, no motion, one humanist typeface and no signature visual, so it risks reading as a compliance form rather than cutting-edge AI. Its D 6.0 claim also rests on an 8-second screen-reader cue cadence that the proposal itself calls a guess, and its library claim of 120-plus personas is only seeded to about 40 by phase 3.

reviews.yes_case: Coach's Field Notebook makes each call an open notebook spread. On paper (#F4EEE1 with faint grain), the transcript is ruled with line numbers, rep lines in deep blue ink and caller lines in graphite. The coach writes in the margin in vermilion handwriting (Caveat, for coach notes only), one note at a time, beside the exact transcript line that moved a score, so coaching is located on the page rather than in a sidebar. Each criterion is a ledger line with a sage or vermilion pencil bar, a weight, a one-line rationale and quotes, and the grade lands as a slightly tilted ink stamp. Quotes are highlighted in pale yellow behind the text, every number in the debrief links to the transcript line it came from, and the fallback state ('LLM grader failed, keyword heuristic used') is explained with a retry rather than hidden in a banner. Three coach channels keep the persona out of the loop: text margin notes, a whisper pill in voice mode, and objection sticky notes linked to talk-track steps. The pre-call briefing is a spread with a talk-track checklist the rep can tick and a handwritten line recalling the last score ('Last time 50. Pricing was thin.'). The library lists 15 sales job families as paper index tabs, and index cards flip to show the talk track and rubric. Against today's three-item dropdown and blurry orb, it turns practice into a notebook the rep returns to, with the most memorable identity of the five. A lamp-lit dark theme and a clean print view keep it usable, and the live footer names the model and its latency so OpenAI's engine is visible without a logo.
reviews.no_case: The look is the least modern of the set and the most likely to read as twee in an enterprise demo: paper grain and handwriting aim at warmth, not at the sleek, cutting-edge tech the brief asks for. Its split system (paper for the live call and debrief, a crisp grid for the library and dashboards) also weakens the coherent total-UI change the brief requires.

reviews.yes_case: Cadence is a one-question-at-a-time studio. Setup, onboarding and persona creation become a Typeform-style sequence: one 48px Geist question per screen ('Who picks up the phone?'), a chip grid, a text field or drop zone, Enter to advance, a progress counter and a permanent 'Skip all to form' escape hatch. A summary card assembles at the edge as answers arrive, and a schema-checked GPT call drafts the persona, which the user edits and then saves or exports as a PR-ready file, with a similarity check that warns about near-duplicates. The library is a faceted three-column grid (job, industry, difficulty dial, objection type, mode) with filters synced to the URL, so a link such as ?job=sdr&industry=solar&difficulty=3 can be shared. The pre-call briefing is a single column with a question card ('How will you open the call?') that gets a three-line pre-flight check on the greeting before the call starts, which is a real improvement on walking in unprepared. The palette is calm (paper #F7F6F2 on light, #0B0E14 on dark) with one colour per meaning. The live call uses a dense, scannable coach rail, and it is honest about its scope: cues from a separate coach stream stay private to the rep and are capped at two on screen. Against today's dropdown and form, persona creation becomes a guided conversation, and a Codex GitHub Action that reviews persona pull requests is a specific, credible story for the Codex programmes.
reviews.no_case: It is the least total change of the five. Phase 1 maps the new tokens onto existing Tailwind class names and restyles landing and pre-call in place, the one-question rhythm stops at setup and persona creation, and the live call and debrief stay a conventional cockpit that the proposal itself rates only at baseline (D 5.2) until a coach engine exists. It also says react-hook-form is already in the repo, but package.json does not list it, so that claim is wrong.

reviews.yes_case: Clay Coach is a warm, tactile call console built around a soft-clay 3D caller rendered with react-three-fiber, which the repo already depends on. The caller's jaw follows the caller's audio level and the halo changes state: sage when the rep is on track, amber when an objection lands, cobalt while the caller speaks. The 3D stays on the persona and the live caller only. Scorecards and dashboards are flat with hairline rules, so the playfulness never gets in the way of the numbers. The live call is a three-part console: a six-step talk-track tracker on the left, captions in speaker lanes with the caller in the centre, and a right rail with five rubric bars that hatch while provisional and lock solid once a transcript quote confirms them. Whisper cards (Ask, Objection, Next question) slide in beside the transcript and tuck into a Coach tray afterwards. A Coach switch (On, Quiet, Off) sets how much the rep sees, and the coach runs on its own channel that never reaches the persona. The debrief adds a cue timeline showing which coaching was followed or missed, a skill radar, and evidence quotes that scrub the audio to the exact second. The library has facets for role, industry, difficulty, objection, mode and source (built-in, mine, community). Its first tile is a New persona card that opens the wizard with the current filters applied. Each persona is one versioned JSON recipe, so a contributor adds one with no 3D skills. Against today's app, a chat window with a three-item dropdown and no feedback until the end, this is the most memorable identity in the set (C scores highest here), and it shows the coaching loop on the first screen. For the OpenAI fund, a Model Ledger chip on every AI surface shows model, latency, tokens and cost per call, and a /contribute page offers a Codex CLI quickstart and a PR-review status tile.
reviews.no_case: Playful clay is the riskiest look for enterprise and call-centre buyers, and the F2 case depends on those buyers, so the identity could cost deals even as it wins attention. A WebGL caller on a live call is a performance and battery problem on low-end Android and embedded webviews. The proposal's fallbacks (pre-rendered thumbnails, one canvas, a static still) are mandatory and not yet built. The two-second cue budget is the whole value of live coaching, and the proposal concedes that a slower backend turns cues into post-turn hints, which weakens the live-coaching claim. D (5.6) and E (5.3) are both marginal and only reach the standard once roughly 120 personas are written and reviewed, which the UI cannot deliver. The parametric clay avatar system (head shapes, palettes, accessories) is a sizeable, unscoped art and engineering job that the phase plan does not show. Moving to Tailwind 4 and copying shadcn in, while enforcing a token lint rule, is a bigger migration than an L effort suggests. Soft 3D is a trend that may age faster than sharp, flat systems, which matters for a repo that wants to look serious in five years.

reviews.yes_case: Geist Signal Console is a monochrome developer-tool console for sales reps. It uses Geist Sans and Geist Mono at 400, 500 and 600 only, 1px hairline borders, black primary buttons and a dark mode designed first. The one colour in the system is a teal signal that appears only when the AI coach has something to say: a 1px ring that pulses while a cue is live, plus a rule and a dot. Nothing else is coloured, so the signal reads as live state rather than decoration, and the blurred orb is retired. The live call is three resizable panes. The left call panel holds the persona name, a state pill (Caller speaking, Your turn, Coach thinking), a mono timer, mic meter and End and grade. The centre is a hairline transcript with mono timestamps and inline markers such as an objection flag. The right coach rail has a Next move card with an evidence link (Why? line 6) and Accept or Dismiss, six rubric meters that tick with a mono delta after each rep turn, and talk-track progress. The coach has concrete budgets: a first cue within two seconds (p50), rubric meters within four seconds, one cue per turn, and every cue offers Not helpful, which feeds a contributor eval set.
